nav.tip_combine_weighted: Weighted hybrid: the four base recommenders (user-based kNN, item-based kNN, matrix factorization, content-based) predict independently; the weights are learned on held-out ratings and the answer is the weighted sum.
nav.tip_combine_switching: Switching hybrid: the same base recommenders predict; a rule picks ONE of them for the case at hand, by a leaderboard on the active user's held-out ratings or by the neighbour rule.
nav.tip_combine_dnn: Feature-combination network: one network reads ids, content features and the user profile together; there is no separate recommender, the content is just more input to a single learner.
nav.tip_combine_meta: Meta-level hybrid (future work): two stages. Stage 1 learns a per-user content profile, a vector of term weights; stage 2 is collaborative filtering whose peers are found by comparing those profiles instead of rating vectors, and the prediction is the user-based formula over the peers' ratings. Same formula, different peers. Not in the lab this week.

formula.sig_weight_info_text: Significance weighting damps a similarity that rests on few co-rated items. The rule used here is one example: factor = min(c / n, 1) with n = 50 — Herlocker et al. (1999) applied n/50 below 50 co-rated items and 1 above. The factor grows linearly with c and stays at 1 beyond the threshold: a clipped linear activation, identity up to the threshold, constant after it. Other rules in the literature: a free threshold γ (Ma, King & Lyu 2007 use γ = 30); shrinkage c / (c + λ) with λ ≈ 100 (Bell & Koren 2007; Koren 2010), smooth and never reaching 1; overlap weighting w × Jaccard (Candillier et al. 2008); a sigmoid of c (Jamali & Ester 2009). This app offers none, raw count (w × c), ratio and adaptive — change them under Parameters → sw.
formula.sig_weight_info_text_cb: In the content-based walk the count is the number of terms the two films share (c); the factor min(c / n, 1) shrinks a cosine that rests on few shared terms.

pitfall.corated_mean: This mean is taken over the co-rated items only — what numpy.corrcoef / scipy.pearsonr / DataFrame.corr compute. In recommender systems the user's mean is taken over ALL of their ratings.
pitfall.item_mean_centring: Centring item vectors by the item mean instead of the user mean is a common fault; the course's measure centres by the user's mean.
pitfall.jaccard_union: This Jaccard variant excluded the target from the intersection but not from the union.
pitfall.signed_denominator: A signed denominator can cancel toward zero when positive and negative neighbours mix; the prediction leaves the scale.
pitfall.rank_foil: Rank correlations ignore both the rating scale and the users' own means — shown for comparison only.
pitfall.static_active_mean: The active user's mean includes the target rating (the static convention); in the lecture scenario that is information the system should not have.
pitfall.no_neighbours: No eligible neighbour exists (nobody else rated the target, or every similarity is undefined or non-positive); the prediction falls back to a mean.
pitfall.negative_weighted_average: Negative weights in an uncentred weighted average subtract whole ratings, not deviations; the prediction can leave the rating scale (toy example -0.02 instead of 4.61).
pitfall.target_below_degree: The target item itself has fewer raters than the degree filter demands; under a strict degree filter it would not appear in the item–item matrix at all. The prediction is still computed from the filtered candidates.
pitfall.no_idf_weighting: Every present tag counts equally (idf = 1): a rare tag like a niche genre carries the same weight as a common one, so this profile loses its ability to tell items apart by their most distinctive tags.
pitfall.valid_too_small: The validation tail would hold very few ratings; early stopping on such a noisy signal would end training almost at random, so it is skipped and the epoch budget is used instead. On a real dataset the tail is large enough and early stopping is on.
pitfall.no_negatives: A user who interacted with every item has nothing to rank below their positives — BPR gets no triple from them and learns nothing about them.
pitfall.ease_big_catalogue: EASE inverts an n_items × n_items matrix: O(n³) time and O(n²) memory. Raise min_raters to shrink the catalogue on large datasets.
pitfall.ease_outside_closed_form: Items with fewer raters than min_raters are excluded from the Gram matrix and cannot be scored by EASE.
pitfall.binarised_point: Thresholding the predictions BEFORE the ROC leaves a single operating point; the 'AUC' of that point is only the balanced accuracy at τ. Sweep the scores, never the labels.
pitfall.no_test_ratings: This user has no relevant held-out rating under the chosen split (fewer than min_ratings ratings, or nothing rated ≥ τ in the test tail): the walk has nothing to hit. Pick a user with relevant test items.
pitfall.few_pairs_for_stats: Very few pairs enter the paired test; with n = 5 seeds a two-sided Wilcoxon signed-rank test can never reach p < 0.05 (its smallest p is 2/2⁵ = 0.0625). Pair over users instead, and read the effect size.
pitfall.deterministic_no_variance: A temporal split and a deterministic engine give the same numbers under every seed: the standard deviation over seeds is 0 and a seed-paired test is undefined. Variation must come from users.
pitfall.unrated_novelty: An item nobody rated in train has popularity 0, so its self-information is unbounded; the evaluator clips it - such items dominate the novelty average.
pitfall.target_outside_filter: The target item itself lies outside the attribute filter: the neighbours are chosen by how the two users agree on OTHER kinds of films, and that agreement is then used to predict a film of a kind the filter never looked at.
pitfall.filter_empty_support: The active user has not rated a single item inside the filter (besides the target): every similarity is undefined and the prediction falls back to a mean. Widen the filter.
pitfall.filter_small_support: The filter shrank the co-rated support: at least one selected neighbour rests on very few shared films inside the filter. Pearson on 1-2 items is ±1 or undefined by construction (Herlocker 1999, Schafer 2007); significance weighting now uses the FILTERED count and shrinks these weights hard.
pitfall.filtered_mean_degenerate: Under the segment mean, both users' centring populations are exactly the co-rated set inside the filter - the 'segment mean' has silently become the co-rated mean of the library convention (numpy.corrcoef), which the course treats as a foil; with two items the value is always ±1.
pitfall.active_outside_user_filter: The active user is outside the user filter: none of their ratings enters the item similarities (their rating of the target is hidden anyway). The prediction still uses their own ratings of the selected items.
pitfall.user_filter_empty_support: Inside the user filter nobody besides the active user rated the target item: every item similarity is undefined and the prediction falls back to a mean. Widen the filter.
pitfall.candidate_filter_empty: The candidate filter left no item: nothing the user rated is related to the target (a target without genres keeps nobody under a genre match). The prediction falls back to a mean.
pitfall.filter_small_support_raters: The user filter shrank the common-rater support: at least one selected item rests on very few shared raters inside the filter. A correlation over 1-2 raters is ±1 or undefined by construction; significance weighting now uses the FILTERED count and shrinks these weights hard.
pitfall.icf_not_user_centred: The course's item-based measure centres each rating by its USER's mean (adjusted cosine, Sarwar et al. 2001); this measure does not.
pitfall.weights_on_train: The weights are fitted on ratings every recommender has already learned from: a recommender that memorised them looks better than it is and is given too much weight. Fit the weights on held-out ratings the recommenders never saw.
pitfall.winner_on_train: The winner is picked on ratings every recommender has already learned from: the one that memorised them looks best, whatever it will do on new ratings. Pick the winner on held-out ratings the recommenders never saw.

pearson.summary: Measures how linearly two users' rating behaviours move together, each centred at their own mean.
pros: Removes rating-scale differences — a user who always gives 4–5 and one who always gives 1–2 can still correlate perfectly.
Captures negative relationships; a value near −1 means opposite taste, which is information too.
cons: Data sparsity — with 2–3 co-rated items the coefficient is misleading or undefined; one or two items produce spurious ±1 values.

cons.Requires the users' means (the course co: over ALL of each user's ratings, not the co-rated subset).

constrained_pearson.summary: Both users are centred at one fixed neutral rating, so agreement is about absolute liking rather than personal habits.
pros: Distinguishes "both liked it" from "both rated it above their own average".
cons: Harsh and generous raters who agree relatively can become negatively correlated.
The neutral centre is a modelling choice (scale midpoint 2.75 here; legacy used 3).

median_robust.summary: Pearson's shape with medians instead of means.
pros: Less sensitive to a few extreme ratings.
cons: Medians are coarse on a half-star scale; ties are frequent.

cosine.summary: Users are vectors in item space; similarity is the cosine of the angle between them.
pros: Cheap — no means are needed; intuitive vector-space model.
Ignores vector magnitude, only the direction (rating pattern) matters.
cons: Blind to rating bias — a 4–5 rater and a 1–2 rater with the same pattern look dissimilar; it cannot separate optimists from pessimists.
Missing ratings act as zeros, so norms depend on how many items each user rated.

adjusted_cosine.summary: Cosine of the user-mean-centred vectors; for user-based CF the numerator equals Pearson's, the norms run over all rated items.
pros: Removes rating bias — the main weakness of raw cosine.
Usually more accurate than both raw cosine and Pearson in practice.
cons: Needs the means (more computation than raw cosine).
In item-based CF centring by the ITEM mean instead of the USER mean is a frequent mistake.

jaccard.summary: Overlap of the sets of rated items; rating values are ignored entirely.
pros: Ideal for implicit / binary data (watched, liked, in watchlist).
Shows how large the shared interest area is.
cons: Discards rating values — (5, 1) and (5, 5) on a shared film are identical, a heavy information loss on explicit data.

euclidean_inv.summary: Straight-line distance between the two rating vectors over the co-rated items, converted with 1/(1+d).
pros: The most intuitive notion of distance; easy to interpret.
cons: Very sensitive to the rating scale — same taste, different habits → far apart.
Curse of dimensionality — as items grow all users become almost equidistant.
Squared differences make a single large disagreement dominate.

manhattan_inv.summary: City-block distance (sum of absolute differences) converted with 1/(1+d).
pros: More robust to outliers than Euclidean (no squaring).
cons: Still ignores rating bias and cannot capture correlation patterns.

sig_weight.summary: Shrinks a similarity toward zero when it rests on few co-rated items.
pros: A ±1 built on one or two shared films no longer outranks a 0.6 built on forty.
cons: The threshold n is a hyper-parameter (50 by default; adaptive variants exist).

dnn_features.pick: The question: one user, one film, a rating to predict - the network takes both ids and every feature the lab knows about them.
dnn_features.holdout: The user's rating of this film is hidden from training, and the newest share of every user's ratings is set aside to watch the validation error.
dnn_features.features: From the training ratings alone: each film's TF-IDF content row and its numbers, each user's taste profile over the same terms and their rating statistics - the hidden rating and the validation rows enter none of them.
dnn_features.build: The network is assembled from the groups that are on: the two embedding tables, a dense tower over the film's terms, one over the user's profile, the numbers straight in, all concatenated into the hidden layers and one output unit.
dnn_features.init: Every weight starts from the seed: embeddings from a normal draw, dense layers from PyTorch's uniform rule, the output bias at the training mean - so the untrained network predicts the mean.
dnn_features.loop: Training is a loop over epochs: every epoch passes once over the training ratings in mini-batches.
dnn_features.update: One mini-batch: predict the ratings, compare, and move every weight a step against the error (Adam).
dnn_features.evaluate: After the epoch: the RMSE on the training ratings and on the validation tail the network never trained on.
dnn_features.early_stop: If the validation RMSE has not improved for `patience` epochs, training stops and the best epoch's weights are kept; with the early-stopping switch off the network runs to the epoch budget and the last epoch's weights predict (the teaching foil).
dnn_features.forward: The prediction: the pair's inputs flow through the network one stage at a time - the walk shows every stage with its numbers.
dnn_features.result: The network's output is the predicted rating; the notes compare it with the ids-only network and count what the embeddings had to learn from.

topk_cb.mmr: Maximal Marginal Relevance (Carbonell & Goldstein 1998): each place of the list takes the film with the highest λ · relevance − (1 − λ) · (largest cosine to the films already listed). λ = 1 keeps the relevance order; a lower λ trades relevance for variety, so near-duplicates move down.

hybrid_switching.pick: The user and the film to predict. Their rating of it, if there is one, is hidden from every recommender and from the choice.
hybrid_switching.split: The newest part of the ACTIVE user's own ratings is held out - at most a fixed number. The choice is made on these ratings, which no recommender ever saw; every other user's ratings stay with the recommenders.
hybrid_switching.fit_bases: Each recommender is fitted on the training ratings only, one after the other, with its own default settings.
hybrid_switching.predict_heldout: Every fitted recommender predicts every held-out rating of the user: one column of the table each. A recommender with nothing to go on answers with its own fallback, the user's mean.
hybrid_switching.score: How far each recommender misses the user's held-out ratings, two ways: MAE (the average miss) and RMSE (the misses are squared first, so big ones count more). One row of the leaderboard per step.
hybrid_switching.choose: A bucket of models keeps the recommender with the lowest error; the cold-start rule asks, for every rating, whether the collaborative recommender had enough neighbours.
hybrid_switching.answer: The chosen recommender answers about the target film; the others' answers are shown to compare.
hybrid_switching.clip: The answer is cut to the rating scale (only when clipping is on).
hybrid_switching.result: The predicted rating, and what the user's held-out evidence says about it.

hybrid_weighted.pick: The user and the film to predict. Their rating of it, if there is one, is hidden from every recommender and from the weights.
hybrid_weighted.split: The newest part of every user's ratings is held out - at most a fixed number per user. The weights are learned on these ratings, which no recommender ever saw.
hybrid_weighted.fit_bases: Each base recommender is fitted on the training ratings only, one after the other, with its own default settings.
hybrid_weighted.predict_heldout: Every fitted recommender predicts every held-out rating: one column of the table each. A recommender with nothing to go on answers with its own fallback, the user's mean.
hybrid_weighted.equal: The start of the weights: every recommender counts the same, one over q, and the intercept starts at the mean residual of that blend.
hybrid_weighted.gd: Gradient descent: measure how the error changes with each weight, move the weights a little against it, repeat. The step size is one over the largest curvature of the loss.
hybrid_weighted.ridge: The closed form: the weights that minimise the same loss in one solve - the check for the descent.
hybrid_weighted.compare: Each recommender alone, equal weights, the descent and the closed form, on the same held-out ratings.
hybrid_weighted.blend: The recommenders' predictions of the target film, weighted, added up and shifted by the intercept.
hybrid_weighted.clip: The blend is cut to the rating scale (only when clipping is on).
hybrid_weighted.result: The predicted rating, and what the held-out evidence says about it.

ucf.similarity_undefined: {sim}({user}, {cand}) is undefined (no co-rated items or zero variance)
ucf.collapsed: {n} more candidates computed the same way (see the table)
ucf.sig_weight: Shrink each similarity by its co-rated count ({mode}): {cand} {w} × {factor} = {w_shrunk}
ucf.rank_select: {n_eligible} eligible neighbours ranked by weighted similarity; keeping {n_used}
ucf.fallback: No usable neighbour ({reason}); falling back to {center}
ucf.filter: Item scope = filter {desc}: {n_f} items; {user} rated {n_a} of them besides the target ({n_a_all} without the filter). Similarities use only these items; the prediction baseline does not change
ucf.dyn_stats_filtered: Segment mean: {user} rated {n} items inside the filter (target excluded), mean {mean} — used to centre the similarities; the prediction baseline stays the mean over all {n_all} other ratings, {mean_all}

icf.pick: Predict {user}'s rating of {item} from the items they rated
icf.user_filter: User scope = filter {desc}: {n_c} of {n_users} users. {n_t} of them rated {item} besides {user} ({n_t_all} without the filter); only their ratings enter the item similarities. The prediction baseline does not change
icf.candidate_filter: Candidate scope = {desc}: {n_after} of the {n_before} items {user} rated are related to {item}; {n_off} dropped before any similarity
icf.corated_filtered: {item} and {cand} share {c} raters inside the user filter (active user excluded; {c_all} without the filter)
icf.filter_support: {n_small} of the {n_used} selected items rest on at most {threshold} shared raters inside the user filter (smallest {c_min}; median {c_median} inside vs {c_all_median} without the filter)
icf.degree_none: No degree filter: all {n} items the user rated stay candidates
icf.degree_fraction: Degree filter (share of users): keep items rated by more than {pct}% of the {n_users} users, i.e. at least {min_raters} raters — {n_after} of {n_before} candidates remain
icf.degree_count: Degree filter: keep items with at least {min_raters} raters — {n_after} of {n_before} candidates remain
icf.similarity_undefined: {sim}({item}, {cand}) is undefined (no common raters or zero variance)
icf.collapsed: {n} more candidate items computed the same way (see the table)
icf.sig_weight: Shrink each similarity by its rater count ({mode}): {cand} {s} × {factor} = {s_shrunk}
icf.rank_select: {n_eligible} eligible items ranked by similarity; keeping {n_used}
icf.predict: Prediction = weighted average of the user's ratings of the selected items = {pred}
icf.fallback: No usable item neighbour ({reason}); falling back to {center}

cb.pick: Predict {user}'s rating of {item} from the items they rated
cb.profile: {item}'s content profile: {n} term(s), each weighted by tf × idf
cb.similarity_undefined: Content similarity({item}, {cand}) is undefined (one of the items has no terms at all)
cb.collapsed: {n} more candidate items computed the same way (see the table)
cb.sig_weight: Shrink each similarity by its shared-term count ({mode}): {cand} {s} × {factor} = {s_shrunk}
cb.sig_weight_off: Significance weighting is off (mode none): the cosine weights go to the ranking unchanged
cb.rank_select: {n_eligible} eligible items ranked by content similarity; keeping {n_used}
cb.predict: Prediction = similarity-weighted average of the user's ratings of the selected items = {pred}; {top_item} adds the most ({top_part})
cb.fallback: No usable content neighbour ({reason}); falling back to {center}
cb.hybrid_cf: Hybrid (switching): CF has {n_cf} ≥ {min_cf} neighbours — using the CF prediction {pred}
cb.hybrid_cb: Hybrid (switching): CF has only {n_cf} < {min_cf} neighbours — falling back to the content prediction {pred}
cb.hybrid_cf_only: The content prediction is undefined; using the CF prediction alone = {pred}
cb.hybrid_cb_only: The CF prediction is undefined; using the content prediction alone = {pred}
cb.text_clean: {item}'s overview and tagline are cleaned into {n_stems} terms: lower-cased and split into {n_words} words, {n_removed} dropped (stop words, one-letter words, plain numbers), the rest cut down to their stems (hopes, hoping → hope)
cb.user_profile: {user}'s taste profile adds up their {n} other films, each weighted by rating − mean ({center}); cos with {item} = {score}: a score in [−1, 1], not a rating
cb.user_profile_undefined_no_other_ratings: {user} has rated nothing besides {item}, so there is no taste profile to compare with it
cb.user_profile_undefined_profile_flat: All {n} ratings of {user} equal their mean, so no film pulls the taste profile up or down: it is undefined
cb.user_profile_undefined_profile_zero: The signed terms of {user}'s {n} films cancel out: the taste profile is the zero vector and has no direction to compare with {item}
cb.user_profile_undefined_target_empty: {item} has no term in the chosen fields, so its cosine with {user}'s taste profile is undefined
cb.result_score: {item}: score {score} for {user} ({terms}). Above 0 it fits their taste, below 0 it does not; not a rating
cb.topk_pick_profile: Recommend {k} films to {user}: score the {n_candidates} films they have not rated against their taste profile, then re-rank with MMR (λ = {lam})
cb.topk_pick_item: Recommend {k} films to {user}: predict a rating for each of the {n_candidates} films they have not rated, then re-rank with MMR (λ = {lam})
cb.topk_score_profile: {item}: cos(profile of {user}, film) = {score} ({terms}); a score in [−1, 1], not a rating
cb.topk_score_item: {item}: predicted rating {pred} for {user}, the weighted average over the {n} similar films they rated
cb.topk_score_rest: The other {n} candidates are scored the same way (see the table)
cb.topk_score_none_all_rated: {user} has rated all {n_items} films: nothing is left to recommend
cb.topk_score_none_no_profile: {user}'s ratings give no taste profile (no rating, or every rating the same), so no film can be scored
cb.topk_score_none_no_prediction: No film has a predicted rating for {user}: there is nothing to rank
cb.topk_rank: Sorted by that number, the best {k} films are the relevance list; their intra-list similarity (mean cosine of {pairs} pairs) is {ils}
cb.topk_rank_one: Sorted by that number, the best film heads the list; one film has no pair to compare
cb.topk_mmr_first: Place {pos}: {item}, the most relevant (rel {rel}); the list is empty, so no penalty: MMR = {value}
cb.topk_mmr_pick: Place {pos}: {item} (was {before}); closest listed film {by}, cos {penalty}; MMR = {value}
cb.topk_mmr_free: Place {pos}: {item} (was {before}) resembles no listed film: penalty 0, MMR = {value}
cb.topk_mmr_rest: The other {n} places are filled by the same rule (see the table)
cb.topk_mmr_done: Intra-list similarity {before} → {after} (λ = {lam}; lower = more varied): {places} of {k} places changed, {n_new} new film(s)
cb.topk_mmr_one: With one film there is nothing to diversify
cb.topk_result: {k} films for {user}: {places} of {k} places changed, {n_new} new film(s) (λ = {lam}); biggest move: {mover}, {before} → {after}
cb.topk_result_same: The list for {user}: {k} films; at λ = {lam} MMR leaves the relevance order as it is
cb.topk_result_empty: No list for {user}: no film could be ranked
cb.feature_selection: Which terms set {user}'s liked films (rating ≥ {theta}) apart? {n_terms} terms scored over {n} films ({n_pos} liked, {n_neg} not) by Gini, entropy, χ², Dev; target left out
cb.feature_selection_weighted: Which terms set {user}'s liked films (rating ≥ {theta}) apart? {n_terms} terms scored over {n} films ({n_pos} liked, {n_neg} not); each weighs ×({a} − Gini); target left out
cb.feature_selection_undefined_no_other_rat: {user} has rated nothing besides the target, so no term can be scored
cb.feature_selection_undefined_flat_ratings: All {n} ratings of {user} are equal, so no term can tell liked films from disliked ones: the scores are undefined

cb.feature_selection_undefined_too_few_disl: Only {n_neg} of {user}'s {n} films are disliked (rating < {theta}); at least 2 liked and 2 disliked films are needed, so the scores are undefined
cb.model_data: {user}'s {n} other films become the rows of X: each film is its TF-IDF vector over {m} terms. The targets y are their ratings minus {user}'s mean ({center}). The model sees only this history, nothing from any other user
cb.model_fit: Ridge regression finds the weights w that fit y from X while a penalty α = {alpha} keeps them small; solved in closed form. On its own {n} films it misses by {rmse} on average (RMSE)
cb.model_fit_lsqr: Ridge regression finds the weights w that fit y from X while a penalty α = {alpha} keeps them small; {n} films are too many for the closed form, so it is solved iteratively ({iterations} steps). On its own films it misses by {rmse} on average (RMSE)
cb.model_fit_flat: Every rating of {user} equals their mean ({center}), so there is nothing to learn: all weights are 0 and the model predicts {center} for every film
cb.model_fit_undefined_no_other_ratings: {user} has no other rating, so there is nothing to train a model on: the prediction falls back to the mean rating of everyone, {center}
cb.model_weights: {user}'s model learned {n_pos} terms that raise a rating and {n_neg} that lower it. Raising: {top_up}. Lowering: {top_down}
cb.model_predict: {item}: the user's mean {center} + {dev} from the film's {n_terms} terms = {pred}. {top_term} moves it most ({top_part}); {n_unseen} of the terms occur in none of {user}'s films and add nothing
cb.model_predict_no_terms: {item} has no term at all, so the model has nothing to add: the prediction is {user}'s mean, {pred}
cb.model_predict_none: No model, no prediction from the films: the prediction is the mean rating of everyone, {pred}
cb.topk_pick_model: Recommend {k} films to {user}: train the user's own model, predict a rating for each of the {n_candidates} films they have not rated, then re-rank with MMR (λ = {lam})
cb.mlp_fit: A small network (one hidden layer of {hidden} units) is trained on {n} of {user}'s {n_all} films: {epochs} steps of Adam (learning rate {lr}) on their squared error, from a seeded start. The other {n_val} films are held out for validation: the network never trains on them. Each film enters as its {n_input} most frequent terms ({n_dropped} rarer ones are left out), scaled to length 1. The error on the training films falls from {rmse0} to {rmse} (RMSE); on the held-out films it ends at {val_rmse}. Early stopping is switched OFF here on purpose, so all {epochs} steps run and the gap between the training and the validation error shows; the usual practice - the switch beside the epochs, on by default - stops at step {best_epoch}, where the validation error is lowest ({val_at_best}), and keeps those weights; here the last step's weights predict. The held-out films are left out of the weights, not of the centre: the centre is still the mean of all of {user}'s other ratings
cb.mlp_fit_best_first: A small network (one hidden layer of {hidden} units) is trained on {n} of {user}'s {n_all} films: {epochs} steps of Adam (learning rate {lr}) on their squared error, from a seeded start. The other {n_val} films are held out for validation: the network never trains on them. Each film enters as its {n_input} most frequent terms ({n_dropped} rarer ones are left out), scaled to length 1. The error on the training films falls from {rmse0} to {rmse} (RMSE); on the held-out films it ends at {val_rmse}. Early stopping is switched OFF here on purpose, so all {epochs} steps run and the gap between the training and the validation error shows; the usual practice - the switch beside the epochs, on by default - would stop after the first step, where the validation error is lowest ({val_at_best}): with {n_train} films and {n_params} parameters the network starts memorising right after step 1, when it is still close to the user's mean. Here the last step's weights predict. The held-out films are left out of the weights, not of the centre: the centre is still the mean of all of {user}'s other ratings
cb.mlp_fit_no_val: A small network (one hidden layer of {hidden} units) is trained on {user}'s {n} films: {epochs} steps of Adam (learning rate {lr}) on their squared error, from a seeded start. Each film enters as its {n_input} most frequent terms ({n_dropped} rarer ones are left out), scaled to length 1. The error on its own films falls from {rmse0} to {rmse} (RMSE). {n} films are too few to hold any out, so there is no validation curve
cb.mlp_fit_es: A small network (one hidden layer of {hidden} units) is trained on {n} of {user}'s {n_all} films: Adam steps (learning rate {lr}) on their squared error, from a seeded start; the other {n_val} films are held out for validation and the network never trains on them. Each film enters as its {n_input} most frequent terms ({n_dropped} rarer ones are left out), scaled to length 1. Early stopping (patience {patience}) ended training after step {epochs_run} of the {epochs} allowed: the held-out error was lowest at step {best_epoch} ({val_at_best}) and had not improved for {patience} steps since, so the weights of step {kept_epoch} are kept and predict (training error {rmse}, held-out error {val_rmse}). The held-out films are left out of the weights, not of the centre: the centre is still the mean of all of {user}'s other ratings
cb.mlp_fit_es_budget: A small network (one hidden layer of {hidden} units) is trained on {n} of {user}'s {n_all} films: Adam steps (learning rate {lr}) on their squared error, from a seeded start; the other {n_val} films are held out for validation and the network never trains on them. Each film enters as its {n_input} most frequent terms ({n_dropped} rarer ones are left out), scaled to length 1. Early stopping (patience {patience}) is on, but the budget of {epochs} steps ran out first: the held-out error was lowest at step {best_epoch} ({val_at_best}), so the weights of step {kept_epoch} are kept and predict (training error {rmse}, held-out error {val_rmse}). The held-out films are left out of the weights, not of the centre: the centre is still the mean of all of {user}'s other ratings
cb.mlp_fit_es_improving: A small network (one hidden layer of {hidden} units) is trained on {n} of {user}'s {n_all} films: Adam steps (learning rate {lr}) on their squared error, from a seeded start; the other {n_val} films are held out for validation and the network never trains on them. Each film enters as its {n_input} most frequent terms ({n_dropped} rarer ones are left out), scaled to length 1. Early stopping (patience {patience}) is on, but the budget of {epochs} steps ran out while the held-out error was still falling: the last step, {kept_epoch}, is the best one ({val_at_best}) and its weights predict (training error {rmse}). A larger epoch budget would let the network keep improving. The held-out films are left out of the weights, not of the centre: the centre is still the mean of all of {user}'s other ratings
cb.mlp_effects: What does the network say about a film made of one term alone? {n_pos} terms push the rating up, {n_neg} push it down. Up: {top_up}. Down: {top_down}. These are single-term effects, not shares of a prediction: a network is not additive, so the terms of a film do not simply add up
cb.mlp_predict: {item}: the user's mean {center} + the network's output {dev} for the film's {n_terms} terms = {pred}. {n_unseen} of the terms are not among the network's inputs (no film of {user} has them, or they are too rare) and add nothing
cb.topk_score_mlp: {item}: predicted rating {pred} for {user} = their mean {center} + the network's output {dev}

mf.holdout: {item}'s rating by the user is hidden from training ({n_hidden} cell); the newest {valid_frac} share of each user's remaining ratings ({n_valid} ratings) is the validation set; {n_train} ratings train the model
mf.holdout_absent: Nothing is hidden: the requested cell is not in the training matrix (evaluation mode); {n_train} ratings train, {n_valid} validate
mf.holdout_no_valid_frac: The target rating is hidden ({n_hidden} cell); no validation set (valid_frac = 0): training runs for every epoch on the remaining {n_train} ratings
mf.holdout_valid_too_small: The target rating is hidden ({n_hidden} cell). A validation tail would hold only {n_valid_available} ratings (< {min_valid}) — too few for a reliable early-stopping signal — so all {n_train} remaining ratings train the model for the full epoch budget
mf.holdout_unrated: {item} has no rating by the user, so nothing is hidden from training; the newest {valid_frac} share of each user's ratings ({n_valid} ratings) is the validation set; {n_train} ratings train the model
mf.holdout_unrated_no_valid_frac: {item} has no rating by the user, so nothing is hidden; no validation set (valid_frac = 0): training runs for every epoch on all {n_train} ratings
mf.holdout_unrated_valid_too_small: {item} has no rating by the user, so nothing is hidden. A validation tail would hold only {n_valid_available} ratings (< {min_valid}) — too few for a reliable early-stopping signal — so all {n_train} ratings train the model for the full epoch budget
mf.binarise: Every rating becomes an interaction (x = 1): {n_pos} positives; {n_no_negative} user(s) interacted with every item and yield no (u, i, j) triple; {n_triples} triples per epoch
mf.init: {k} latent factors per user and item drawn from N(0, {std}²) with seed {seed}; biases start at 0; μ = train mean = {mu}
mf.init_als: {k} latent factors per item drawn from N(0, {std}²) with seed {seed}; user factors start at 0 and are solved first; μ = train mean = {mu}
mf.sgd_demo: Epoch {epoch}, one update: {user} rated {item} {r}; the model said {pred}, error e = {e}; biases and both vectors move by η = {lr} (λ = {reg})
mf.als_demo: Sweep {epoch}: {user}'s vector solved exactly from the {n} items they rated (ridge λ = {lam}, a {k} × {k} system)
mf.bpr_demo: Epoch {epoch}, one triple: {user} interacted with {item_i} but not {item_j} — the gradient pushes the first above the second (batch of {batch})
mf.epoch: Epoch {epoch}: train {loss} = {train}, validation {metric} = {valid}; current prediction for the target = {pred}
mf.epoch_no_valid: Epoch {epoch}: train {loss} = {train}; current prediction for the target = {pred}
mf.epochs_collapsed: {n} more epochs ran the same way (see the table and the curve)
mf.early_stop: Validation {metric} did not improve for {patience} epochs: stopped after epoch {n_epochs}; the weights of epoch {best_epoch} ({metric} = {metric_best}) are restored
mf.max_epochs: Reached the epoch budget ({max_epochs}); the best validation {metric} was at epoch {best_epoch} ({metric_best}), whose weights are kept
mf.no_validation: No validation set, so no early stopping: all {n_epochs} epochs ran and the final weights are used
mf.score: Score x_ui = b_i + p_u·q_i = {b_i} + {dot} = {score} (not a rating — only its order matters)
mf.result_score: {item} ranks {rank} of {n} unseen items for this user (score {score}, {ties} tie(s))
mf.result_undefined: No score: {item} is outside the closed form
mf.ease_binarise: Every rating becomes an interaction x = 1 ({n_users} users × {n_kept} items in the closed form, min {min_raters} rater(s); {n_hidden} cell hidden); {user} has {n_user_items} interactions to score from
mf.ease_ratings_input: Ratings enter X as they are ({n_users} users × {n_kept} items in the closed form, min {min_raters} rater(s); {n_hidden} cell hidden); {user} has {n_user_items} ratings to score from
mf.ease_binarise_unrated: Every rating becomes an interaction x = 1 ({n_users} users × {n_kept} items in the closed form, min {min_raters} rater(s)); {item} has no rating by the user, so nothing is hidden; {user} has {n_user_items} interactions to score from
mf.ease_ratings_input_unrated: Ratings enter X as they are ({n_users} users × {n_kept} items in the closed form, min {min_raters} rater(s)); {item} has no rating by the user, so nothing is hidden; {user} has {n_user_items} ratings to score from
mf.ease_gram: Gram matrix G = XᵀX over the {n_kept} items: G_tt = {g_tt} raters for {item}; off-diagonal entries count common raters
mf.ease_inverse: Invert once: P = (G + λI)⁻¹ with λ = {lam}; P_tt = {p_tt}; the weights of {item}'s column are B_jt = −P_jt / P_tt with B_tt = 0
mf.ease_weights: {n} weights for {item}, one per interaction of the user; strongest: {top_item} (B = {top_b})
mf.ease_score: Score s_ut = Σ x_uj B_jt over {user}'s {n} interactions = {score}
mf.ease_outside: {item} has fewer than {min_raters} raters and is outside the closed form: no score

dnn.pick: Predict {user}'s rating of {item} with {algorithm}: a neural rating model takes (userId, movieId) in and gives a rating out. We open that box now - what is inside it, and how it learns, are the next steps.
dnn.build: Inside the box ({architecture}): {n_layers} stages from the two ids to the rating - embeddings of size {k}, hidden layers [{layers}], {n_params} trainable parameters; stage sizes {sizes}
dnn.init: Embeddings drawn from N(0, {std}²) with seed {seed}, dense layers with PyTorch's default initialisation, the output bias set to μ = {mu}; {n_params} parameters in total
dnn.batch_demo: Epoch {epoch}, first mini-batch of {batch} ratings ({users} users): MSE {loss_before} before the {optimizer} step (η = {lr}), {loss_after} on the same batch after it
dnn.layer_embedding_user: Stage {layer}/{n_layers}: look up {user}'s embedding, a learned vector of {size} numbers
dnn.layer_embedding_item: Stage {layer}/{n_layers}: look up {item}'s embedding, a learned vector of {size} numbers
dnn.layer_features: Stage {layer}/{n_layers}: the item's genre multi-hot input ({n_genres} genres): {genres}
dnn.layer_product: Stage {layer}/{n_layers}: GMF — the element-wise product of the user and item embeddings ({size} values): MF's dot product with a learned weight per factor (the output unit holds the weights)
dnn.layer_concat: Stage {layer}/{n_layers}: concatenate into one vector of {size} values
dnn.layer_dense: Stage {layer}/{n_layers}: dense layer {n_in} → {n_out} with ReLU; {zeros} of {n_out} units are off (0)
dnn.layer_output: Stage {layer}/{n_layers}: the linear output unit gives the rating {pred}
dnn.features: Side inputs, from the {n_train} training ratings alone ({n_groups} input groups on: {groups}): the film's content row over {n_fields} field(s) ({fields}) cut to the {n_terms} most frequent terms ({n_dropped} rarer ones left out) and scaled to length 1; the user's taste profile over the same terms (their training films, liked ones push terms up, disliked ones down); {n_numeric} film number(s) and {n_stats} user statistic(s), each standardised. The hidden target rating and the validation tail enter none of them
dnn.layer_item_content: Stage {layer}/{n_layers}: {item}'s content row — {n_terms_film} of the {size} terms are non-zero (TF-IDF over the selected fields, scaled to length 1); the heaviest: {terms}
dnn.layer_user_profile: Stage {layer}/{n_layers}: {user}'s taste profile over the same {size} terms, from their {n_films} training ratings ({n_terms_profile} terms non-zero): a liked film pushes its terms up, a disliked one down, then the vector is scaled to length 1. Up: {pos}. Down: {neg}
dnn.layer_user_stats: Stage {layer}/{n_layers}: {user}'s rating statistics from their training ratings — {raw} — each standardised over all users (mean 0, std 1) to {z}
dnn.layer_item_numeric: Stage {layer}/{n_layers}: {item}'s numbers — {raw} (release year and training raters; the count enters as log(1 + n)) — each standardised over all films to {z}
dnn.layer_dense_user: Stage {layer}/{n_layers}: the profile tower's dense layer {n_in} → {n_out} with ReLU compresses the user's profile; {zeros} of {n_out} units are off (0)
dnn.layer_dense_item: Stage {layer}/{n_layers}: the content tower's dense layer {n_in} → {n_out} with ReLU compresses the film's terms; {zeros} of {n_out} units are off (0)

pretrained.early_stop: Trained at home ({n_train} ratings, {seconds} s): no live epoch walk here - the curve and the epoch table show the stored history. Validation {metric} did not improve for {patience} epochs: training stopped after epoch {n_epochs} and the weights of epoch {best_epoch} ({metric} = {metric_best}) are kept
pretrained.max_epochs: Trained at home ({n_train} ratings, {seconds} s): no live epoch walk here - the curve and the epoch table show the stored history. It ran to the epoch budget ({max_epochs}); the best validation {metric} was at epoch {best_epoch} ({metric_best}), whose weights are kept
pretrained.no_validation: Trained at home ({n_train} ratings, {seconds} s): no live epoch walk here - the curve and the epoch table show the stored history. There is no validation set, so all {n_epochs} epochs ran and the final weights are used
pretrained.topk: This {algorithm} was fitted at home ({n_epochs} epochs, {seconds} s) and read from disk: nothing is trained for this request

topk.pick: Recommend the top {k} films to {user}: score every film they have not rated, then keep the best {k}
topk.pick_all: Rank all films for {user} and show the top {k}. Display only: films this user has rated stay in the ranking, marked “seen” — a recommender would not offer them
topk.model: {algorithm}, fitted once on every rating ({k} latent factors, {epochs} epochs, μ = {mu}). Nothing is hidden: the films scored here have no rating, so no rating can leak
topk.model_score: {algorithm}, fitted once on every interaction ({k} latent factors, {epochs} epochs). It gives a ranking score, not a rating — only the order of the scores matters
topk.model_closed: {algorithm}: the closed-form item-to-item weights B, computed once from every interaction. A film's score is Σ x·B over the films this user has rated
topk.model_dnn: {algorithm} network ({n_params} parameters), fitted once on every rating ({epochs} epochs). Nothing is hidden: the films scored here have no rating, so no rating can leak. One batched forward pass gives the score of all {n_items} films for this user
topk.score_implicit: {item}: score = b_i + p_u·q_i = {b_i} + {dot} = {raw} (not a rating — only its order matters)
topk.score_ease: {item}: score = Σ x_uj B_jt over the films {user} has rated = {raw}
topk.score_rest: The same rule scores the other {n} candidate films: every film's score comes from the same factors
topk.score_none: Nothing to score: {user} has rated all {n_items} films
topk.exclude: {n_seen} films {user} has already rated drop out; {n_candidates} of the {n_items} films remain as candidates
topk.exclude_unscored: {n_seen} films {user} has already rated drop out and {n_unscored} more have no score; {n_candidates} of the {n_items} films remain as candidates
topk.exclude_all: Nothing drops out (display only): {n_seen} of the {n_candidates} ranked films are ones {user} has rated, marked “seen”
topk.rank: Sort the {n_candidates} candidates by score, best first; a tie goes to the film with the smaller index
topk.cut: Keep the first {n_listed} (K = {k}): {n_relevant} of them score at least {threshold}, the relevance threshold
topk.cut_implicit: Keep the first {n_listed} (K = {k}). A ranking score has no rating threshold, so no film is judged relevant here
topk.cut_empty: No candidate is left, so there is nothing to keep
topk.list: {user}'s top-{k} list is ready: {n_relevant} of the {n_listed} films are relevant (score ≥ {threshold})
topk.list_implicit: {user}'s top-{k} list is ready: {n_listed} films, best score first
topk.list_empty: {user} has no candidate film left, so the list is empty

metrics.split: {method} split ({unit}, test share {test_frac}, users with fewer than {min_ratings} ratings stay in train), seed {seed}: {n_train} train and {n_test} test ratings from {n_users_test} users; the recommender never sees the test cells
metrics.fit: {engine} fitted on the {n_train} train ratings only ({seconds} s)
metrics.relevant_none: {user} has {n_test} held-out rating(s) but none is relevant (≥ {tau}): recall, nDCG and AP are undefined for this user
metrics.no_test: {user} has no held-out rating under this split (fewer than {min_ratings} ratings): nothing to hit
metrics.candidates: {user} has {n_candidates} unseen items in train; {n_ranked} of them received a score and form the ranked list L (the {n_unscored} unscored ones are never recommended)
metrics.rank_hit: Rank {k}: {item} (score {score}) is relevant — a hit; TP = {tp}
metrics.rank_miss: Rank {k}: {item} (score {score}) is not relevant — a miss; FP = {fp}
metrics.rank_collapsed: {n} more ranks walked the same way (see the table and the curves)
metrics.ndcg: Cut-off K = {K}: DCG@K = {dcg} (gain 1 per hit, discount 1/log2(k+1)), IDCG@K = {idcg} over min(K, |Rel|) = {n_ideal} ideal hits → nDCG@{K} = {ndcg}
metrics.ap: Cut-off K = {K}: AP@K sums P@k over the hit ranks ({hit_ranks}) and divides by min(K, |Rel|) = {norm} → AP@{K} = {ap}
metrics.rr: First hit at rank {first_hit} → RR = {rr}; HR@{K} = {hr}; P@{K} = {precision}, R@{K} = {recall}
metrics.rr_none: No hit within K = {K}: RR = 0, HR@{K} = 0, P@{K} = 0, R@{K} = 0
metrics.aggregate: Averaged over the {n_users} test users with at least one relevant item (K = {K}): P@K {precision}, R@K {recall}, HR@K {hr}, nDCG@K {ndcg}, MAP@K {map}, MRR {mrr}
metrics.aggregate_sampled: Averaged over {n_users} seeded-sampled test users of {n_total} with at least one relevant item (K = {K}): P@K {precision}, R@K {recall}, HR@K {hr}, nDCG@K {ndcg}, MAP@K {map}, MRR {mrr}
metrics.aggregate_none: No test user has a relevant held-out item under this split: the ranking metrics are undefined
metrics.rating_errors: Rating accuracy on the same {n} test cells: MAE {mae}, RMSE {rmse} ({coverage} predicted)
metrics.rating_errors_implicit: {engine} returns ranking scores, not ratings: MAE and RMSE are skipped (AUC and the @K metrics remain)
metrics.beyond: Beyond accuracy over the {n_users} top-{K} lists: catalogue coverage {coverage} ({n_recommended} of {n_items} items), Gini {gini}, mean popularity {avg_pop} raters, novelty {novelty} bits
metrics.result_rank: {user}: P@{K} = {precision}, nDCG@{K} = {ndcg}; over all test users nDCG@{K} = {ndcg_mean}
metrics.scores: {engine} scored {n_test} test cells: {n_pos} relevant (≥ {tau}) and {n_neg} not; {n_unscored} unscored cells are left out; prevalence {prevalence}
metrics.threshold: Threshold t = {t}: the {n_predicted} cells with score ≥ t are predicted relevant → TP {tp}, FP {fp}, FN {fn}, TN {tn}
metrics.threshold_collapsed: {n} more thresholds swept the same way (see the table and the curves)
metrics.auc: Trapezoids under the {n_points} ROC points give AUC = {auc}; the pairwise check P(score_pos > score_neg) + ½ P(tie) = {pairwise}; a random ranker scores 0.5
metrics.single_point: Binarising the predictions at τ = {tau} first collapses the sweep to the single point (FPR {fpr}, TPR {tpr}); the 'AUC' of that point is (TPR + 1 − FPR)/2 = {bal_acc}, the balanced accuracy — not the area under a curve
metrics.result_threshold: AUC = {auc} over {n_test} test cells ({n_pos} relevant); MAE {mae}

hybrid_switch.pick: Predict {user}'s rating of {item} by choosing ONE of {q} recommenders ({bases}) - the one that did best on {user}'s own ratings. {user} rated it {actual}: that rating is hidden from every recommender and from the choice
hybrid_switch.pick_unrated: Predict {user}'s rating of {item} by choosing ONE of {q} recommenders ({bases}) - the one that did best on {user}'s own ratings. {user} has not rated it, so there is no rating to compare with
hybrid_switch.pick_rule: Predict {user}'s rating of {item} with the cold-start rule: {cf} answers when it has at least {m} neighbours for the film, {cb} otherwise. {user} rated it {actual}: that rating is hidden from both recommenders and from the rule
hybrid_switch.pick_rule_unrated: Predict {user}'s rating of {item} with the cold-start rule: {cf} answers when it has at least {m} neighbours for the film, {cb} otherwise. {user} has not rated it, so there is no rating to compare with
hybrid_switch.split: The newest {frac} % of {user}'s own ratings are held out - {n_heldout} of {n_user}, at most {cap}. The recommenders learn only from the other {n_train} ratings (every other user's included), and {item} is in neither group. What follows is about {user} alone
hybrid_switch.predict_heldout: Each of the {q} recommenders predicts all {n_heldout} of {user}'s held-out ratings: one column of the table per recommender. Where one has nothing to go on (no neighbour who rated the film) it answers with its own fallback, the user's mean; rows answered that way: {fallbacks}
hybrid_switch.predict_heldout_rule: {cf} and {cb} predict all {n_heldout} of {user}'s held-out ratings; next to {cf}'s answer the table counts the neighbours it used for each film. Where it found none it answers with its own fallback, the user's mean ({n_fallback} rows)
hybrid_switch.score: {base} misses {user}'s {n_heldout} held-out ratings by {mae} on average (MAE) and by {rmse} (RMSE: the misses are squared before they are averaged, so big misses count more)
hybrid_switch.score_train: {base} misses {n_fit} of {user}'s TRAINING ratings - ratings every recommender has already learned from - by {mae_fit} (MAE) and {rmse_fit} (RMSE). On the {n_heldout} held-out ratings it misses by {mae} (MAE) and {rmse} (RMSE)
hybrid_switch.choose: On {user}'s {n_heldout} held-out ratings the lowest {criterion} is {winner}'s, {value}; {second} is second, {gap} behind. The other error measure, {other}, picks {winner} too
hybrid_switch.choose_split: On {user}'s {n_heldout} held-out ratings the lowest {criterion} is {winner}'s, {value}; {second} is second, {gap} behind. The other error measure, {other}, would pick {winner_other} instead: the two errors weigh the misses differently
hybrid_switch.choose_train: {user}'s TRAINING ratings (every recommender has learned from them) crown {winner}: {criterion} {value}. On the {n_heldout} held-out ratings the best is {winner_right} ({criterion} {value_right}); {winner} misses them by {value_heldout} ({criterion})
hybrid_switch.choose_rule: The rule on {user}'s {n_heldout} held-out ratings: {cf} answers {n_cf_used} of them (it had at least {m} neighbours), {cb} the other {n_cb_used}. The rule misses by {rule_mae} (MAE) and {rule_rmse} (RMSE); {cf} alone by {cf_mae} and {cf_rmse}, {cb} alone by {cb_mae} and {cb_rmse}
hybrid_switch.answer: {winner} answers about {item}: {pred}. The others say {others_text}. The choice was made on {user}'s history, not on this film: it never looks at {item}
hybrid_switch.answer_cf: {cf} found {n_cf} neighbours for {item} (the rule needs {m}) and answers: {pred}. {cb} would have said {other_pred}
hybrid_switch.answer_cb: {cf} found {n_cf} neighbours for {item}, fewer than the {m} the rule needs, so {cb} answers: {pred}. {cf} would have said {other_pred}

hybrid.pick: Predict {user}'s rating of {item} by blending {q} recommenders ({bases}). {user} rated it {actual}: that rating is hidden from every recommender and from the weights
hybrid.pick_unrated: Predict {user}'s rating of {item} by blending {q} recommenders ({bases}). {user} has not rated it, so there is no rating to compare with
hybrid.split: The newest {frac} % of every user's ratings are held out, at most {cap} per user: {n_heldout} ratings of {n_users} users ({n_heldout_user} of them {user}'s; the largest user share is {top_share} %). The recommenders learn only from the other {n_train} ratings, and {item} is in neither group. The weights are learned on the held-out ratings of EVERY user: the newest ratings of each student (at most {cap} per user, {n_heldout} pairs in all), {user}'s included; one set of weights serves the whole class, and the target rating is never among them. Switching differs: its bucket scores the bases on the active student's own held-out ratings only
hybrid.split_no_user: The newest {frac} % of every user's ratings are held out, at most {cap} per user: {n_heldout} ratings of {n_users} users, none of them {user}'s ({user} has fewer than {min_ratings} ratings, so all of theirs stay with the recommenders; the largest user share is {top_share} %). The recommenders learn only from the other {n_train} ratings, and {item} is in neither group. The weights are learned on the held-out ratings of EVERY user: the newest ratings of each student (at most {cap} per user, {n_heldout} pairs in all); one set of weights serves the whole class, and the target rating is never among them. Switching differs: its bucket scores the bases on the active student's own held-out ratings only
hybrid.fit_bases: Fit {base} ({i} of {q}) on the {n_train} training ratings alone, with its own default settings: {ms} ms. It never sees a held-out rating, nor {item}
hybrid.predict_heldout: Each of the {q} recommenders predicts all {n_heldout} held-out ratings: one column of the table per recommender. Where one has nothing to go on (no neighbour who rated the film) it answers with its own fallback, the user's mean; rows answered that way: {fallbacks}. Alone, the best is {best}, with an RMSE of {rmse_best}
hybrid.equal: The weights start equal, 1/{q} each, and the intercept starts at the mean residual of that blend: β₀ = {beta0}, the average shift that makes it meet the {n_heldout} held-out ratings. Plain averaging misses them by {rmse_plain} (RMSE), the blend with the intercept by {rmse_equal}; the best recommender alone, {best}, by {rmse_best}
hybrid.equal_free: The weights start equal, 1/{q} each. Their blend misses the {n_heldout} held-out ratings by {rmse_equal} (RMSE); the best recommender alone, {best}, by {rmse_best}
hybrid.equal_train: The weights start equal, 1/{q} each. On the {n_fit} TRAINING ratings the weights are fitted on (ratings the recommenders have already learned from) their blend misses by {rmse_equal} (RMSE); the best recommender alone, {best}, by {rmse_best}
hybrid.gd_first: Gradient descent, step 1 of {K}: the gradient says how the error changes with each weight, and the weights move a little against it - projected onto the plane where they add up to 1, so the blend stays a weighted average. The step size is the step scale {gss} over the largest curvature of the loss along that plane, with the intercept solved out: {eta} = {gss} / {lambda_max} (a scale of 1 is one over the largest curvature). The intercept is not a step of its own: after every move it is set again to the mean residual of the new weights ({beta0_prev} → {beta0}). The error falls from {rmse_prev} to {rmse}
hybrid.gd_first_free: Gradient descent, step 1 of {K}: the gradient says how the error changes with each weight, and the weights move a little against it. The step size is the step scale {gss} over the largest curvature of the loss: {eta} = {gss} / {lambda_max} (a scale of 1 is one over the largest curvature). The error falls from {rmse_prev} to {rmse}; the weights now add up to {sum}
hybrid.gd_first_train: Gradient descent, step 1 of {K}, on the {n_fit} training ratings (the foil): the weights move a little against the gradient. The step size is the step scale {gss} over the largest curvature: {eta} = {gss} / {lambda_max}. The error on those ratings falls from {rmse_prev} to {rmse}
hybrid.gd_step: Step {k} of {K}: the error goes from {rmse_prev} to {rmse}; the weights add up to {sum}, the intercept is {beta0}
hybrid.gd_step_free: Step {k} of {K}: the error goes from {rmse_prev} to {rmse}; the weights add up to {sum}
hybrid.gd_collapsed: Steps {first} to {last} ({n} steps) work the same way; after step {last} the error is {rmse} (the table lists them all)
hybrid.ridge: The closed form finds the best weights in one solve - the ones that minimise the same loss while adding up to 1: a column of ones joins the table (its weight is the intercept, which the penalty leaves alone) and a Lagrange system, with a multiplier for the constraint, gives both. Weights {alpha_text}, intercept β₀ = {beta0}. The error is {rmse_ridge}; after {k} gradient steps the descent is at {rmse_gd}, {gap} behind
hybrid.ridge_free: The closed form finds the best free weights in one solve - the ones that minimise the same loss with no constraint and no intercept (the textbook's recipe): {alpha_text}. Its error is {rmse_ridge}; after {k} gradient steps the descent is at {rmse_gd}, {gap} behind. The usual practice - weights held to add up to 1, plus an intercept - reaches {rmse_tied}
hybrid.ridge_ols: Plain least squares, no penalty (λ = 0): with {n} held-out ratings the weights can swing to fit their noise: {alpha_text} (error {rmse_ols}). The usual practice keeps a small ridge penalty (λ = {lam_ref}): {alpha_ref_text} (error {rmse_ref}) - steadier weights for the same data
hybrid.ridge_train: The weights were fitted on {n} TRAINING ratings - ratings every recommender has already learned from - so they trust the recommenders that memorised them: {alpha_text}. On those ratings the blend misses by {rmse_fit}; on the {n_heldout} held-out ratings the same weights miss by {rmse_heldout}, while weights fitted on the held-out ratings (the right way) reach {rmse_right}
hybrid.compare: On the same {n_heldout} held-out ratings (RMSE): the best recommender alone, {best}, {rmse_best} ({rmse_best_level} once it too gets an intercept); plain averaging {rmse_plain}; equal weights with the intercept {rmse_equal}; the gradient steps {rmse_gd}; the closed form {rmse_ridge}. Against {best} alone the closed form changes the error by {gain} (positive: better). From plain averaging to the closed form the error falls by {gain_total}: {gain_level} of it is the intercept, {gain_weights} the learned weights
hybrid.compare_free: On the same {n_heldout} held-out ratings (RMSE): the best recommender alone, {best}, {rmse_best}; equal weights {rmse_equal}; the gradient steps {rmse_gd}; the closed form {rmse_ridge}. Against {best} alone the closed form changes the error by {gain} (positive: better). The usual practice - weights that add up to 1, plus an intercept - reaches {rmse_tied}
hybrid.blend: Blend for {user} and {item}: the recommenders say {p_text}; the weights {alpha_text} and the intercept {beta0} turn that into {pred}
hybrid.blend_gd: Blend for {user} and {item}: the recommenders say {p_text}; the weights of the gradient steps, {alpha_text}, and their intercept {beta0} turn that into {pred} (the closed form would give {pred_ridge})
hybrid.blend_equal: Blend for {user} and {item}: the recommenders say {p_text}; equal weights and their intercept {beta0} turn that into {pred} - the learned (closed-form) weights would give {pred_ridge}
hybrid.blend_free: Blend for {user} and {item}: the recommenders say {p_text}; the weights {alpha_text} turn that into {pred}
hybrid.blend_gd_free: Blend for {user} and {item}: the recommenders say {p_text}; the weights of the gradient steps, {alpha_text}, turn that into {pred} (the closed form would give {pred_ridge})
hybrid.blend_equal_free: Blend for {user} and {item}: the recommenders say {p_text}; equal weights turn that into {pred} - the learned (closed-form) weights would give {pred_ridge}

diag.fallback: No neighbour shares a term with the target under the chosen fields, so the prediction falls back to the user's mean {center}.
diag.favourite_outlier: A neighbourhood method predicts what the user gave the look-alikes: the {n_used} most similar film(s) average {pred}, while {actual} is one of the user's {n_fav} ratings at or above {q_fav}. The largest errors of such methods land on a user's favourites.
diag.dislike_outlier: The look-alikes average {pred}, while {actual} is one of the user's {n_dis} ratings at or below {q_dis}. The largest errors of a neighbourhood method land on a user's outliers.
diag.wide: {n_used} of the user's {n_rated} rated films count as neighbours ({share} %), so the weighted average sits near the user's mean {center}. Fewer fields or a smaller k let the closest films speak.
diag.thin: This prediction rests on {n_used} neighbour(s) only; a single rating decides it.
diag.hit: The look-alikes carried the rating: {pred} against {actual}.
diag.large_error: The look-alikes miss the rating by {abs_error}: what the user felt about this film is not in its attributes.

diag_model.favourite_outlier: The model, trained on the user's other films, predicts {pred}, while {actual} is one of the user's {n_fav} ratings at or above {q_fav}: a favourite is an outlier of the user's own history, and a model fitted to that history predicts the usual, not the exception.
diag_model.dislike_outlier: The model, trained on the user's other films, predicts {pred}, while {actual} is one of the user's {n_dis} ratings at or below {q_dis}: a strong dislike is an outlier of the user's own history, and a model fitted to that history predicts the usual, not the exception.
diag_model.hit: The model carried the rating: {pred} against {actual}.
diag_model.large_error: The model misses the rating by {abs_error}: what the user felt about this film is not in its attributes, and the attributes are all the model sees.

diag_dnn.valid: Validation RMSE {rmse} at the kept epoch {kept_epoch}, on {n_valid} held-out ratings the network never trained on.
diag_dnn.ids_only: The same settings with ids only: validation RMSE {rmse_ids}; with the content and user features: {rmse} — {gain} lower. The features carry information an id cannot.
diag_dnn.ids_only_better: The same settings with ids only: validation RMSE {rmse_ids}; with the content and user features: {rmse} — {gain} higher. On this data the features did not help; more inputs are not a guarantee.
diag_dnn.cold_item: The film's embedding had {n_item} training rating(s) to learn from — nearly untrained — while the content tower reads its terms, learned from every film that shares them; the user's embedding had {n_user}.
diag_dnn.examples: The film's embedding learned from {n_item} training ratings and the user's from {n_user}; the content and profile towers read every film that shares their terms.
diag_dnn.examples_ids: The film's embedding learned from {n_item} training ratings and the user's from {n_user}; no content or profile tower helps them out here.

diag_hybrid.gain_positive: On the {n_heldout} held-out ratings the blend misses by {rmse_blend} (RMSE), {gain} less than the best single recommender, {best} ({rmse_best}).
diag_hybrid.gain_zero_or_negative: On the {n_heldout} held-out ratings the blend misses by {rmse_blend} (RMSE) and the best single recommender, {best}, by {rmse_best}: the blend is not better (difference {gap}). A blend pays off only when the recommenders make different mistakes.
diag_hybrid.target_older: {user} rated this film {days} days before {user}'s held-out ratings began. The intercept (β₀ = {beta0}) was learned on newer ratings: if the level drifted, it moves this prediction the wrong way.
diag_hybrid.target_fallback: {bases} had nothing to go on for this film - nobody else rated it - and answered with their own fallback, {user}'s mean. The blend's real evidence comes from the others.
diag_hybrid.few_heldout_user: {user} contributed only {n} of the {n_heldout} held-out ratings, so the weights hardly reflect this user's taste.
diag_hybrid.heldout_dominant: One user supplies {share} % of the held-out ratings (the cap is {cap} per user): the weights mostly reflect that user.
diag_hybrid.alpha_negative: {base} received a negative weight ({alpha}): the regression uses it to correct the others rather than to predict.
diag_hybrid.alpha_dominant: {base} carries {share} % of the weight: the others mostly correct it.
diag_hybrid.gd_converged: The gradient steps reached the closed form in {k} steps: with the weights held to add up to 1 the loss has no steep direction left, so descent and closed form agree.
diag_hybrid.gd_short: After {k} steps the descent is still {alpha_gap} from the closed form in the weights ({gap} in RMSE): it creeps along the flat directions of the loss, the closed form jumps to the end.
diag_hybrid.level_free: The textbook's free recipe (no constraint, no intercept) would give weights adding up to {sum} and an error of {rmse_free} (RMSE): without an intercept the weights themselves must rescale the level of the predictions. Here the weights add up to 1 and the intercept, β₀ = {beta0}, corrects the level instead: {rmse_blend}.
diag_hybrid.heterogeneous: The recommenders mix rating-based and content-based models, which see different data: weighting matters more when the data types differ.
diag_hybrid.homogeneous: All the recommenders learn from the same ratings, so their mistakes are alike and a blend gains little.
diag_hybrid.switch_winner: On {user}'s {n_heldout} held-out ratings {base} has the lowest RMSE, {rmse_winner}; the runner-up is {gap} behind.
diag_hybrid.switch_winner_mae: On {user}'s {n_heldout} held-out ratings {base} has the lowest MAE, {mae_winner}; the runner-up is {gap} behind.
diag_hybrid.switch_older: {user} rated this film {days} days before the held-out ratings the leaderboard rests on began: if {user}'s taste moved since, the winner on the newest ratings may not be the best one for this film.
diag_hybrid.switch_winner_fallback: {base} won on {user}'s ratings but had nothing to go on for this film - nobody else rated it - and answered with {user}'s mean: a switch that looks at the user's history never looks at the film.
diag_hybrid.switch_train: Picked on the training ratings the winner is {base}; on the held-out ratings it is {best}. Ratings a recommender has learned from flatter it.
diag_hybrid.switch_few: Only {n} held-out ratings of {user} decide the leaderboard: one rating more or fewer could change the winner.
diag_hybrid.switch_close: A close call: the runner-up is {gap} behind {base}, and on {n} ratings that is within the noise - the two answer the same ratings and their misses differ by about as much as the gap itself.
diag_hybrid.switch_disagree: The two errors disagree about the winner: {base} by the one the choice used, {best} by the other.
diag_hybrid.rule_coverage: On the held-out ratings {base} had at least {m} neighbours for {n_cf_used} of {n_heldout}; the content recommender answered the other {n_cb_used}.
diag_hybrid.rule_gain: The rule misses by {rmse_rule} (RMSE), {gain} less than the better of the two alone ({best}, {rmse_best}).
diag_hybrid.rule_no_gain: The rule misses by {rmse_rule} (RMSE) and the better of the two alone, {best}, by {rmse_best}: the rule does not help here (difference {gap}). A switch pays off only when the second recommender is better exactly where the first is thin.
diag_hybrid.rule_cb_fallback: The content recommender had nothing to go on for this film either and answered with {user}'s mean.

col_tip.user: The neighbour: a user who rated the target item. Its row in the matrix carries the same name.
col_tip.item: The candidate item: an item the active user has rated.
col_tip.n_raters: raters: how many users rated this candidate item (its support on its own).
col_tip.c: co-rated: how many items this neighbour and the active user both rated (the target excluded) - the basis of w.
col_tip.c_all: co-rated without the attribute filter: how many items the two users share before the filter on the item attributes is applied.
col_tip.c_raters: common raters: how many users rated BOTH this candidate item and the target item, the active user excluded - the support s is computed over; the item-based mirror of the co-rated films in the user-based table (there the candidates are users and the shared things are films; here the candidates are films and the shared things are users).
col_tip.c_raters_all: common raters without the user filter.
col_tip.mean_f: The neighbour's mean rating inside the filtered segment F - the centre this similarity used.
col_tip.item_mean_f: The item's mean rating inside the segment C - the centre this similarity used.
col_tip.w: w: the similarity between the active user and this neighbour, before significance weighting.
col_tip.s: s: the similarity between the target item and this item, before significance weighting.
col_tip.factor: Shrink factor min(c / n, 1): damps a similarity resting on few co-rated items; n is the threshold (Parameters, n; 50 by default).
col_tip.w_shrunk: w′ = w × factor: the similarity after significance weighting - the weight used to rank the candidates and in the prediction.
col_tip.s_shrunk: s′ = s × factor: the item similarity after significance weighting - used to rank and in the prediction.
col_tip.rating: r(u, t): the neighbour's rating of the target item; a neighbour must have rated t.
col_tip.rating_uj: r(a, j): the active user's rating of this item.
col_tip.mean: mean(u): the neighbour's mean rating over all their ratings - the centre of the deviation r(u, t) − mean(u).
col_tip.item_mean: mean(j): this item's mean rating over all its raters.
col_tip.status: What became of this candidate: kept as a neighbour, or why not (beyond k, w ≤ 0, too few co-rated ...).
col_tip.rank_raw: Rank by the raw similarity w, before significance weighting (1 = most similar).
col_tip.rank: Rank by the weighted similarity w′ (1 = best); the k best become the neighbours. ▲ / ▼ marks a move against the raw rank.
col_tip.c_shared_terms: shared terms: how many terms this item has in common with the target (the terms both profiles hold) - the cosine is built from them.
col_tip.term: The term: a word of one of the film's fields, written with the field's prefix in the profile (kw:heist, genre:Crime).
col_tip.field: The field the term comes from; one word in two fields is two terms.
col_tip.tf: tf: how often the term occurs in the film's field. A tag is there or not, so tf = 1 for genres, keywords, themes and people (a name credited twice in the cast is the rare exception); only the overview text can repeat a word (the overview and the tagline are counted together, so a word in both has tf = 2). The column shows the raw count whatever the damping: the damping changes x, not this column.
col_tip.tf_sqrt: √tf: the damped count that enters x; the square root tames a word that repeats many times (√1 = 1, so tags are unchanged).
col_tip.tf_log: 1 + ln tf: the damped count that enters x; the logarithm tames repeats and the added 1 keeps a single occurrence at 1 (ln 1 = 0 would erase every tag).
col_tip.df: df: in how many films of the dataset the term occurs.
col_tip.idf: idf = ln(N_field ÷ df): the term's rarity - the rarer, the larger. N_field is the number of films that carry the field at all (the coverage chip).
col_tip.g: g(t) = a − Gini(t), with a = {a}: this user's supervised weight of the term. Gini(t) is how mixed the user's rated films that carry the term are between liked and disliked (0 = the term sorts them perfectly, 0.5 = not at all), so g runs from a − 0.5 (useless) to a (decisive); a term none of the user's films carries gets a − 0.5. It multiplies x.
col_tip.tfidf_weight: x = field weight × damp(tf) × idf × g(t): the term's weight in the film's profile, the number in the Profile matrix. With raw damping damp(tf) = tf, and without the Gini weighting g(t) = 1, so x = field weight × tf × idf.
col_tip.preference: p(t): how much the user likes films that carry this term - above zero for terms of films rated above their mean, below zero for the others.
col_tip.weight_in_film: x(t): this term's weight in the target film's profile (field weight × damp(tf) × idf × g(t); see the TF-IDF tab).
col_tip.profile_contribution: p·x share: what this term adds to the score, p(t)·x(t) ÷ (|p| |x|). The shares of all terms add up to the score.
col_tip.sim_part: adds to s: the part of the cosine that comes from the terms of this field that both films hold - the sum of (target weight × candidate weight) over them, ÷ (length of the target's profile × length of the candidate's). The parts of all fields add up to the candidate's similarity s.
col_tip.shared_terms: shared terms: the terms of this field that the candidate and the target film both hold (the first few are listed) - the ones that make the part.
col_tip.pred_contribution: s·r ÷ Σs: what this neighbour adds to the prediction - its similarity times the user's rating of it, over the sum of the similarities. The shares of all neighbours add up to the predicted rating.
col_tip.df_u: df(u): in how many of the films the user rated (the target left out) the term occurs.
col_tip.p_like: P(liked): of those films, the share the user liked (rating at or above the threshold the step names).
col_tip.gini: Gini = 1 − (P² + (1 − P)²): how mixed the films that carry the term are between liked and disliked. 0 = the term sorts them perfectly, 0.5 = not at all; lower is better.
col_tip.entropy: Entropy = −Σ P log₂ P over liked / disliked: the same question in bits. 0 = pure, 1 = an even split; lower is better.
col_tip.chi2: χ²: how far the counts (term present or absent × liked or disliked) are from what chance would give. Larger = the term is more tied to liking.
col_tip.dev: Dev = |μ⁺ − μ⁻| ÷ σ: how far apart the mean ratings are of the films with the term and without it, in standard deviations of the user's ratings. Larger is better.
col_tip.topk_film: A film the user has not rated: in the list after MMR re-ranking, or one that has just left it.
col_tip.rank_before: Place in the relevance list (1 = the highest score).
col_tip.rank_after: Place in the list after MMR re-ranking; empty for a film that left the list.
col_tip.rel: rel: the relevance MMR mixes - the score (taste profile), or the predicted rating rescaled to 0-1 (kNN item similarity).
col_tip.penalty: penalty: this film's largest cosine to a film already placed above it, i.e. how much it would repeat what the list already shows. MMR takes (1 - λ) × penalty off the film's relevance, so a film whose look-alike is already listed drops a few places and a different kind of film comes up: the list shows the breadth of the taste, not five variations of its top film. 0 for the first place.
col_tip.penalised_by: penalised by: the listed film this one resembles most - the source of its penalty. Read it as "the list already has this one's look-alike": with that film above it, this film counts as repetition and yields its place to something different. Empty when it resembles no listed film.
col_tip.mmr_value: MMR = λ × rel − (1 − λ) × penalty: what the film scored in the round it was placed (a film that left: in the last round).
col_tip.moved: What the re-ranking did to the film against the relevance list: ▲ up, ▼ down, = same, + entered the list, − left it.
col_tip.weight: w_t: how much one unit of term t moves this user's predicted rating, learned from their rated films with ridge penalty α; positive raises, negative lowers.
col_tip.effect: The network's output for a film made of this term alone (term weight 1, nothing else): positive raises this user's predicted rating, negative lowers it. Not a share of a prediction: the network is not additive, so the terms of a film do not add up.
col_tip.model_contribution: w_t × x_{it}: this term's share of the prediction for the target film.
col_tip.df_user: In how many of the user's films the term occurs.
col_tip.alpha: The ridge penalty: larger α shrinks every weight towards 0 (safer with few films), smaller α fits the films more closely (and the noise).
col_tip.hybrid_base: The recommender: the method of an earlier page (its badge and name say which), with that page's defaults, fitted on the training part of the ratings only. The link opens that page for this user and film.
col_tip.hybrid_n_fallback:
Fallbacks: held-out pairs the base could not answer on its own.
What this lab sends then:
• the user's own mean rating (the neighbourhood methods)
• the mean training rating (the content method)
The factorization model always has an answer.
Alternatives a system could send instead:
• the user's mean within the film's genres
• the film's mean
• the global mean
• a popularity prior
• no prediction at all, leaving the pair to the other bases
col_tip.hybrid_rmse_alone: RMSE alone: the root mean squared error of this base's own predictions on the held-out ratings - how well it does without the blend (lower is better).
col_tip.hybrid_fit_ms: Fit time in milliseconds, on the training part of the ratings.
col_tip.alpha_equal: Equal weight: every base counts the same (1/q) - where the descent starts. The β₀ row is the intercept of that start.
col_tip.alpha_gd: The weight after the gradient steps: where the descent has got to (the last row of the trajectory).
col_tip.alpha_ridge: The closed-form weight: the exact minimum of the same loss with the ridge penalty - where the descent is heading.
col_tip.hybrid_step: The gradient step (0 = the equal start).
col_tip.alpha_of: α for {base}: the weight the blend gives to the prediction of the {base} recommender, after this step.
col_tip.alpha_sum: Σα: the weights added up - 1 for a weighted average (the descent walks that plane), anything else for free weights.
