trace.cb_profile_info:
How to read the taste profile: the top row is the user's taste profile p - one number for each term of the target film; the second row is the film's own weights x (tf × idf × field weight, the same numbers as the first tab). A term that the user's well-rated films carry has p above zero, a term their poorly rated films carry has p below zero; the sign is in the figure and in the hue (the two hues of the centred sub-matrix on the user- and item-based pages), the strength is the size.
The score is the cosine of the two rows, Σ p·x ÷ (|p| |x|). It lies between −1 and 1 and it is a SCORE, not a rating: it says how closely the film matches what the user likes. Turning it into a rating would need a regression model on top of it; the lab stops at the score. The table under the rows breaks the score into its terms - each term's share p·x ÷ (|p| |x|), the largest effect first - and the shares add up to the score, so it says why the film scored what it did.
## How to present it
1. **Build p.** Take every film the user rated except the target; centre each rating on the user's mean rating; weight the film's term vector by that difference; add them up and divide by the sum of the differences' sizes. Liked films pull their terms up, disliked ones pull theirs down.
2. **Compare with the film.** One cosine between p and the film's vector: the score.
3. **Read the table.** The terms at the top moved the score most, up or down; a term whose p is near zero did not matter.
## If asked
- **Why not a rating?** The score compares two vectors; putting it on the 1-5 scale needs a model fitted to the user's ratings, which the lab does not build.
- **Why is the target's own rating left out?** It is the answer the walk predicts; with it in, the profile would already know it.
- **What if the user rated nothing else?** There is no profile to build: the tab says so and the walk goes on without it.
trace.cb_tfidf_info:
How to read the TF-IDF table: it lists the target film's terms - the words of its description that the profile keeps. tf is how often the term occurs in the film's field (a tag is there or not, so 1; the words of the overview can repeat). df is in how many films of the dataset the term occurs. idf = ln(N_field ÷ df) is the term's rarity: N_field is the number of films that carry the field at all (the coverage chip says it), and the logarithm turns "rare" into a larger number without letting a one-off dominate. The weight x = field weight × damp(tf) × idf × g(t) is the number in the first row of the Profile matrix: the same table, read sideways. With √tf or 1 + ln tf a column shows the damped count that enters x; with the Gini weighting a g(t) column shows the user's term weight; x is always the product of the columns to its left (the damped count in place of tf), times the field weight. A word that appears in two fields is two terms (kw:heist, txt:heist), because the prefix keeps the fields apart.
## How to present it
1. **A film becomes a list of terms.** Its genres, keywords, people and, if you tick it, the text of its overview.
2. **Rare terms say more.** "Drama" is on most films and says little; "heist" is on few and says a lot: that is idf.
3. **Weight = damp(tf) × idf × g(t), with damp(tf) = tf and g = 1 unless you switch them on** (times the field's own weight from the Parameters panel). Two films are then compared by the cosine of their weight lists.
## If asked
- **Why a logarithm?** It softens rarity: a term in 1 film of 100 is not 100 times as informative as one in all 100.
- **Why is there no smoothing?** Every term in the table occurs in at least one film, so df is never 0 and idf never divides by zero; the table shows the plain formula.
trace.cb_features_info:
How to read the Feature selection table: it scores every term of the films the user rated (the target film left out) by how well it tells the films the user LIKED (rating at or above the threshold the step names) from the rest. df(u) is in how many of those films the term occurs and P(liked) the share of them the user liked. Gini and entropy measure how mixed those films are (0 = the term sorts them perfectly; lower is better); χ² and Dev measure how far the liked and the disliked films differ (larger is better). The table is sorted in two groups: the terms that occur in at least two of the user's films come first (lowest Gini, then the most films, then the largest Dev), the terms seen in one film follow. A term in one film always has Gini 0 - the film has it or not, and it is the only one - which is no evidence: one film cannot tell a signal from an accident. In this lab the scores EXPLAIN which terms carry the user's taste; the profile and the similarity are built from all terms either way.
## How to present it
1. **Which words explain this user's taste?** A term in several liked films and in no disliked one (P(liked) = 1, Gini 0) is a good clue.
2. **A term that is in every film tells nothing:** it has no "absent" side, so its scores are undefined (—).
3. **It needs both sides:** at least 2 liked and 2 disliked films, and ratings that are not all equal. Otherwise the tab says why.
## If asked
- **Does this change the recommendation?** Not here: it explains. Weighting the terms with it (a − Gini) is an option of the engine that this page does not draw.
- **Why is the target film left out?** Its rating is what we try to predict; the scores must not see it.
trace.cb_topk_info:
How to read the top-K view: the page asks the content-based model another question - not "what would this user rate the film?" but "which K films would you put at the top of their list?". Every film the user has not rated gets a number (the score of the taste profile, or the rating the item-similarity walk predicts), the films are sorted by it and the first K are the relevance list. That list is then re-ranked with MMR (maximal marginal relevance): each place goes to the film with the highest λ × relevance − (1 − λ) × penalty, where the penalty is the film's largest cosine to a film already placed. The table at the lower right is that second list: the place before and after, the relevance MMR mixed, the penalty, the film it resembled and what moved. The summary bar's ILS (intra-list similarity, the mean cosine between every two films of a list) says how much more varied the second list is - lower means more varied - and its changes chip counts the films the re-ranking moved, brought in or dropped.
## How to present it
1. **Rank first.** The sorted list is what a plain recommender returns.
2. **Then diversify.** A list of near-duplicates is a poor recommendation: MMR gives up a little relevance for variety, and λ is the dial (1 = no change, 0 = variety only).
3. **Read the table row by row.** A film that "entered" was too far down the relevance list to make it, but is unlike what was already placed; one that "left" was too similar to a film placed above it.
4. **Turn the dial.** Keep the user and K and compare λ = 1.0 (nothing changes), 0.9 and 0.7: the changes chip and the ILS move with it.
## If asked
- **Is the taste-profile score a rating?** No: it is a cosine in [−1, 1] that orders films. Turning it into a rating takes a regression model.
- **Why do so many films move?** When the scores lie close together (the taste-profile scores often do), a small penalty is enough to reorder many places. Raise λ to keep more of the relevance order and watch the ILS change.
- **Can the ILS go up after MMR?** Occasionally. The ILS is a mean over the films in the list, so putting the same films in another order never changes it, and MMR penalises a film by its single most similar listed film, not by the average: a swap that removes one close pair can still add a few mild ones. "Lower is more varied" holds as a rule, not as a guarantee.
- **Does it depend on the method?** Yes: item similarity ranks by the predicted rating (rescaled to 0-1 for MMR), the taste profile by its score. The two numbers are never mixed with each other.

This model sees only this user's history: the features of the films they rated and their own ratings - nothing from any other user. That is the sense in which a black box can be user-specific: the box is trained per user, from that history alone, and asked about a new film's features.
A film made only of terms the user never rated scores exactly their mean: the model has nothing to say about it.

trace.dnn_features_guide:
## The idea
A feature-combination hybrid: one network over ids and content. It reads everything at once: who the user is (an id), what the film is (its terms, year and popularity), what the user likes (a taste profile built from their own training ratings) and how they rate (count, mean, spread). There is no separate recommender - the content is just more input to a single learner. In the lecture's tree this is the monolithic hybrid, the feature-combination type.
## What each part adds
- **ids (embeddings).** A learned list of numbers per user and per film: what the ratings alone say. A film with few ratings has a barely trained list.
- **Content tower.** The film's terms (genres, keywords, themes) squeezed into a short vector: what the film is about, known before anyone rates it.
- **Profile tower.** The same for the user: what they like, in the film's own terms.
- **Numbers.** The film's year and popularity, the user's rating count, mean and spread: straight into the join.
- **Join and MLP.** The pieces are laid side by side and the dense layers mix them. This is the only place the parts meet: there is no separate dot product.
## Reading the diagram
The inputs are at the top, the user's side on the left and the film's on the right; each column runs down its own tower, they all meet at the join, the MLP below it mixes them and the output at the bottom is the rating. The user's statistics and the film's numbers have no tower: they enter the join from the side. A box shows its name, its width (n), its activation and |θ|, the number of parameters in it; hover it for what it does and what switching it off does. “n” is how many numbers a box holds (“16 of 2000” where only some of them are non-zero for this pair). The small bars are the box's first six values for this user and this film - the two wide inputs show their six largest - and the Values tab lists them as numbers, stage by stage.
## The comparison with the ids-only network
Switch every group except ids off and you get the ids-only network: the same network with no content at all. Its error per epoch - training and validation - is the pair of faint dashed lines on the training curve (a stored network without its history shows only its final validation error, one dashed line). A validation line below it means the content helps. For a film with few ratings the ids carry almost nothing, and the content is all the network has.
## Reading the training curve
One epoch is one pass over the training ratings. The training error keeps falling; the validation error falls and then stops improving. Early stopping ends the run when it has not improved for Patience epochs and keeps the weights of the BEST epoch (the dotted line). The caption under the chart says how the run ended.
## The foil beside the right way
Switch early stopping off and the run goes on to its epoch budget: the training error keeps falling while the validation error rises - that is overfitting - and the last epoch's weights predict. The page names where the usual practice would have stopped.
## Why these training settings
- **Learning rate 0.001** — the size of every update step. Alternative: 0.01, the neural page's default, with everything else unchanged: the error reaches 0.851 at epoch 3 and then jumps about (0.877, 0.882, 0.858, 0.880, 0.864) — the steps are too large to settle, and even the training error wobbles; with the neural page's whole recipe (batches of 16, no regularisation) the jump went from 0.850 to 0.928. 0.0003: the same best error (0.845) at the same epoch (5) and a tail as flat — the descent only starts higher (0.893 against 0.864 after the first epoch) and runs without a wobble.
- **Batch size 128** — the ratings averaged into one update. Alternative: 16, the default of the neural page: a noisier gradient and eight times more updates per epoch (a fit took 209 s instead of 58 s); 512: the same best error (0.846, at epoch 3) in 34 s with a quarter of the updates — the first epoch lands higher (0.888 against 0.864) and after the best epoch the validation error creeps up steadily (0.846, 0.847, 0.850, 0.853, 0.857) instead of staying flat.
- **Weight decay 0.0001** — at every update each weight is pulled a little towards zero (L2), so no single rating can be memorised by one large weight. Alternative: almost none (0.00001, dropout off): the validation error starts rising right after the best epoch (0.843 → 0.871 in five epochs with the same rate and batch); ten times more (0.001): the same validation error (0.847 against 0.845) and a tail as flat (0.849–0.855 over the five epochs after the best one), while the training error stays higher (0.760 against 0.732 at the best epoch) — the stronger pull mostly holds the network back from the training ratings.
- **Dropout 0.1** — at every update one hidden unit in ten of the MLP layers is switched off, so no unit can rely on a particular other one. Alternative: 0: slightly faster learning and earlier overfitting (0.843 → 0.871 with weight decay 0.00001); 0.5: both errors stay higher (validation 0.853 against 0.845, training 0.786 against 0.732 at the best epoch) — with half of the units off at every update too little of the network is left to learn the ratings.
- **Early stopping, patience 5** — after every epoch the error on the validation tail is measured; five epochs without an improvement of at least 0.0001 end the run, and the weights of the best epoch are kept. Alternative: off (the foil beside it on the page): the run uses its whole budget and the last epoch predicts — at 60 epochs the validation error is 0.914 against 0.845 at the best epoch while the training error keeps falling (0.732 → 0.546); patience 2 would have stopped this very run at epoch 4 and kept epoch 2 (0.846), one step short of the minimum at epoch 5 (0.845): a wobble between neighbouring epochs (0.848, 0.855) looks like the end of the descent.
- **Epoch budget 30** — the most epochs a run may use; early stopping ends it earlier (at epoch 10 on the lecture data). Alternative: 60 without early stopping is the foil.
- **Validation tail 10 %** — each user's newest ratings (users with at least five ratings), carved out before training starts; the held-out pair of the walk and the test ratings never decide when training stops.
## If asked
- **Why one network and not a blend of recommenders?** A blend (the weighted hybrid) combines finished predictions; here the ratings and the content are inputs of one learner, so it can learn how they go together.
- **Where is the interaction?** After the join: the MLP mixes the user's and the film's numbers. There is no explicit user-film product in this network.
- **What is a tower?** A small sub-network for one kind of input; it shortens that input to a few numbers before the join.
- **What does a bigger embedding or a wider layer do?** More capacity: the network fits the training ratings more closely and overfits sooner when ratings are few.
- **What changes for a brand-new film?** Its id list is untrained, but its content row is complete: the content tower still has something to say.

trace.hybrid_info_switch_bases_label: About the bases and the split
trace.hybrid_info_switch_bases:
How to read the Bases tab: a switching hybrid does not blend, it lets ONE recommender answer. The recommenders are the lab's own: user-based kNN (uCF), item-based kNN (iCF), matrix factorization (MF) and content-based item similarity (CB), each with its default settings. What decides which one answers is how each did on ratings of THIS user that no recommender had seen: the newest share of the user's own ratings (a quarter by default, the course's rule of thumb is a quarter to a third; at most a fixed number) is held out, and the recommenders are fitted on everything else, every other user's ratings included. The target film's own rating is hidden from all of it. The held-out table shows each held-out rating next to what every recommender predicted for it, and how often a recommender had nothing to go on and answered with its own fallback (no neighbour had rated the film, so it says the user's mean).
## How to present it
1. **Hold the user's newest ratings out.** The choice is about one student, so the evidence is that student's own ratings; everyone else's, the newest included, stay in training.
2. **Fit the recommenders on what is left.** None of them sees a held-out rating or the target.
3. **Read the table.** Each row is a rating the recommenders have not seen: the film, the true rating and one answer per recommender.
## If asked
- **Why only this user's ratings?** A bucket of models chooses per user - the winner changes from student to student - so the evidence has to be the user's own.
- **Why the newest ratings?** Time order is what a deployed recommender faces: trained on the past, asked about the future.
- **Is a held-out rating really unseen?** By the recommenders and the choice, yes: it is out of training. But the lab's split is per user, not one cut in time: another user's LATER rating of the same film stays in training and can help predict it. A single global date would be stricter; this page does not use one.
- **Why do the neighbourhood recommenders so often answer with the mean?** On a small class data set most films were rated by one person; with nobody to compare with they fall back to the user's mean. Matrix factorization and the content recommender always have an answer.
- **How is this split different from the weighted walk's?** Only the active student's newest ratings are held out; everyone else's, the newest included, stay in training. In the weighted walk every user's newest ratings are held out, because the weights are learned on all of them.
trace.hybrid_info_switch_board:
How to read the Leaderboard tab: every recommender's misses on the held-out ratings, two ways. MAE is the average size of a miss; RMSE squares the misses before it averages and takes the root, so a few large misses count for more. The lecture's criterion is the lowest MSE or MAE; the page picks the winner by the error set in the parameters (RMSE by default, which ranks the recommenders like MSE) and shows both. The foil picks the winner on the training ratings instead: the recommender that memorised them wins. In the cold-start rule's walk the same two errors are shown for the two recommenders alone, next to the rule's own: the rule helps only if it beats both.
## How to present it
1. **Score every recommender** on the held-out ratings, one row at a time.
2. **Rank them.** The lowest error wins; a tie keeps the order of the list.
3. **Check the margin.** A runner-up a hair behind is a close call, and a handful of held-out ratings cannot tell them apart: the notes say so.
## If asked
- **Is the winner the best recommender?** The best on THESE ratings of this user. With few held-out ratings one more or fewer can change the winner.
- **Why both MAE and RMSE?** They weigh the misses differently; when they disagree about the winner, a note says so.
- **Does the winner stay the same for every user?** No, that is the point of a bucket of models: save the walk for several students and compare.
- **What does the foil change?** It picks the winner on the training ratings, which every recommender has already learned from: the one that memorised them wins. The right way picks on the held-out ratings.
- **How does the cold-start rule choose?** Per pair, not per user: the collaborative base answers when it has neighbours for the pair, the content base otherwise. This is the cold-start lesson.
trace.hybrid_info_switch_answer:
How to read the Answer tab: every recommender's answer about the target film and which one counts. A bucket of models chooses once for the user, so the winner answers whatever the film: it never looks at the film, only at the user's history. The cold-start rule chooses per film: the collaborative recommender answers when it found enough neighbours for the film, the content recommender when it did not. The number is an offline estimate: the film's real rating was kept out of everything, so the error is honest, but a better error offline does not guarantee a better result with real users.
## How to present it
1. **Ask every recommender** about the target film.
2. **Take the chosen one's answer.** The others are shown only to compare.
3. **Compare with the truth.** The rating was hidden from all of it.
## If asked
- **What if the winner has nothing to go on for this film?** It answers with its own fallback, the user's mean, and a note says so: a switch on the user cannot see the film. The cold-start rule exists for exactly that case.
- **Why not blend?** That is the weighted hybrid: it learns one weight per recommender. A switch keeps one recommender and drops the rest.
- **Does switching beat always using the best single recommender?** The winner's prediction for the target is the page's answer. In this cohort the bucket does not beat always-MF: the rule's gain is at the noise level; switching earns its keep in cold start.
trace.hybrid_info_switch_switches:
How to read the switches: each one shows a way to do the choice WRONG next to the right way, on the same screen. The winner of a bucket of models must be picked on ratings the recommenders have not seen; picked on the user's TRAINING ratings (the switch for it) it favours the recommender that memorised them, and the walk names the winner of the right way beside it. The criterion switch (RMSE or MAE) changes how misses are weighed, not the protocol. The cold-start rule has settings of its own: which collaborative recommender, and how many neighbours are enough.
## How to present it
1. **Flip one switch at a time** and watch the choice step and the notes.
2. **Keep the right way in view:** the foil's sentence names the right way next to it.
## If asked
- **Which setting is the usual practice?** The defaults: the winner picked on held-out ratings, by RMSE (MAE is shown as well).
trace.title_hybrid_weighted: Weighted hybrid: learned blend of base recommenders
trace.hybrid_info_bases:
How to read the Recommenders tab: a weighted hybrid is a parallel ensemble - several recommenders predict the same rating independently, and a final step weighs their answers. The recommenders here are the lab's own: user-based kNN (uCF), item-based kNN (iCF), matrix factorization (MF) and content-based item similarity (CB), each with its default settings. The table lists, for each, how many held-out ratings it had nothing to go on for (a fallback: no neighbour had rated the film, so it answered with the user's mean), its error alone on the held-out ratings and how long it took to fit.
The weights need ratings the recommenders have never seen. So the newest part of every user's ratings is held out first (at most a fixed number per user, so that one very active user cannot supply most of them) and the recommenders are fitted on the rest; the target film's own rating is hidden from everything. The held-out table shows each held-out rating next to what every recommender predicted for it.
## How to present it
1. **Hold out first.** The weights must be learned on ratings no recommender trained on; otherwise the one that memorised its training ratings would look best.
2. **Fit the recommenders on what is left.** None of them sees a held-out rating or the target.
3. **Read the table.** Each row is a rating nobody had seen: the film, the true rating and one prediction per recommender.
## If asked
- **Why the newest ratings?** Time order is what a deployed recommender faces: it is trained on the past and asked about the future. A random hold-out would let the future leak into the training part.
- **Why do some recommenders fall back so often?** On a small class data set most films were rated by one person: a neighbourhood method has nobody to compare with and answers with the user's mean. Matrix factorization always has an answer.
- **Is the blend fitted on the training ratings too?** Only with the switch for it, as a labelled foil: the weights then trust whichever recommender memorised the training ratings.
- **Is a held-out rating really unseen?** By the recommenders and the weights, yes: it is out of training. But the lab's split is per user, not one cut in time: another user's LATER rating of the same film stays in training and can help predict it. A single global date would be stricter; this page does not use one.
trace.hybrid_info_weights:
How to read the Weights tab: the blend is r̂ = β₀ + Σ α_b · r̂_b, one weight α_b per recommender and an intercept β₀. The weights start equal (1/q each) and are then moved to where the error on the held-out ratings is smallest. The curve is that error after each gradient step: the descent measures how the error changes with each weight (the gradient) and moves the weights a little against it. The step size is one over the largest curvature of the loss - the largest step that is still stable. By default the weights are held to add up to 1, so the blend is a weighted average and the descent walks the plane where they do. An average cannot move the LEVEL of the recommenders' predictions, so the blend carries an intercept: for any weights the best β₀ is the mean residual, the average amount by which the blend misses the held-out ratings (signed), so it is set again after every step instead of being stepped. The small penalty λ (ridge) pulls the weights gently towards equal weights and keeps them steady when the held-out data is thin; it never touches the intercept.
The closed form gets to the end in one solve (the "regression alternative"): the weights that minimise the same loss, by a Lagrange system on the table with a column of ones added (its weight is the intercept) when they must add up to 1. The three flat lines on the curve are the equal start (with its intercept), the closed form and the best single recommender. When the descent has reached the closed form the two agree.
## How to present it
1. **Start equal.** Every recommender counts the same.
2. **Descend.** Each step moves the weights against the gradient and the error falls.
3. **Check with the closed form.** One solve gives where the descent is heading.
4. **Compare.** The blend should beat the best recommender alone; sometimes it does not, and the page says so.
## If asked
- **Why must the weights add up to 1?** Then the blend is an average of the recommenders' predictions and stays on the rating scale, and the intercept does the one thing an average cannot: shift the level. The textbook's free recipe (no constraint, no intercept) makes the weights rescale the level themselves; the note under the comparison says what they would add up to.
- **Why an intercept?** The held-out ratings are each user's newest, and the recommenders learned from the older ones: if the level drifted in between, they all sit above (or below) the held-out ratings together, and no weighted average of them can follow. The comparison step separates what the intercept earns from what the learned weights earn.
- **Is the intercept right for every film?** It is one number, learned on the newest ratings and applied to every target - also to a film the user rated long ago. If the level drifted, that favours the newest period.
- **Can a weight be negative?** Yes: a recommender that is wrong in a systematic way is subtracted to correct the others. A note says when it happens.
- **Why a penalty?** With few held-out ratings and recommenders that resemble each other, plain least squares swings; the penalty keeps the weights steady. λ = 0 is the switch that shows the swing.
- **Why can the descent be slower than the closed form?** The loss is flat along some directions (recommenders that are alike): descent creeps there, the closed form jumps.
trace.hybrid_info_blend:
How to read the Blend tab: the target film's predictions of the recommenders, each multiplied by its weight, added up and shifted by the intercept. The table shows every recommender's prediction, its weight, what it adds (the intercept's share last), and whether it answered with its own fallback (no neighbour had rated the film). A recommender that fell back says nothing about this film; the blend then leans on the others.
The number is an offline estimate: the recommenders were fitted on the training part only, the weights learned on held-out ratings they never saw, and the target's own rating was hidden from all of it. A production system would refit the recommenders on all the ratings before applying the weights. A better error offline does not guarantee a better result with real users.
## How to present it
1. **Ask each recommender.** Each one answers about the target film on its own.
2. **Weigh and add.** The weights learned on the held-out ratings say how much each answer counts.
3. **Compare with the truth.** The film's real rating was kept out of everything: the error is honest.
## If asked
- **Does the blend always win?** No. It beats the best single recommender only when the recommenders make different mistakes; the notes say how this blend fared.
- **Why does one weight vector serve every user?** One global set of weights, learned on all users' held-out ratings, is steady; a set per user would rest on a few dozen ratings.
- **What if a recommender has no answer?** It answers with its own fallback, the user's mean; the table flags it.
trace.hybrid_info_switches:
How to read the switches: each one shows a way to do the blend WRONG next to the right way, on the same screen. Equal weights are only the start; learned weights are what the held-out ratings call for. Weights fitted on the TRAINING ratings (the switch for it) trust the recommenders that memorised those ratings: the error on the ratings they were fitted on looks better, on the held-out ratings it is worse than with weights fitted on held-out ratings. A penalty of 0 (plain least squares) lets the weights swing with the noise of a small held-out set; the default keeps a small penalty. Free weights without an intercept (the textbook's recipe, the constraint switch) rescale the level of the predictions through their sum; the usual practice keeps the sum at 1 and lets an intercept correct the level - the comparison step shows both.
## How to present it
1. **Flip one switch at a time** and watch the comparison step and the notes.
2. **Keep the right way in view:** every foil sentence names the right way next to it.
## If asked
- **Which setting is the usual practice?** The defaults: weights learned on held-out ratings, a small ridge penalty, weights that add up to 1 with an intercept.

params.title: Parameters
params.sim_group_icf_other: Other measures: not centred by the user's mean
params.measure_icf_note: On item-based pages the measure compares two items' rating vectors (over the users who rated both) instead of two users'.
params.icf_mc_note: In item-based CF the mean convention applies to the item means (item-centred fault, generic measures); the user-centred adjusted cosine always uses each user's own mean, the active user's without the target.
params.cf_any: shares a genre with the target
params.cf_all: carries every genre of the target
params.filter_note: An attribute filter restricts the ratings the SIMILARITY sees (reduction-based pre-filtering, D7); who is eligible and the prediction baseline still come from the whole matrix. Global mean: every centre over all of a user's or item's ratings; segment mean: over the ratings inside the filter.
params.fields_none: Tick at least one field first: the item profiles are built from the fields.
params.weights_zero: Give at least one ticked field a weight above 0: with every weight at 0 there is no profile.
params.hybrid_bases_min: Tick at least two bases: a blend of one is no blend.
params.hybrid_note: Every base is fitted on the ratings the split leaves for training; the weights are fitted on the held-out entries; the target film's rating is in neither. The two choices that would flatter the blend - weights fitted on the training entries, and the textbook's free weights (no constraint, no intercept) that rescale the level themselves - stand beside the right way, labelled.
params.hybrid_sw_note: The recommenders are fitted on every rating but the active user's newest ones and the target film's; the bucket's winner is picked on those newest ratings. The choice that would flatter a recommender - the winner picked on the training ratings it has already learned from - stands beside the right way, labelled. The cold-start rule has no winner: it chooses per film, by how many neighbours the collaborative recommender found.
params.min_cf_neighbours: Min CF neighbours to trust it
params.cb_note: Content similarity (TF-IDF cosine) is never negative, so there is no similarity/mean-convention/denominator/keep-negative choice to make here.
params.mf_note: The target rating is hidden and the model is refitted for this pair (a factor model is global). Early stopping uses only a validation tail of the training ratings; when that tail would be tiny it is skipped and the epoch budget applies.
params.early_stopping: Early stopping (usual practice; off = teaching foil)
params.dnn_note: Rating regression with MSE. The traced forward pass is recomputed in plain numpy from the weights and matches the network to 1e-12 on the CPU (float64).
params.model_global_tip: The model is global: its parameters (for the factor models one P, one Q and the biases) are learned from all ratings together; there is no model per user. In the lesson's honest mode the chosen pair's own rating is hidden and the model is trained again without it, so every new pair with a rated film costs one training run. A film the user has not rated needs no refit: a stored model answers at once.
params.model_source_tip: Where the model of the next trace comes from: one fitted beforehand on every rating of the dataset (pretrained), or trained now for this request. Nothing pressed is automatic: the stored model answers wherever it may, otherwise the model is trained. Press a choice to fix it, press it again to hand it back to automatic.
params.model_source_tip_pretrained: Use the model fitted beforehand on every rating of this dataset. It answers top-K lists and films this user has not rated; a film the user has rated is always answered by a model trained without that rating.
params.model_source_tip_fit: Train the model now for this request, as the walk-through always did. It takes seconds on the class data and minutes on a large dataset.
params.model_source_tip_auto_pretrained: Automatic uses the stored model here. Press to fix the choice, then Apply.
params.model_source_tip_auto_fit: Automatic trains the model here. Press to fix the choice, then Apply.
params.model_source_tip_refit: A film this user has rated is the held-out cell: a model that has seen its rating cannot answer for it, so the model is trained again without it, whatever is chosen here. Films the user has not rated, and top-K lists, may use the stored model.
params.model_source_tip_ease: EASE is not stored: its closed form is a dense items × items matrix, far larger than the other models.
params.model_source_tip_missing: No model is stored for these settings on this dataset. Fit one beforehand and it appears here.
params.model_source_state_ease: trained for each trace (EASE is not stored)
params.model_source_state_missing: no stored model for these settings
params.model_source_auto_tip: Nothing is pressed: the page picks the source itself - the stored model where it may answer, training where it must. Press a choice to fix it, then Apply.

param_tip.groups: Which inputs the network reads. A group that is off is absent from the network (no zero vectors), so the parameter count changes. Effect: with every group except ids off you get the ids-only network, the comparison this page shows next to the full one; with ids off the network cannot tell one user or film from another by name, only by content and numbers. Default: all five on.
param_tip.group_ids: The user id and the film id, each looked up in an embedding table: a learned list of k numbers per user and per film. An id carries nothing by itself; its numbers are learned from the ratings. Effect: switch it off and the network cannot memorise a particular user or film, it can only generalise from content and numbers; a film with few ratings has a barely trained list here, which is where content helps.
param_tip.group_item_content: The film's TF-IDF row over the content fields (genres, keywords, themes), through the content tower. Catalogue data: the same for every user, no rating in it. Effect: switch it off and the network stops seeing what the film is about, and the content tower disappears from the diagram.
param_tip.group_item_numeric: The film's release year and how many training ratings it has (log), both standardised (0 = the average film): two numbers that go straight into the join. Effect: lets the network use how old and how widely rated a film is; off = it no longer sees them.
param_tip.group_user_profile: The user's taste profile over the same terms (Rocchio), built from their TRAINING ratings only: terms of films they rated above their own mean push up, terms of films below it push down. It goes through the profile tower. Effect: switch it off and the network stops seeing what this user likes in terms of content, and the profile tower disappears from the diagram.
param_tip.group_user_stats: The user's rating count (log), mean and spread over their training ratings, standardised (0 = the average user): three numbers that go straight into the join. Effect: lets the network know whether a user rates high or low and how widely; off = it no longer sees that.
param_tip.item_fields: Which film description fields the content row and the user profile are built from (comma list: genres, keywords, themes, ... the content page's field names). Effect: more fields = a richer, longer vocabulary (cut at Max terms); fewer = less for the towers to learn from. At least one. Default genres,keywords,themes.
param_tip.item_max_terms: The vocabulary is cut to this many terms (the most frequent ones); the film row and the user profile have exactly this width. Effect: larger = more terms visible and more parameters in the towers' first layer (terms × width), slower; smaller = rare terms are left out. Default: 2000; a whole number from 1.
param_tip.item_layers: The content tower: a small sub-network that squeezes the film's long content row (one TF-IDF number per term) into a short vector before it is joined with the rest. Widths of its dense layers, first layer first, e.g. 32,16 = 2000 terms → 32 → 16, ReLU after each. Effect: wider = more room to learn what the content says and many more parameters (the first layer costs terms × width); the LAST width is how many numbers the join receives from this tower. Default 32,16.
param_tip.user_layers: The profile tower: the same kind of sub-network over the user's taste profile (their Rocchio vector over the same terms). Widths of its dense layers, first layer first, e.g. 32,16 = terms → 32 → 16, ReLU after each. Effect: as the content tower - wider = more capacity and more parameters; the LAST width is how many numbers the join receives. Default 32,16.
param_tip.early_stopping: On (the usual practice): training stops after `patience` epochs without a validation improvement and the best epoch's weights predict. Off (the teaching foil): every epoch runs and the last epoch's weights predict - the curves part, the page still names where the usual practice would have stopped.
param_tip.net_architecture: Which network is built. Feature network (this page): the ids, the film's content, the user's taste profile and activity numbers go into ONE network. MLP: user and film embeddings joined and mixed by dense layers. GMF: the two embeddings multiplied element by element (the matrix factorization idea, no hidden layers). NeuMF: GMF and MLP side by side. Hybrid MLP: the MLP plus a small tower over the film's genres. Effect: decides which of the fields below exist. Default NeuMF; the feature-combination page opens on Feature network.
param_tip.net_embedding_size: Embedding size k: how many numbers describe each user and each film inside the network (the length of their embedding vectors; the diagram's embedding boxes show n = k). Effect: larger = more capacity and more parameters (the film table has one row of k numbers per film), so it fits the training ratings more closely and overfits sooner when ratings are few; smaller = coarser but steadier. Default 8; a whole number from 1.
param_tip.net_mlp_layers: The widths of the MLP's dense layers, first layer first, separated by commas (32,16 = a 32-unit layer, then a 16-unit layer; ReLU after each). The MLP sits after the join and mixes everything that went in; this mixing is where the network learns how who, what and content go together. Effect: wider or more layers can learn more complex interactions and overfit sooner; fewer or narrower = simpler and steadier. Default 32,16; at least one layer, every width at least 1.
param_tip.net_dropout: During training each unit of the MLP's hidden layers is switched off at random with this probability (the others are scaled up so the average stays the same); at prediction nothing is dropped. The towers and the embeddings are not dropped. A brake on overfitting. Effect: larger = a stronger brake but noisier, slower training; 0 = off. Default {dropout}; from 0 up to 0.9 in this box.
param_tip.net_optimizer: How the weights are changed from the gradient. Adam (default) scales the step of every weight by its own recent gradients; SGD takes the plain gradient step for all. Effect: the curves change shape, and with SGD the learning rate usually has to be tuned again.
param_tip.net_lr: Learning rate η: how far every weight moves at each update. Effect: too large and the validation error jumps around or rises; too small and training crawls and can run out of epochs while still improving (the curve caption then says so). Default {lr}; above 0.
param_tip.net_weight_decay: L2 penalty: every update also pulls each weight a little towards zero (the optimizer's weight decay; every weight of the network, embeddings included). Effect: larger = smoother, smaller weights and less overfitting, but too large underfits (both curves stay high); 0 = off. Default {weight_decay}; 0 or more.
param_tip.net_batch_size: How many training ratings go into each weight update. Effect: smaller = more updates per epoch, each noisier, so an epoch takes longer; larger = fewer, smoother updates per epoch. Default {batch_size}; a whole number from 1.
param_tip.net_init_std: Embeddings start as random numbers from a normal distribution with this standard deviation (seeded). The dense layers use PyTorch's default start rule and the output starts at the mean rating, so the untrained network predicts the average. Effect: a tiny value starts every user and film near the same point; a large one starts with more scatter. Default 0.1; above 0.
param_tip.net_device: Where the arithmetic runs: CPU (default; float64, so the traced forward pass matches a hand calculation to 1e-12), GPU (CUDA, when the machine has one) or auto (GPU if there is one, else CPU). Effect: speed only.
param_tip.net_clip: Clips the final prediction into the rating scale (the dataset's; 0.5–5 on the class data). Effect: changes only predictions that fall outside the scale. Off by default, so that an overshoot stays visible as a symptom. Default off.
param_tip.net_max_epochs: The most passes over the training ratings (one pass = one epoch); with early stopping on, training can end sooner. Effect: too few and the validation error is still falling when training ends (the curve caption says 'still improving'); more epochs only help while the validation error keeps improving. Default {max_epochs}; a whole number from 1.
param_tip.net_early_stopping: The validation share of each user's remaining ratings is held out to watch the error. Effect: on (the usual practice) = training stops when that error has not improved for Patience epochs in a row, and the weights of the BEST epoch predict; off (the teaching foil, shown beside the right way) = every epoch runs and the last epoch's weights predict - the training error keeps falling while the validation error rises, which is overfitting; the page still names where the usual practice would have stopped. Default on.
param_tip.net_patience: How many epochs in a row without a validation improvement are allowed before training stops (early stopping on). Effect: small = stops sooner and may stop on a small bump; large = waits longer, more epochs run. Default 5; a whole number from 1; unused while early stopping is off.
param_tip.net_valid_frac: The newest share of each user's remaining ratings (the target pair is in neither set) that is held out to watch the error: the validation set. Effect: larger = a steadier error curve but fewer ratings to train on; 0 = none, so early stopping has nothing to watch and is skipped (the epoch budget applies). A validation set under 20 ratings is skipped too. Default 0.1 (10 %); from 0 to below 1.
param_tip.net_seed: The random seed. It fixes the embeddings' start, the dense layers' start, the batch order and the dropout masks, so the same seed repeats a run exactly. Effect: another seed gives a different start and slightly different curves; compare seeds to see how much of a result is luck. Default 0; a whole number from 0.
param_tip.patience_es: Epochs without a validation improvement after which training stops (while early stopping is on).
param_tip.hidden_units: Units of the per-user network's one hidden layer (ReLU).
param_tip.reveal: When the held-out rating - the answer the walk predicts - shows.
param_tip.reveal_step: Reveal at the prediction step (the default): the held-out rating and the prediction stay hidden - as ? in the sub-matrix cell, in the Prediction / Actual / Error chips and in the picker chip - until the step that predicts it. Stepping back hides them again.
param_tip.reveal_start: Show from the start: the held-out rating, the prediction and the error are visible from the first step.
param_tip.reveal_hidden: Held out: shown at the prediction step. Switch the Held-out setting in the Parameters row to show it from the start.
param_tip.fields: Which columns of the film card become terms of its profile. Every term is written with its field's prefix, so the same word in two fields is two terms. The number beside a field is its weight: how much the field counts (1 by default, 0 switches it off, 2 doubles it).
param_tip.fields_all: Tick every field of the registry, or none; a square means a partial choice. Weights stay as they are.
param_tip.cb_alpha: The ridge penalty: larger α shrinks every weight towards 0 (safer with few films), smaller α fits the films more closely (and the noise).
param_tip.cb_kind: The kind of per-user model: a ridge regression (a linear model with a penalty) or a small neural network (one hidden layer, trained with Adam on this user's films alone).
param_tip.cb_kind_ridge: A linear model over the TF-IDF features, fitted in closed form with the penalty α.
param_tip.cb_kind_mlp: One hidden layer of units, trained with Adam for a fixed number of epochs from a fixed seed. It has no penalty α.
param_tip.hybrid_bases: Which recommenders are blended. Every base is fitted on the training part of the split and asked about the held-out entries; at least two are needed. Default: all four.
param_tip.hybrid_base_ucf: User-based collaborative filtering (the uCF page): a weighted average of the neighbours' ratings, with the lab's defaults.
param_tip.hybrid_base_icf: Item-based collaborative filtering (the iCF page), with the lab's defaults.
param_tip.hybrid_base_mf: Matrix factorization (FunkSVD), fitted once on the training part.
param_tip.hybrid_base_cb: Content-based filtering by item similarity (the content page's kNN item-similarity method), with the lab's defaults.
param_tip.hybrid_weights: Which weight vector predicts the target film: the closed-form (regression) solution, the weights after the gradient steps, or the equal start (1/q each, no learning). The walk shows all three; this choice is the one the blend uses.
param_tip.hybrid_w_ridge: The closed-form solution of the same loss (the regression alternative): the weights in one solve.
param_tip.hybrid_w_gd: The weights after the gradient steps, as far as the descent got.
param_tip.hybrid_w_equal: The start: equal shares (1/q each) plus the intercept of those shares. It is the foil - no learning of the weights - and the walk compares it with the learned weights.
param_tip.hybrid_constraint: Whether the weights add up to one. Adding up to one (the default) makes the blend a weighted average of the bases plus an intercept that absorbs the level of the predictions; free weights have no intercept - the textbook's recipe - and must rescale the level themselves.
param_tip.hybrid_c_sum: The weights add up to one, with an intercept that absorbs the level: a weighted average of the bases plus a constant. The descent walks along the plane where the weights sum to one, and the closed form is the constrained solution.
param_tip.hybrid_c_none: The textbook's free recipe: no constraint, no intercept. The weights alone must rescale the level of the predictions (the compare step says by how much).
param_tip.hybrid_fit_on: Where the weights are fitted. The held-out entries are the right way; the training entries are the foil, beside it.
param_tip.hybrid_fit_heldout: The right way: the newest ratings of each user, which no base was fitted on. The weights see how the bases do on ratings they have not seen.
param_tip.hybrid_fit_train: The foil: the ratings the bases were fitted on. Every base looks better there than on new ratings, so the weights trust the bases that overfit most; the error on the held-out entries is worse than the one the weights were fitted on.
param_tip.hybrid_holdout_frac: The newest share of each user's ratings that is held out for the weights (the lab's temporal rule). Default 0.2.
param_tip.hybrid_holdout_cap: At most this many held-out ratings per user (the newest); empty = no cap. Without a cap one user with thousands of ratings would supply most of the held-out entries, and the "global" weights would be that user's.
param_tip.hybrid_min_ratings: A user with fewer ratings keeps all of them for the bases and contributes no held-out entry.
param_tip.hybrid_gd_steps: How many gradient steps the walk shows (1 to 200). Default 30.
param_tip.hybrid_gd_scale: The step size as a multiple of one over the largest curvature of the loss. 1 corrects the steepest direction in a single step; 2 is the stability limit (the descent oscillates for ever); a smaller scale walks more slowly.
param_tip.hybrid_ridge: The penalty on the size of the weights. 0 is plain least squares (the foil: with few held-out ratings, or bases that agree with each other, the weights jump); the default 0.01 keeps them stable.
param_tip.hybrid_clip: Clips the blend to the rating scale (off by default, so that an overflow stays visible).
param_tip.hybrid_sw_rule: How ONE recommender is chosen. A bucket of models scores every recommender on the active user's own held-out ratings and lets the best one answer; the cold-start rule lets the collaborative recommender answer when it has enough neighbours for the film and the content recommender otherwise.
param_tip.hybrid_sw_rule_bucket: One winner for the user: the recommender with the lowest error on the user's newest held-out ratings answers, whatever the film.
param_tip.hybrid_sw_rule_neighbours: One choice per film: the collaborative recommender when it found at least the minimum number of neighbours for the film, the content recommender when it did not. The bases are then that collaborative recommender and the content one.
param_tip.hybrid_sw_bases: Which recommenders compete in the bucket. Every one is fitted on the training ratings and scored on the user's held-out ratings; at least two are needed. Default: all four.
param_tip.hybrid_sw_criterion: The error that ranks the recommenders. RMSE squares the misses before it averages, so big misses count more; MAE is the average size of a miss. The leaderboard shows both.
param_tip.hybrid_sw_cr_rmse: Root mean squared error: the course's usual choice; it ranks the recommenders like the mean squared error does.
param_tip.hybrid_sw_cr_mae: Mean absolute error: every miss counts by its size.
param_tip.hybrid_sw_cr_not_in_lab: Not in the lab: selection rules used in the literature. The lab picks the winner by held-out error (MAE or RMSE).
param_tip.hybrid_sw_select_on: Where the winner is picked. The user's held-out ratings are the right way; the training ratings are the foil, beside it.
param_tip.hybrid_sw_select_heldout: The right way: the user's newest ratings, which no recommender was fitted on. The winner is the one that predicts ratings it has not seen.
param_tip.hybrid_sw_select_train: The foil: a sample of the user's training ratings, which every recommender has already learned from. The one that memorised them looks best; the walk names the right way's winner beside it.
param_tip.hybrid_sw_cf_base: The collaborative recommender of the cold-start rule: item-based or user-based kNN. The content recommender is the other side.
param_tip.hybrid_sw_cf_icf: Item-based collaborative filtering (the iCF page), with the lab's defaults.
param_tip.hybrid_sw_cf_ucf: User-based collaborative filtering (the uCF page), with the lab's defaults.
param_tip.hybrid_sw_holdout: The newest share of the ACTIVE user's own ratings that is held out for the leaderboard (a quarter to a third is the course's rule of thumb). Default 0.25.
param_tip.hybrid_sw_holdout_cap: At most this many of the user's newest ratings are held out; empty = no cap. The older part of a longer share stays with the recommenders.
param_tip.hybrid_sw_min_ratings: A user with fewer ratings cannot have any held out, and the walk says so instead of choosing.
param_tip.hybrid_sw_min_neighbours: How many neighbours the collaborative recommender needs for a film before it answers; below that the content recommender answers. Default 1.
param_tip.hybrid_sw_clip: Clips the chosen recommender's answer to the rating scale (off by default, so that an overflow stays visible).
param_tip.field_weight: Weight w of the field: a term's weight in the profile is w × tf × idf. At least one ticked field needs a weight above 0.
param_tip.field_weight_model: The model learns a weight per term; a field weight only scales that whole field before the penalty (a per-field prior) and does nothing at 1.
param_tip.tf: How a term that occurs more than once in a field counts. Tags occur once, so this only matters for the overview text.
param_tip.tf_sqrt: The square root of the count: a word said four times counts twice.
param_tip.tf_log: 1 + ln(count). A plain ln would turn a term that occurs once into 0 and every tag would vanish, so the course uses 1 + ln.
param_tip.feature_weighting: Off by default. Ticked, every term's weight - in the films' vectors and in the user's taste profile - is multiplied by g(w) = a − Gini(w), with a = {a}. The Gini of a term says how mixed it is among the films this user liked and disliked (their ratings; in a prediction the film being predicted is left aside): a term that separates the two groups (Gini near 0) counts almost a, a term that tells nothing (Gini 0.5) counts a − 0.5. It is the soft version of feature selection; the Feature selection tab lists the Gini of every term.
param_tip.field_genres: One term per genre of the film (genre:Drama). On the lecture's toy it is the only field.
param_tip.field_keywords: The film's plot keywords (kw:heist), one term each.
param_tip.field_themes: Letterboxd's community themes for the film (theme:...), one term each.
param_tip.field_minithemes: Letterboxd's finer community themes for the film (mtheme:...), one term each.
param_tip.field_directors: The film's director or directors (dir:...). A director who also acts is two terms: the prefix keeps the fields apart.
param_tip.field_cast: The first names of the cast (cast:...); the engine keeps ten by default.
param_tip.field_writers: The film's writers (writer:...), one term each.
param_tip.field_cinematographers: The film's cinematographers (cine:...), one term each.
param_tip.field_composers: The film's composers (comp:...), one term each.
param_tip.field_studios: The production studios (studio:...), one term each.
param_tip.field_collection_name: The collection or series the film belongs to (coll:...): one term, or none.
param_tip.field_countries: The countries of production (country:...), one term each.
param_tip.field_languages: The spoken languages (lang:...), one term each.
param_tip.field_original_language: The film's original language (olang:...): one term.
param_tip.field_release_date: The decade of the release date (era:1990s). The date itself is on the film's card; the profile keeps only the decade.
param_tip.field_overview: The overview and tagline as text: lower-cased, cut into words, stop words dropped, the rest cut down to stems (hopes and hoping both become hope). One term per stem; tf counts how often it appears.
param_tip.alg_funk_svd: FunkSVD: an unconstrained matrix factorization trained by SGD on the observed entries only; not an SVD (no orthogonality, no imputation of the missing ones).
param_tip.similarity: How alike two users are (item-based pages: two items). Pearson is the course default; the Similarity atlas shows every measure on the same pair.
param_tip.mean_convention: Which mean the active user is centred at (ū_a); hover a choice for what each one does. The convention enters in two places: the similarity, only for measures that centre on a user mean (Pearson, adjusted cosine, median-robust); and the user-based prediction baseline r̂ = ū_a + Σ w (r − ū_u) / Σ|w|, for every measure. Co-rated only changes the similarity alone (the baseline stays the dynamic mean), so it is the only chip disabled for centre-less measures.
param_tip.mean_convention_icf: Item-based pages: the convention applies to the means of the item vectors (the item-centred fault, generic measures). The user-centred adjusted cosine always uses each user's own mean, the active user's without the target (see the note below the controls).
param_tip.mc_dynamic: The active user's mean over all their ratings except the target's: the held-out rating is not used to centre the user. The course definition; the neighbours' means are over all their ratings.
param_tip.mc_static: The active user's mean over all their ratings. This includes the held-out rating of the target in the mean: a small leak of the answer into the predictor. Shown beside the course convention as a contrast, so the difference is visible.
param_tip.mc_identical: Identical here: the active user has not rated the target, so there is no rating to leave out of the mean. Dynamic (target excluded) and static (target included) give the same numbers on this pair.
param_tip.mc_corated_only: Both users' means are taken over the co-rated items only. This is what numpy.corrcoef, scipy.stats.pearsonr and DataFrame.corr compute: a fallacy for recommenders, because it throws away how each user rates in general. Shown as the teaching foil.
param_tip.mc_no_centre: No user centre in this measure: identical to dynamic here.
param_tip.cosine_support: The classic definition uses the full vectors with missing = 0 (the default here); several libraries compute over the co-rated items only; the two can differ a lot on sparse data. Co-rated items only cuts both vectors to the films they share first, so the norms see only those; the norms in the formula and the prediction change with it (lecture 5×6 toy, U1–U2: 0.6751 against 0.9753).
param_tip.centre: Fixed centre z of the constrained Pearson: ratings above z count as positive, below z as negative, for every user alike (Shardanand & Maes 1995 used 4 on their 1–7 scale, the labelled neutral). Default = the scale midpoint (2.75 on 0.5–5; some sources use the integer 3 on 1–5). Summed over the co-rated items; the mean convention does not apply.
param_tip.denominator: What the weighted sum over the neighbours is divided by. User-based: r̂ = ū_a + Σ w (r − ū_u) / D; item-based weighted average: Σ s r / D.
param_tip.den_abs: D = Σ|w|: every weight counts by its size, whatever its sign, so positive and negative weights cannot cancel in the divisor. The course default.
param_tip.den_signed: D = Σw: positive and negative weights cancel, so D can come close to 0 and the prediction leaves the rating scale (lecture 5×6 toy: 7.94 against 5.11 with Σ|w|). Shown beside the course divisor as a contrast, so the difference is visible.
param_tip.sig_mode: Damps a similarity that rests on few co-rated items c (item-based pages: common raters). none: no damping. min(c/n, 1): a linear ramp that reaches 1 at n co-rated items (Herlocker et al. 1999 used n = 50; the course default). c: the raw count with no cap, so the weights leave the −1…1 range.
param_tip.sig_n: The significance-weighting threshold n: the number of co-rated items c at which the damping stops (factor 1). Below it w is multiplied by c/n: with n = 50, a pair that shares 20 items keeps 40 % of its similarity. Only min(c/n, 1) uses n.
param_tip.k: How many neighbours the prediction uses: the k highest after ranking by the shrunk similarity (ties: more co-rated items first). Empty or 0 = all candidates (users who rated the target; item-based pages: the items the active user rated).
param_tip.clip: Clips the prediction to the rating scale (0.5–5 on the class data). Off by default so that an overflow stays visible: a prediction outside the scale is a symptom, for instance of the Σw denominator.
param_tip.keep_negative: Keeping negative similarities lets a dissimilar neighbour push the prediction the other way: a negative w flips the sign of that neighbour's deviation (r − ū), and the Σ|w| denominator keeps the weights well-scaled — the course default, because the effect is visible in the walk. The literature is mixed: Breese, Heckerman and Kadie (1998) used all correlations; Herlocker et al. (1999) selected neighbours by |w| thresholds, so negative correlates stayed in without being studied separately; several later systems keep only positive neighbours (e.g. Jamali & Ester 2009), and top-k selection drops negatives whenever enough positive neighbours exist.
param_tip.keep_negative_icf: Item-based pages start with this off: the weighted average Σ s r / Σ|s| has no centring, so a negative s would subtract a whole rating, not a deviation (lecture 5×6 toy: −0.02 with all four neighbours, 4.61 with the positive ones). Switching it on is allowed; when a negative similarity actually enters the weighted average, the step shows a pitfall flag; the item-mean baseline prediction handles negative similarities like the user-based formula.
param_tip.centering: Which mean the adjusted cosine subtracts before it takes the cosine.
param_tip.ctr_user: Each user's own mean over all their ratings (the active user's without the target): removes how generously a user rates. The course definition.
param_tip.ctr_item: The item's mean instead: a common mistake (adjusted_cosine_item_centred), kept as a contrast so the difference is visible. It subtracts how well the item is rated overall and leaves the users' own scales in the numbers.
param_tip.prediction: How the neighbours' ratings are combined into the prediction.
param_tip.pred_wavg: The weighted average Σ s · r(a, j) / Σ|s| of the active user's own ratings of the neighbouring items. No centring, so a negative s would subtract a whole rating.
param_tip.pred_baseline: The item-mean form: the target item's mean (without the active user) + Σ s (r(a, j) − mean of j) / Σ|s|. It mirrors the user-based formula and tolerates negative similarities.
param_tip.degree: Keeps only items with enough raters as candidates. Fraction: raters > value × the number of users, a strict “>” (so exactly half does not pass, although “at least half” is the looser reading). Count: raters ≥ the value. Filtered items stay in the table, marked low-degree.
param_tip.deg_value: A fraction between 0 and 1 (0.5 = more than half of the users) or, in count mode, a minimum number of raters.
param_tip.filter_genres: Restricts the ratings the SIMILARITY sees to films with any of these genres (reduction-based pre-filtering): it is computed as if the catalogue were only these films. Who may be a neighbour, and the prediction baseline, still use the whole matrix.
param_tip.filter_year_min: Earliest release year of the same filter. A film without a year never passes a year bound.
param_tip.filter_year_max: Latest release year of the same filter. A film without a year never passes a year bound.
param_tip.mean_scope: Which ratings the centres are taken over while a filter is on. Global: all of a user's (or item's) ratings, the course rule. Segment: only the ratings inside the filter.
param_tip.user_filter: Restricts the item-item similarity to the ratings of these users (the class cohort only, or everyone): pre-filtering on the user side.
param_tip.uf_min_ratings: Users with fewer ratings than this are left out of the item-item similarity.
param_tip.cand_genres: Cuts the candidate list relative to the target, after the similarity (post-filtering): “shares a genre” keeps films with at least one genre of the target, “carries every genre” keeps films that have all of them.
param_tip.cand_year_window: Keeps candidates released within this many years of the target's release year.
param_tip.k_top: How many films the list keeps: the model scores every candidate and the K highest-scoring ones are the recommendation.
param_tip.mmr_lambda: How far the list gives up relevance for variety: each place goes to the film with the highest λ × relevance − (1 − λ) × (its largest cosine to a film already placed). λ = 1 keeps the relevance order; the lower λ, the more variety and the more films change places; 0 = variety only. To see what it does, keep the user and K and compare λ = 1.0, 0.9 and 0.7: the changes chip and the ILS in the summary bar move with it. A film's relevance is its score (taste profile) or its predicted rating rescaled to 0-1 (kNN item similarity), so λ never trades a 1-5 rating against a cosine.
param_tip.candidates_unseen: Only films this user has not rated: what a recommender would actually offer. The default.
param_tip.candidates_all: Every film, the ones this user has rated included (marked “seen”). For display only: the model was fitted on those ratings, so a high score there says little.

param_group_tip.architecture:
## What the network is made of
- **Embedding.** A learned list of k numbers for each user and each film. Training adjusts the numbers so that similar users and films end up with similar lists. Effect: a larger k = more capacity and more parameters, so the network fits the training ratings more closely and overfits sooner when ratings are few.
- **Tower.** A small sub-network that turns ONE kind of input into a short vector before the parts are joined: the content tower reads the film's genres, keywords and themes, the profile tower reads the student's taste profile. Effect: switch a tower's input group off and the network stops seeing that input; wider layers = more capacity for it.
- **Join (concatenation).** The vectors from the embeddings, the towers and the two number groups are laid side by side into one long vector. No arithmetic, no parameters.
- **MLP (dense layers).** Layers that mix the long vector: every output is a weighted sum of all inputs, then ReLU. This mixing is where the network learns how who, what and content go together; the feature network has no separate dot product. Effect: wider or more layers learn more complex interactions and overfit sooner.
- **ReLU.** The rule after every hidden layer: keep a positive value, turn a negative one into zero. It is what makes the stack non-linear - without it the layers would collapse into one linear model and could not learn how user, film and content interact. A unit that outputs zero for a pair is off for it: “19 of 32” in a box counts the units that are on.
- **Dropout.** A brake on overfitting: during training some MLP units are switched off at random. Effect: larger = stronger brake, noisier training.
## Network type
The other types (MLP, GMF, NeuMF, Hybrid MLP) are the neural-models page's; they have no towers and no side inputs.
param_group_tip.side:
## Which inputs the network sees
- **ids.** The user id and the film id, each looked up in an embedding table (a learned list of numbers). Effect: without them the network cannot memorise a particular user or film.
- **Film terms (TF-IDF).** The film's description as a long row with one number per term (genres, keywords, themes); the number is high when the term is typical for this film and rare among films. It goes through the content tower. Catalogue data: the same for every user.
- **Film numbers.** The release year and the number of training ratings (log), standardised.
- **User profile.** The student's taste profile over the same terms (Rocchio): terms of films they rated above their own mean push up, terms of films below it push down. Built from their TRAINING ratings only: the target and the validation share never enter. It goes through the profile tower.
- **User statistics.** The student's rating count (log), mean and spread, standardised.
## Effect of switching a group off
The group is removed from the network (no zero vectors), so the parameter count changes. With every group except ids off you get the ids-only network, the comparison this page shows next to the full one.
## The two numbers
**Content fields** choose the vocabulary's source; **Max terms** cuts it to its most frequent terms and sets the width of the film row and the profile.
param_group_tip.training:
## How the network learns
- **Epoch.** One pass over all training ratings; the curve shows the error after each pass.
- **Batch size.** How many ratings go into one weight update. Effect: smaller = more, noisier updates per epoch.
- **Learning rate.** How far every weight moves at each update. Effect: too large = the error jumps around, too small = slow.
- **Weight decay.** Pulls every weight towards zero a little at each update. Effect: less overfitting, too much underfits.
- **Validation share.** The newest share of each user's remaining ratings, held out to watch the error. The target pair is in neither the training nor the validation set.
- **Early stopping.** Training stops when the validation error has not improved for Patience epochs in a row, and the weights of the best epoch are kept. Effect: with it off the network keeps training and the validation error rises (overfitting); the page shows the usual practice beside it.
- **Seed.** The same seed repeats the run exactly; another seed gives a different start.

measure_info.pearson: Correlation of the two users' deviations from their own means over the co-rated items; the means follow the mean convention (dynamic: target excluded). Undefined with fewer than two co-rated items or when either user's ratings on them are constant; such pairs are dropped with a visible step.
measure_info.constrained_pearson: Pearson with a fixed neutral centre at the scale midpoint (2.75 on 0.5–5) instead of each user's mean; the mean convention does not apply.
measure_info.median_robust: Pearson's form with medians instead of means: one extreme rating moves a median less than a mean.
measure_info.cosine: Angle between the raw rating vectors, a missing rating counting as 0. Full-vector norms (the classic definition) make a user who rated many other films look less similar than the shared films alone suggest; co-rated norms see only the shared films. Ratings are not centred, so two users who rate everything high look alike. A definition, not a fallacy. On sparse data the two norms can put the same neighbours an order of magnitude apart.
measure_info.adjusted_cosine: Cosine of ratings centred by each user's mean over ALL their ratings, removing the users' different scales: the item-based measure.
measure_info.jaccard: Overlap of the two users' rated sets |A∩B| / |A∪B|; rating values are ignored and the target item is left out of both sets.
measure_info.euclidean_inv: 1 / (distance + 1) over the co-rated items; a single strong disagreement weighs more under Euclidean than under Manhattan.
measure_info.manhattan_inv: 1 / (distance + 1) over the co-rated items; a single strong disagreement weighs more under Euclidean than under Manhattan.
measure_info.spearman: A foil: a deliberately contrasting option, a valid statistic a recommender should not use, placed next to the course measure so the difference is visible. Correlation of ranks: ignores both the rating scale and the users' means — for comparison only (a rank foil).
measure_info.kendall: A foil: a deliberately contrasting option, a valid statistic a recommender should not use, placed next to the course measure so the difference is visible. Kendall's tau-b over the co-rated items: the share of item pairs the two users order the same way minus the share they order the opposite way, ties handled by tau-b. Like Spearman it ignores the rating scale and the users' means, and with few co-rated items it takes only a handful of values. A rank foil for comparison, not a recommender default; undefined below two co-rated items or with constant ratings.
measure_info.adjusted_cosine_item_centred: A common mistake, kept as a contrast so the difference is visible: the adjusted cosine centred by each ITEM's mean instead of each user's. It subtracts how well the item is rated overall and leaves the users' own scales in the numbers.
measure_info.library_pearson: A foil: a deliberately contrasting option, a valid statistic a recommender should not use, placed next to the course measure so the difference is visible. What numpy.corrcoef / pandas.corr compute on the co-rated sub-vectors: both means over the shared items only, discarding how each user rates in general — the course's fallacy foil.

memory_cf.title: Memory-based collaborative filtering
memory_cf.beta_note: Beta: {n} cells of the comparison table still say TBD and wait for a literature check; every other cell either cites its source or shows the course focus (the last column says which).
memory_cf.beta_note_sourced: Beta: every cell of the comparison table now carries a source (last column); the text may still change before the page is signed off.
memory_cf.intro: Memory-based (neighbourhood) collaborative filtering predicts a rating **straight from the rating matrix**, with **no trained model**: it finds the users most like the active user (user-based) or the items most like the target item (item-based) and combines their ratings. This page compares the two views, lists the similarity measures of this lab with their formulas and says how a prediction is formed. Nothing on it depends on the selected dataset.
