memory_cf.cmp_intro: One rating matrix, two ways to read it: its rows (users) or its columns (items). “lit. § N” in the last column is section N of the literature notes behind this page, where every statement is marked verified or unverified; “course focus” marks a row that shows what this course examines first, not a finding of the literature.
memory_cf.offline_note: All findings cited here are offline results on 2000-era MovieLens samples with random, not temporal, splits; none reports variation across folds or seeds, and none shows an online gain.

cmp.rule: Item-based CF: centre every rating by its USER's mean (adjusted cosine); centring by the item mean is the named fault; plain cosine is not centred. (The item-based Pearson entry below centres on item means; the default measure of the item-based page is adjusted cosine.)
cmp.rule_src: Source: Sarwar et al. 2001 §3.1.3 and §4.3.1 (offsetting the user average gives adjusted cosine a clear advantage over plain cosine, which ignores differences in rating scale between users); Ekstrand et al. 2011 p. 99 (plain cosine is the most popular item-based choice). “Named fault” is this course's own label (course focus), not a term from those works.

unit.label: Similarity unit
unit.ucf: Two **users**, over the films both rated (the target left out): I_au = (I_a ∩ I_u) without the target.
unit.icf: Two **films**, over the users who rated both (the active user left out): U_ij = (U_i ∩ U_j) without the active user.

support.label: Support of one similarity
support.ucf: In sparse data a user pair shares **few co-rated films**: about 1 common rating per pair in the worked example (10 000 ratings, 1 000 users, 100 items, uniform), against about 650 candidate neighbours.
support.icf: An item pair shares **many common raters** when users outnumber items: about 10 common ratings per pair in the same example, 99 candidate neighbours. The example assumes uniform ratings, which its authors call unrealistic.

scale.label: Precomputation & scale
scale.ucf: The similarities depend on the active user and are **computed when asked** (the lab does this); a user–user table can be precomputed too, but its space grows with the square of the number of users. Tractable when items outnumber users.
scale.icf: The item–item table is **precomputed offline** and only the k most similar items per item are kept (the “model size”); its space grows with the square of the number of items. Tractable when users outnumber items. Amazon's item-to-item system: the online part does not grow with the catalogue or the customer count (a system description, no accuracy reported).
scale.src: lit. § 1: Sarwar et al. 2001 §3.3; Ekstrand et al. 2011 p. 112; Nikolakopoulos et al. 2021 Table 2; Linden et al. 2003 p. 77

stability.label: Stability over time
stability.ucf: Could prove **more stable** when the catalogue changes constantly (the example given: an online article recommender).
stability.icf: Item relationships are **relatively static**, so the precomputed table stays useful; preferred when the items are fairly static.
stability.src: lit. § 1, § 5: Sarwar et al. 2001 pp. 285–286; Nikolakopoulos et al. 2021 p. 13

cold_start.label: Cold start (new user / new item)
cold_start.ucf: A new user has no co-rated films with anyone until they rate, so **no similarity is defined** (from the support above). An item with no ratings cannot be recommended (inference, no source).
cold_start.icf: Answers a new user from **as few as two or three rated items**, and needs no retraining once the item similarities exist. An item with no ratings cannot be recommended (inference, no source).
cold_start.src: lit. § 5: Linden et al. 2003 p. 79; Nikolakopoulos et al. 2021 p. 5; the user-based clause and the last sentence are inference

explanation.label: Explanation style
explanation.ucf: **Less amenable**: the neighbours are other users whom the active user does not know.
explanation.icf: The neighbour films can be shown as the reason: **“because you liked X”**.

serendipity.label: Serendipity
serendipity.ucf: More likely to be **serendipitous**, particularly with a small number of nearest neighbours; on MovieLens this went with greater user satisfaction.
serendipity.src: lit. § 3: Nikolakopoulos et al. 2021 p. 13; Ekstrand et al. 2011 p. 113 (qualitative: no number is given)

measure.label: Typical measure
measure.ucf: **Pearson**, each user centred on the mean of all their own ratings. In general reported to give the best results for user-based CF.
measure.icf: **Adjusted cosine**, user-centred (centring by the item's mean instead is a named fault). Its advantage over plain cosine is an item-based result; Ekstrand et al. call plain cosine the most popular item-based choice and report that Pearson does not seem to work as well.
measure.src: lit. § 4: Ekstrand et al. 2011 pp. 94, 99; Sarwar et al. 2001 §3.1.3, §4.3.1

accuracy.label: Head-to-head accuracy
accuracy.both: **Small differences**, and the direction **depends on data density and task**. Rating prediction (MAE, MovieLens 943 users × 1 682 films, random splits): user-user 0.732, item-item 0.726 at 60 neighbours and 80 % train; the authors call the improvement “not significantly large” (§4.5, p. 293). Top-N recall on nine datasets: item-based is worse on the denser sets (MovieLens among them), better on the sparser ones, and 6 to 391 times faster at recommendation time.
accuracy.src: lit. § 6: Sarwar et al. 2001 p. 292, §4.5; Deshpande & Karypis 2003 (technical report) §5.2.6

rule.label: Prediction rule
rule.ucf: r̂ = ū_a + Σ w (r_ut − ū_u) / Σ|w|: the active user's own mean plus the neighbours' **weighted deviations** from their own means.
rule.icf: Default: r̂ = Σ s r_uj / Σ|s|, the **weighted average** of the active user's own ratings of the neighbouring items. Option: r̂ = r̄_t + Σ s (r_uj − r̄_j) / Σ|s|, the item-mean baseline.

tag_tip.core: A measure the course teaches and the engines use.
tag_tip.foil: A foil: a deliberately contrasting option, a valid statistic a recommender should not use, placed next to the course measure so the difference is visible.

pearson.pro_1: **Centres each user at their own mean**, so a generous and a strict rater who agree in direction look alike: the course's core lesson.
pearson.pro_2: Bounded in [−1, 1]; the sign separates agreement from opposition, and the mean-centred prediction uses a negative weight correctly.
pearson.con_1: **Defined only on the co-rated items**: with fewer than two of them, or constant ratings on them, it is undefined and the pair is dropped with a visible step.
pearson.con_2: A value that rests on two or three co-rated items is easy to push to ±1; significance weighting damps it.
pearson.note: The mean convention (dynamic / static / co-rated only) changes the number; the library correlation (co-rated only) is the fallacy shown next to it.

constrained_pearson.pro_1: **Measures agreement about absolute liking**: both users are centred at the same neutral rating, so 'both liked it' differs from 'both disliked it'.
constrained_pearson.pro_2: No user mean to estimate; the mean convention does not apply.
constrained_pearson.con_1: **Assumes the scale midpoint is neutral for everyone**: a generous rater's 3.0 counts as a dislike.
constrained_pearson.con_2: The sign can flip against Pearson: toy U1–U2 is +0.7620 under Pearson and −0.0899 here.

median_robust.pro_1: One extreme rating moves a median **less than a mean**.
median_robust.pro_2: Keeps Pearson's form, so it reads like the course measure.
median_robust.con_1: A coarse rating scale produces **many ties**, and the median is a coarse centre.
median_robust.con_2: Which ratings the median is taken over still depends on the mean convention.

cosine.pro_1: **Rating values count** (unlike Jaccard) and no mean has to be estimated: it is defined whenever both vectors are non-zero.
cosine.pro_2: Reads the same on explicit ratings and on binary (implicit) vectors.
cosine.con_1: Not centred: two users who rate everything high look alike (raw ratings, a missing rating counts as 0).
cosine.con_2: Support matters: the numerator sums over the co-rated items, but the classic norms run over each user's **full vector**, so a user who rated many other films looks less similar than the shared films suggest.
cosine.note: cosine_support = full (default, the classic definition) takes the norms over the full vectors; cosine_support = corated cuts both vectors to the shared films first. On sparse data the two can put the same neighbours an order of magnitude apart (Parameters panel, 'norms').

adjusted_cosine.pro_1: **Removes each user's own rating scale** before the comparison, using the user's mean over ALL their ratings.
adjusted_cosine.pro_2: The course's item-item measure: two item vectors are compared over their common raters, each rating centred by its rater's mean.
adjusted_cosine.con_1: The numerator runs over the common raters but the norms over each item's full rater set (the same support distinction as the cosine), so it is **not a Pearson on the common raters**: toy U1–U2 is 0.6124 against Pearson's 0.7620.
adjusted_cosine.con_2: A user with few ratings gives a noisy mean, and every rating of that user is centred by it.
adjusted_cosine.note: Its advantage over plain cosine is an empirical result of ITEM-based CF (Sarwar et al. 2001 §4.3.1, Fig. 4, MAE about 0.73 against 0.83, read off the figure); it is not evidence that adjusted cosine beats Pearson for user-based CF (lit. § 4).

jaccard.pro_1: **Needs no rating values**: works on implicit data (rated / not rated) as well as on ratings.
jaccard.pro_2: Bounded in [0, 1] and easy to explain: the share of what either rated that both rated.
jaccard.con_1: **Ignores what the users thought**: 'both watched it' is not 'both liked it'.
jaccard.con_2: Heavy raters overlap with everyone, so a large overlap is weak evidence of taste.
jaccard.note: The target item is left out of BOTH sets; keeping it in the union would deflate Jaccard (toy 0.6667 against 0.8000).

euclidean_inv.pro_1: Intuitive: a distance in rating units over the co-rated items, turned into a similarity by 1 / (1 + d).
euclidean_inv.pro_2: No centring and no variance: **defined with a single co-rated item**.
euclidean_inv.con_1: d is a SUM over the co-rated items, so it grows with their number: **a well-supported pair looks less similar than a one-item pair**.
euclidean_inv.con_2: Raw differences leave each user's own scale in the number, and one big disagreement weighs more here than under Manhattan.

manhattan_inv.pro_1: Intuitive: the summed absolute rating gap over the co-rated items, turned into a similarity by 1 / (1 + d).
manhattan_inv.pro_2: **One big gap dominates less** than under the Euclidean distance.
manhattan_inv.con_1: d is a SUM over the co-rated items, so it grows with their number: **a well-supported pair looks less similar than a one-item pair**.
manhattan_inv.con_2: Raw differences leave each user's own scale in the number.

library_pearson.pro_1: **Convenient**: one call to numpy.corrcoef, scipy.stats.pearsonr or DataFrame.corr.
library_pearson.con_1: **Both means are taken over the shared items only**: it throws away how each user rates in general.
library_pearson.con_2: With exactly two shared items it is always ±1 (or undefined), whatever the users think.

spearman.pro_1: **Does not depend on the rating scale**: only the order a user gives the shared items matters.
spearman.con_1: **Ignores the scale and the users' means**, and a ten-level scale produces many ties.
spearman.con_2: Undefined below two co-rated items or when either user's ratings on them are constant. For comparison only.

kendall.tex_note: n_c / n_d: pairs of shared items the two users order the same / the opposite way; n_1 / n_2: tie corrections of the two users; c: the number of co-rated items.
kendall.pro_1: **Counts how often two users order item pairs the same way**: a direct, scale-free reading of agreement.
kendall.con_1: **Ignores the scale and the users' means**; with few co-rated items it takes only a handful of values.
kendall.con_2: Undefined below two co-rated items or when either user's ratings on them are constant. For comparison only.

adjusted_cosine_item_centred.what: The item-centred variant: each rating is centred on the mean of its item instead of its user's mean; kept so the difference is visible.
adjusted_cosine_item_centred.pro_1: **Easy to compute**: one mean per item, which is the column mean.
adjusted_cosine_item_centred.con_1: **Subtracts how well the item is rated overall** and leaves each user's own scale in the numbers: it is not the user-centred measure the course teaches.
adjusted_cosine_item_centred.con_2: Harmless-looking on a small matrix: on the toy, sim(I5, I1) is 0.7121 user-centred and 0.7123 item-centred.

memory_cf.predict_intro: How the neighbours' ratings become one prediction. The formulas are the ones the lab traces; the numbers quoted come from the lecture 5×6 toy example.

predict_user_deviation.title: Mean-centred weighted deviation
predict_user_deviation.text: The active user's own mean plus the neighbours' weighted deviations from their own means. ū_a is the active user's mean over all their ratings, the target excluded; a negative weight flips the sign of that neighbour's deviation, which the mean-centred form handles correctly, so negative similarities are kept.

predict_item_weighted_average.title: Weighted average of the neighbouring items
predict_item_weighted_average.text: The weighted average of the active user's own ratings of the neighbouring items: no centring, no user mean. A negative similarity would subtract a whole rating, not a deviation, so the page starts with negative similarities off (toy: −0.0228 with all four neighbours, 4.6056 with the two positive ones).

predict_item_mean_baseline.title: Item-mean baseline with weighted deviations
predict_item_mean_baseline.text: The item-mean form: the target item's mean (without the active user) plus the weighted deviations of the user's ratings from their item means. It mirrors the user-based rule and tolerates negative similarities (toy target mean 3.25).

signed.label: Denominator variant
signed.text: D = Σ|w| (default): every weight counts by its size, so positive and negative weights cannot cancel in the divisor. The alternative D = Σw lets them cancel: the divisor can come close to 0 and the prediction leaves the scale (toy: 7.9387 against 5.1066).

clip.label: Clipping to the rating scale
clip.text: Optional, off by default so that an overflow stays visible: a prediction outside the scale is a symptom, for instance of the Σw denominator.

neighbours.label: Which neighbours
neighbours.text: User-based: the users who rated the target; item-based: the items the active user rated. They are ranked by the similarity after significance weighting; k cuts the list (empty or 0 = all).

memory_cf.when_intro: The six measures most often compared, side by side. Each cell restates the card above in one line.

pearson.idea: Agreement of the deviations from each user's own mean, over the co-rated items.
pearson.data: Explicit ratings; **at least two co-rated items**
pearson.con: Unstable on few co-rated items; undefined for constant ratings.

cosine.idea: Angle between the raw rating vectors, missing = 0.
cosine.con: Everything-high raters look alike; full-vector norms penalise heavy raters (cosine_support).

adjusted_cosine.idea: Cosine of user-centred ratings; two item vectors over their common raters.
adjusted_cosine.pro: The item-item measure that removes the users' scales.
adjusted_cosine.con: Needs the users' means; norms over the full rater sets, so not a Pearson on the common raters.

jaccard.idea: Overlap of the two rated sets, |A ∩ B| / |A ∪ B|.
jaccard.pro: Needs no rating values at all.
jaccard.con: Value-blind: both watched is not both liked; heavy raters overlap with everyone.

euclidean_inv.pro: Intuitive; defined with one co-rated item.
euclidean_inv.con: The distance grows with the number of co-rated items, so well-supported pairs look less similar.

manhattan_inv.idea: 1 / (1 + summed absolute gap) over the co-rated items.
manhattan_inv.pro: One big gap dominates less than under Euclidean.
manhattan_inv.con: The same growth with the number of co-rated items.

memory_cf.when_note_distance: Why Euclidean and Manhattan are not the default: d is a sum over the co-rated items, so a pair that shares many films looks LESS similar than a pair that shares one, and the raw differences keep each user's own scale in the number.

model_cf.title: Model-based collaborative filtering
model_cf.beta_note: Beta: {n} cells of the comparison table still say TBD and wait for a literature check; every other cell names its source in the last column (the literature, the lecture slides or the course focus).
model_cf.beta_note_sourced: Beta: every cell of the comparison table now carries a source (last column); the text may still change before the page is signed off.
model_cf.intro: Model-based collaborative filtering **learns a compact model from the ratings first** and predicts from that model, instead of looking the neighbours up in the rating matrix each time. This page sets the two families side by side, shows what a matrix factorization is on two small worked examples, says how this lab finds the factors, lists the factorization family and opens the “black box” of a neural rating model. Nothing on it depends on the selected dataset.
model_cf.col_resize_hint: Drag to resize the column (arrow keys: 2 points); double-click to reset the columns of this table
model_cf.offline_note: Statements here come from the literature and the lecture slides, and the results behind them are offline (held-out ratings of a fixed dataset); none shows an online gain, and an offline gain does not guarantee one.
model_cf.cmp_intro: One rating matrix, two ways to use it: look the neighbours up each time (memory-based) or fit a compact summary of it first and predict from that (model-based). “lit. § N” in the last column is section N of the literature notes behind this page, where every statement is marked verified or unverified; “course slides” marks a statement of this course's lecture slides and “course focus” what this lab does; a row with several labels names the source of its left cell first.

unit.label: What is kept
unit.memory: **Lazy learning**: the work is specific to the instance being predicted, so the neighbours are looked up in the rating matrix itself.
unit.model: A **summarized model of the data is built up front** (here: factors and weights), as in supervised or unsupervised learning.

phases.label: Training vs prediction
phases.memory: **No model-building phase**: the neighbours are found from the matrix when a prediction is asked for (a precomputed table only speeds this up).
phases.model: **Training is clearly separated from prediction**: the model is fitted first, then used to predict.

entries.label: Train / test unit
entries.both: In CF the split is over **entries**, not rows: any entry of the rating matrix may be missing, so one speaks of training and test entries rather than training and test rows.

space.label: Space and time
space.memory: Pre-processing is **quadratic** in either the number of users or the number of items; a user-based method might need O(m²) space for m users (the pre-processing can be skipped, at the price of slower queries).
space.model: The size of the learned model is **much smaller than the rating matrix**, so the space needed is often quite low.

overfit.label: Overfitting
overfit.both: Overfitting is a prediction **overly influenced by random artifacts** in the data. The textbook says model-based methods **can often help avoid it**; for unconstrained factorization the guard is regularization (family table below).

support.label: Similarity without common ratings
support.memory: A similarity exists only on the **co-rated items**: the textbook's user-based Pearson sums over the items both users rated (I_u ∩ I_v) and over nothing else, notes that this set is often empty because rating matrices are sparse, and that a similarity over few mutually rated items is less robust. Over an empty set the coefficient is undefined: a pair with no common rating has no similarity and cannot be neighbours.
support.model: Every user and every item gets a factor vector learned from all observed ratings, and a prediction is the dot product of two of them, so it exists for any pair. The textbook says a distance between two users' latent vectors can be computed **even when they have very few items rated in common**, and that the low-rank structure is estimated from a small subset of the entries, filling the whole matrix in one shot; Koren et al. describe the factors as inferred from the rating patterns, 20 to 100 per user and item.
support.src: lit. § 1: Aggarwal 2016 §2.3.1, §2.5, §3.6; lit. § 2: Koren et al. 2009

explanation.label: Explanation
explanation.memory: The **neighbours themselves** can be shown as the reason; in the classroom lab the user-based and item-based pages listed them with their ratings.
explanation.model: Interpretability **depends on the method**: the family table below ranks them (NMF and PLSA: high semantic interpretability; unconstrained: poor).

accuracy.label: Accuracy
accuracy.both: The textbook calls latent factor models **state-of-the-art** (2016) and says some of the most accurate methods are model-based; Koren et al. (2009) state that matrix factorization is superior to classic nearest-neighbour techniques for product recommendations. Since then a **tuned dot product** has been shown to beat learned MLP similarities on the same sampled protocol (HR@10 / NDCG@10, 100 sampled negatives, binarised MovieLens 1M and Pinterest), and the original NCF numbers were reported at the best iteration on the test set (Rendle et al. 2020). All of it is offline evidence.
accuracy.src: lit. § 1: Aggarwal 2016 §3.1, §3.6, §3.8; lit. § 2: Koren et al. 2009; lit. § 6: Rendle et al. 2020 §3.3, §3.4

rule.label: Prediction rule
rule.memory: User-based: r̂ = ū_a + Σ w (r_ut − ū_u) / Σ|w|, the active user's own mean plus the neighbours' **weighted deviations** from their own means.
rule.model: r̂ = μ + b_u + b_i + p_u · q_i: the **dot product of two learned factor vectors** plus the global mean and two biases.
rule.src: course focus; lit. § 2: Koren et al. 2009, Eq. (4)

decomp.zero_note: **0 is a value here.** In these tables a 0 is an ordinary rating; in the lab's own data an empty cell means a missing rating, never a zero. That is why the two examples are fixed tables on this page and not datasets of the lab.

item_matrix.label: Item-factor matrix
item_matrix.deck: V (n × k); the product uses Vᵀ
item_matrix.lab: Q (n × k); the product uses Qᵀ

latent.label: “Latent factors”
latent.deck: A ROW of U or V is a latent factor; a COLUMN is a latent vector (a component)
latent.lab: “k latent factors” means the k COMPONENTS of every vector, that is the number of columns of P and Q

mf_lowrank.title: The low-rank model
mf_lowrank.text: A rating matrix R (m users × n items) is approximated by the product of two thin matrices: P has one row of k numbers per user, Q one row of k numbers per item. One rating is the **dot product** of a user's row and an item's row. This is the lecture's R ≈ UVᵀ in this lab's letters.
mf_lowrank.src: course slides; lit. § 2: Koren et al. 2009, Eq. (1)

mf_predict.title: Prediction
mf_predict.text: A predicted rating is the **global mean μ**, plus the user's bias b_u, plus the item's bias b_i, plus the dot product of the two factor vectors. The biases carry how generous a user is and how well liked an item is on average, so the factors describe what is left. Switching the Biases setting off drops b_u and b_i.

mf_objective.title: What the factors minimise
mf_objective.text: The factors are chosen to make the **squared error over the observed ratings** small, plus a penalty of weight λ on the size of the factors and biases (regularization). The sum runs over the observed (training) ratings K only: a missing cell is not a zero, it is simply not in the sum. That is the difference from the SVD of a full matrix, which is undefined when the matrix is incomplete. The curve on the Matrix factorization page shows RMSE, which has no penalty term, so it is not this objective.
mf_objective.src: lit. § 2: Koren et al. 2009, Eq. (2) and (5)
mf_objective.note: In this lab λ is the “{reg}” setting for FunkSVD and BPR and the “{lam}” setting for ALS and EASE.

mf_sgd_update.title: One SGD step (FunkSVD)
mf_sgd_update.text: For **one observed rating** the error e = r − r̂ is computed; then the biases and both factor vectors take a step of size η that reduces it, and λ pulls them back toward zero. The Matrix factorization page shows one such update with live numbers, then repeats it over the training ratings, epoch by epoch.
mf_sgd_update.src: lit. § 2: Koren et al. 2009 (SGD rules), Funk 2006
mf_sgd_update.note: The printed rules are for q_i and p_u; the bias updates in the formula are derived by this lab from the biased objective. Funk's own recipe trains one factor at a time; this lab updates all k at once. “FunkSVD” is this app's name for unconstrained factorization trained by SGD; Funk's 2006 post does not use it.

als_solve.title: One ALS solve
als_solve.text: ALS has no learning rate: with the item factors held fixed, each user's factor vector is the closed-form solution of a small **ridge regression** over the items that user rated; then the roles swap and the items are solved. λ is the page's “{lam}” setting.
als_solve.src: lit. § 3: Zhou et al. 2008 (author's preprint), Eq. (4) with simple λ regularization
als_solve.note: This is the simple-λ form, not the weighted-λ variant of the paper (ALS-WR, preprint Eq. (5)); and this lab centres the ratings on μ, which the paper's model does not.

bpr_gradient.title: One BPR step (implicit feedback)
bpr_gradient.text: BPR learns from **which items a user interacted with, not from rating values**: for a triple (user u, an item i they interacted with, an item j they did not) it pushes the score of i above the score of j: x_uij = x_ui − x_uj. It optimises a ranking, so its curve is a loss and a validation AUC, not an RMSE.
bpr_gradient.note: The paper maximises BPR-Opt; this lab writes the same step as a loss. The paper's BPR-MF has no item bias; the lab's “{setting}” setting adds one.

ease_closed_form.title: EASE: a linear model with a closed form
ease_closed_form.text: **EASE is a linear model, not a matrix factorization**: it learns one weight B_jt from every item j to the target item t (a linear item-item model without a hidden layer) and finds the weights in closed form from the item Gram matrix G: invert (G + λI) and rescale. It sits beside the factor models because the lab traces it on the same page, on the same implicit data.
ease_closed_form.note: The closed form needs the item Gram matrix: its cost grows with the cube of the number of items and does not depend on the number of users.

dnn_output.title: The neural model's output unit
dnn_output.text: The neural models end in **one linear unit** that outputs the predicted rating, r̂ = wᵀh + b, where h is whatever the layers before it (embeddings, element-wise product, dense layers with ReLU) make of the user and the item. It is a regression output, trained on squared error.
dnn_output.note: The paper trains on binarised implicit data with log loss; this lab trains the network on ratings with squared error, a variant of the paper's setup.

model_cf.family_intro: Five ways to factorize a rating matrix, told apart by their constraints and their objective; the “In this lab” column says which of them this lab implements. Drag the edge between two column headings to resize; double-click it to reset.

unconstrained.label: Unconstrained
unconstrained.pro: **Highest quality**; good for most matrices; regularization prevents overfitting.
unconstrained.lab: **FunkSVD** (SGD, the lab's default) and **ALS** (ridge), both on explicit ratings; λ is the “{reg}” setting for FunkSVD and the “{lam}” setting for ALS.

svd.label: SVD
svd.pro: Good visual interpretability; out-of-sample recommendations; **good for dense matrices**.
svd.con: Poor semantic interpretability; **suboptimal in sparse matrices**.
svd.lab: Not implemented; see the note on the name below.

max_margin.label: Max-margin
max_margin.pro: Highest quality; **resists overfitting**; similar to unconstrained; good for discrete ratings.

nmf.label: NMF
nmf.pro: Good quality; **high semantic interpretability**; less overfitting in some cases; best for implicit feedback.
nmf.con: **Loses interpretability** with both like and dislike ratings.

plsa.label: PLSA
plsa.pro: Good quality; **high semantic interpretability**; probabilistic interpretation; less overfitting in some cases; best for implicit feedback.
plsa.con: **Loses interpretability** with both like and dislike ratings.

family.svd_note: **About the name “SVD”.** The “SVD” of the Netflix Prize era is unconstrained factorization fitted to the observed ratings only; a true SVD of a rating matrix needs every entry. Koren et al. say conventional SVD is undefined when the matrix is incomplete and that earlier systems filled the gaps by imputation; Funk's 2006 post says the result is exactly an SVD only if the training set covers the matrix completely. Aggarwal calls using “SVD” for unconstrained factorization an incorrect, widespread practice and keeps the two apart, as does this table.
family.svd_note_src: lit. § 1: Aggarwal 2016 §3.6.4, §3.6.5; lit. § 2: Koren et al. 2009, Funk 2006
family.also_note: Also on the classroom lab's Matrix factorization page, but not rows of this table: **BPR** (implicit feedback: a factor model trained to rank, not to minimise squared error) and **EASE** (a linear item-to-item model without a hidden layer).
family.note: The table follows the lecture's Table 3.3. The literature notes confirm that its five rows and its cell phrases occur in the textbook, but not which phrase sits in which row, so the assignment shown is the slide's.

model_cf.blackbox_intro: The lecture draws any classification or regression model as a black box: ratings go in as (user, movie) rows, a rating comes out. In the classroom lab the Neural models page opened that box.

flow.out_sub: A test row (user, movie, ?) gets a number

framing.title: The framing: rows in, a rating out
framing.text: The lecture draws the network as a **black box**: training rows of (user, movie, rating) go in, and for a test pair (user, movie) with no rating a number comes out. Any classification or regression model can sit in the box; this lab opens it for a neural network, and the cards below say what is inside.

embedding.title: Inside, step 1: an embedding per user and per item
embedding.text: The first layer is a **lookup**: every user id and every item id owns a learned vector, the same kind of object as a row of P or Q. In the plain architectures nothing else is fed in: the network sees ids only.

gmf.title: GMF: the dot product, opened up
gmf.text: GMF multiplies the two embeddings **element by element** and feeds the product to a linear output unit; with one weight per factor that is a dot product with per-factor weights. **MF is a special case of the NCF framework**: with an identity output and every weight fixed to 1, GMF is exactly the dot product of the low-rank model card above.
gmf.src: lit. § 6: He et al. 2017 §3.2, Rendle et al. 2020 §3.3
gmf.note: The paper's trained GMF has a sigmoid output and learns the weights with log loss; the exact recovery of MF needs the identity output and weights of 1. Rendle et al. note that the learned weights can be absorbed into the embeddings, so GMF is no more expressive than a dot product.

mlp.title: MLP: let the layers find the interaction
mlp.text: The MLP **concatenates** the two embeddings and passes them through dense layers with ReLU. The NCF paper's argument: a plain concatenation says nothing about how user and item features interact, so hidden layers are added to learn that.
mlp.note: In the 2020 re-evaluation a tuned dot product beat the MLP on every dataset, metric and embedding size it tested; an MLP can approximate a dot product only with enough data and capacity.

neumf.title: NeuMF: both towers, one output
neumf.text: NeuMF gives GMF and the MLP **separate embeddings** and joins the two towers' outputs in the final linear unit, combining the linearity of MF with the non-linearity of the network.
neumf.src: lit. § 6: He et al. 2017 §3.4, Rendle et al. 2020 §3.3
neumf.note: Rendle et al. found NeuMF only slightly better than the MLP and much worse than a tuned dot product; the pre-trained variant was competitive on one dataset.

hybrid.title: Hybrid inputs: “later”
hybrid.text: The lecture's picture marks a user profile and item information as **hybrid, later**: extra inputs next to the ids. This lab's one extra input so far is the item's genres, the “Hybrid” architecture of the classroom lab's Neural models page.

task.title: Regression, not classification
task.text: A star rating is a number, so predicting it is **regression**, and this lab trains on squared error. The NCF paper instead binarises the ratings and trains a classifier with log loss (did the user interact with the item?), a different task. The textbook treats CF as a generalization of both classification and regression.
task.note: The paper itself argues that squared loss may not tally well with implicit data; the lab's network is a variant of the paper's setup, not a reproduction.

optimizer.title: How it is trained
optimizer.text: The network is fitted by **mini-batch gradient steps** on the squared error: the θ ← θ − η∇ idea of the SGD card above, applied to every weight and embedding. The page's “{optimizer}” setting chooses Adam (the default) or plain SGD.

model_cf.when_intro: Neighbourhood, factorization, implicit-feedback ranking and neural models side by side: what each learns, what it needs, when to reach for it and what to watch. Drag the edge between two column headings to resize; double-click it to reset.

neighbourhood.label: Neighbourhood (memory-based)
neighbourhood.learns: Nothing in advance: the rating matrix is the data and the similarities are computed when a prediction is asked for.
neighbourhood.needs: Overlap: items both users rated, or users who rated both items.
neighbourhood.when: You want the **neighbours as the explanation** and the user base or the catalogue is small enough for the search; the Memory-based CF page compares the user-based and item-based forms.
neighbourhood.watch: Pre-processing is **quadratic** in the number of users or of items.

factorization.label: Factorization (FunkSVD, ALS)
factorization.learns: k factors for every user and every item (and biases), fitted to the observed ratings.
factorization.needs: Explicit ratings, and enough of them to fit k numbers per user and per item.
factorization.when: You have explicit ratings and want a compact model with a fast dot-product score; **start from a tuned dot product** before anything deeper.
factorization.watch: Tune the hyper-parameters, the stopping epoch included, on data that **excludes the test item**; the family table lists regularization as the guard against overfitting.
factorization.src: course focus; lit. § 6: Rendle et al. 2020 §7, App. A.2

implicit.label: Implicit ranking (BPR, EASE)
implicit.learns: BPR: factors that score what the user interacted with above what they did not. EASE: one weight per item pair, in closed form.
implicit.needs: Interactions (who touched what), no rating values.
implicit.when: You have **views or clicks, not stars**, and the goal is a ranked list; EASE when the catalogue is small enough for its item Gram matrix.
implicit.watch: EASE's cost grows with the **cube of the number of items** (not with the users); the BPR paper argues that fitting 0 to every unobserved pair gives a model that, if expressive enough, predicts only 0s and cannot rank, so it compares pairs.
implicit.src: course focus; lit. § 5: Steck 2019 §3.4; lit. § 6: Rendle et al. 2009 §3.2

neural.label: Neural (GMF, MLP, NeuMF)
neural.learns: Embeddings plus dense layers, fitted by mini-batch gradient steps.
neural.needs: Enough data and capacity, and more computation than a dot product.
neural.when: **The dataset is large** or the embedding dimension is very small; side information (the lecture's “hybrid, later”) is the other reason to open the box.
neural.watch: In the 2020 re-evaluation a tuned dot product **beat the MLP and NeuMF**; an MLP learns a dot product only with enough data and capacity, scoring an item costs O(d²) against O(d), and nearest-neighbour retrieval tricks do not apply.
neural.src: lit. § 6: Rendle et al. 2020 §1, §3.3, §4, §5, §7; course slides

when.note: Read the table top to bottom as increasing machinery. The 2020 re-evaluation suggests a dot product as the better default choice unless the dataset is large or the embedding dimension is very small.

tip.weighted: How the ratings are split for this walk. The newest share of every user's ratings is held out (settings holdout_frac and holdout_max_per_user; a user with fewer than min_ratings ratings keeps all of theirs in training); the bases train on the rest and the weights are learned on the held-out ratings. The target rating is in neither group. The counts come from the split step of the trace; before a trace the row shows the settings.
tip.switching: How the ratings are split for this walk. Only the ACTIVE user's newest ratings are held out (settings switch_holdout_frac, holdout_max_per_user and min_ratings); every other rating - the other users' newest included - is training data, and the leaderboard is scored on the held-out ones. The target rating is in neither group. The counts come from the split step of the trace; before a trace the row shows the settings.
tip.trained: The target rating is hidden and the model is trained again without it (setting holdout = in_matrix); for a film the user has not rated nothing is hidden. The newest valid_frac share of each user's remaining ratings (only users with at least valid_min_ratings ratings; a validation tail smaller than min_valid_size is not used, and then everything trains) is the validation set that early stopping watches. A closed-form model (EASE) has no validation set. A stored model, used only for a film the user has not rated, was fitted beforehand on every rating. The counts come from the holdout step of the trace; before a trace the row shows the settings.
tip.model: The per-user model learns from ONE student's own rated films, the target film left out. A share of those films (setting model.mlp.val_fraction, at least val_min; the same films for the same student whatever the target is; fewer than twice val_min films: none) is held out as validation: the small network is watched by early stopping on it, the ridge keeps every film for its weights and only reports a validation error from a separate fit. The test is the target film. The counts come from the trace; before a trace the row shows the settings.
tip.profile: The taste profile is built from this student's own rated films with the target film left out (setting holdout = in_matrix): nothing is trained, nothing is validated, and no other user's rating is read.
tip.target: The target rating is hidden (setting holdout = in_matrix) and the prediction is computed from every other rating. Nothing is fitted here, so there is no validation set.

tip.activity: Number of films the user has rated, drawn on a logarithmic scale.
tip.generosity: How many stars above or below other raters this user scores the same films, after allowing for each film's own appeal; short profiles are pulled toward zero.
tip.spread: Standard deviation of the user's own ratings, in stars: how widely they use the scale around their personal average. A low spread is not a defect: clustered ratings draw a sharper personal scale.
tip.mainstream: Share of the user's films that belong to the catalogue's short head of most-rated titles, not counting the user's own rating.
tip.agreement: Correlation between the user's ratings and the other users' average rating of the same films.
tip.diversity: How evenly the user's films spread across the catalogue's genres: genre entropy divided by its largest possible value.
tip.polarised: Uses both ends of the scale: a sizeable share of the user's ratings sits at the very bottom and at the very top.
tip.selective: Generous and narrow: watches only what they would rate highly.

word_tip.light: Light rater: few films rated, below the Activity cut-off. Few ratings mean few co-rated films with anyone, so every similarity of this user rests on little evidence - the case significance weighting is there for.
word_tip.heavy: Heavy rater: many films rated, beyond the Activity cut-off. A heavy rater shares films with almost everyone and can turn up in many users' neighbourhoods.
word_tip.harsh: Harsh rater: scores the same films lower than other raters do, at or below the Generosity cut-off. A middling rating from a harsh rater is already a good one for them, which is why user-based CF predicts from deviations from each user's own mean, not from raw ratings. The idea is the user bias b_u of baseline predictors (Koren).
word_tip.generous: Generous rater: scores the same films higher than other raters do, at or above the Generosity cut-off. A high rating from a generous rater can be an ordinary one for them, so raw ratings of generous and harsh users are not comparable until each is centred on their own mean. The idea is the user bias b_u of baseline predictors (Koren).
word_tip.narrow: Narrow rater: keeps close to their own average - a small spread of ratings, below the Spread cut-off. Not a defect: it is a sharper personal scale. A correlation with this user leans on very few differences between films, and it is undefined when all their ratings on the co-rated films are the same.
word_tip.wide: Wide rater: uses the scale widely around their own average - a large spread of ratings, beyond the Spread cut-off. Wide is not extreme: using both ends of the scale is the polarised chip. In a mean-centred prediction a wide neighbour's deviations are large, so the same similarity moves the prediction more.
word_tip.niche: Niche viewer: most of their films are long-tail films that few people rated - a small share of their films belongs to the popular head, below the Mainstream cut-off. They share few films with others, so they have few co-rated films and few possible neighbours. The word follows the niche user group of Abdollahpouri et al.
word_tip.mainstream: Mainstream viewer: rates mostly popular films. This is the older, percentile-based name of the blockbuster end of the Mainstream axis; the default reading says blockbuster.
word_tip.blockbuster: Blockbuster-focused viewer: most of their films are popular titles from the head of the catalogue - a large share, beyond the Mainstream cut-off. Many other users rated the same films, so co-rated films are plentiful. The word follows the blockbuster-focused user group of Abdollahpouri et al.
word_tip.grey_sheep: Grey sheep: agrees little with the other raters of the same films, below the Agreement cut-off - the correlation between their ratings and the others' average rating is low. Classic CF struggles most with such users: there is no group of similar users to borrow ratings from. The term is Claypool et al.'s - a user whose opinions agree or disagree consistently with no group; here it is a classroom proxy, and a user who agrees with a sub-group only can still score low.
word_tip.consensual: Consensual rater: rates films the way the other raters do, beyond the Agreement cut-off - a high correlation between their ratings and the others' average rating. Their neighbours' ratings are good evidence for predicting theirs.
word_tip.focused: Focused viewer: concentrates on a few genres, below the Diversity cut-off - their films are spread unevenly across the catalogue's genres. Their neighbours tend to be users of the same few genres, and films outside those genres are hard to predict for them.
word_tip.omnivore: Omnivore: spreads their films evenly across the catalogue's genres, beyond the Diversity cut-off - as varied as the whole audience. "Cultural omnivore" is cultural sociology's term (Peterson) for someone who consumes many kinds of culture. In a neighbourhood an omnivore overlaps with users of many different tastes.
word_tip.polarised: Polarised rater: uses both ends of the scale - a sizeable share of their ratings sits at the very bottom and a sizeable share at the very top. Not the same as wide: wide says how far ratings stray from the user's own average, polarised asks whether both ends are used.
word_tip.selective: Selective viewer: generous and narrow at once - rates high and stays close to one level, watching only what they would rate highly. Their stars vary little around a high level, so telling films apart from their ratings is hard.

library_corr.title: Library correlation: means over the co-rated items only
library_corr.why: numpy.corrcoef, scipy.pearsonr and DataFrame.corr centre each user on the mean of the co-rated items alone. In recommender systems the centre is the user's habit over ALL their ratings (the active user's without the held-out target). Every similarity shifts — on the toy U1–U2 goes from 0.7620 to 0.8528 — and the neighbourhood and the prediction move with it.

static_active_mean.title: Static mean: the held-out rating inside the active user's centre
static_active_mean.why: The legacy static convention keeps the target rating in the active user's mean. In the classroom scenario that rating is exactly what the system must not know: the centre moves (4.0 → 4.1 on the toy), every similarity changes and the prediction leaks information about its own answer.

jaccard_legacy_union.title: Legacy Jaccard: target removed from the intersection but not from the union
jaccard_legacy_union.why: Removing the target from the numerator only biases the ratio downwards for every neighbour who rated it (4/6 instead of 4/5 on the toy) — one event counted once above the line and twice below it. Both sets must drop the target.

item_mean_centring.title: Adjusted cosine centred by the item mean
item_mean_centring.why: Adjusted cosine centres each rating by the USER who gave it, removing rating habits. Centring by the ITEM mean instead (Q2ij_possibleFaults) measures how items deviate from their own average — a different quantity: on the toy the I5–I2 similarity moves from −0.7478 to −0.4781 and the prediction follows.

few_corated_spurious.title: One or two co-rated items give a perfect ±1
few_corated_spurious.why: A correlation over one or two co-rated items can be ±1 by chance. Significance weighting w·min(c/n, 1) shrinks such coefficients before ranking. On the toy every pair shares four items, so the factor is the same for everyone and the prediction does not change under Σ|w| — on real data the c = 1–2 pairs fall down the ranking.

signed_denominator.title: Signed denominator Σw instead of Σ|w|
signed_denominator.why: Dividing by Σw lets positive and negative weights cancel: the denominator approaches zero and the prediction leaves the scale (toy: 7.94 instead of 5.11). Clipping hides the symptom, not the cause.

negative_weighted_average.title: Negative weights in the uncentred weighted average
negative_weighted_average.why: The item-based weighted average Σ s·r / Σ|s| has no centring, so a negative similarity subtracts a whole RATING, not a deviation. Keeping negative neighbours drives the toy prediction to −0.02. Drop non-positive neighbours (the default) or use the item-mean baseline form.

kcore_before_split.title: k-core fitted on all data before the split
kcore_before_split.why: Fitting the k-core filter on every rating lets the test rows decide which users and items survive — the test set shapes its own training data. Fit the filter on train only and apply the surviving ids to the evaluation rows (docs/experiment-protocol.md).

random_vs_temporal.title: Random split instead of a temporal one
random_vs_temporal.why: A random split trains on the future: later ratings help predict earlier ones, which never happens in deployment. The per-user random twin keeps exactly the temporal split's sizes, so every difference in the table is due to time alone — usually optimistic accuracy.

preprocess_before_split.title: Statistics fitted on all data (test ratings inside the means)
preprocess_before_split.why: Any statistic fitted on the whole matrix — here the per-user means — carries the test ratings into the model. The numbers improve, but the gain is a leak, not learning. Preprocessing is fitted on train and applied to the evaluation rows.

zero_as_rating.title: Missing ratings counted as 0
zero_as_rating.why: A missing rating is not a rating of 0. Counting empty cells as zeros drags every mean towards zero and wrecks the deviations and the predictions; the legacy needed getMeanMediaStdOfNonZeroValues.m to avoid exactly this. Watch MAE and RMSE.

binarised_auc.title: AUC on binarised predictions
binarised_auc.why: The week-06 script called roc_auc_score on binarised predictions. Thresholding the scores collapses the ROC curve to a single operating point, so the 'AUC' is just balanced accuracy at that threshold. Only the AUC row moves — every other metric is untouched — which is how you spot it.

mf.explained: axes carry {a} + {b} of the factor energy
mf.network_info:
How to read the network: each box is one stage of the model, left to right in the order the data flows; the arrows are the wiring. A box's first line is the stage's name, the second its width (n = how many numbers it holds) and, where the stage has them, its activation (ReLU or linear) and |θ|, the number of trainable parameters in it. The two boxes at the far left are not layers: they hold the traced user and film (the name and its row number) that the embedding tables are looked up with, in the red the app gives users and the blue it gives films everywhere else. Hover a box, or tab to it, for a sentence on what it does.
NeuMF learns a separate embedding table for each of its two branches (GMF and MLP); the same user id indexes both, so one id box has an arrow to each table. The two branches: GMF multiplies its user and item vectors element by element (the matrix factorization inside the network, a linear interaction read off like a dot product); MLP concatenates its own pair of vectors and passes them through dense ReLU layers (a non-linear interaction the network shapes freely); the output layer weighs the two.
The small bars inside a box are the first few numbers that stage holds for this user and film (its output vector): the baseline is zero, a bar above it is a positive value (purple, the colour the mean-centred sub-matrix of the user- and item-based pages uses above its centre), a bar below it a negative one (orange-brown, its colour below); a ReLU stage has no bars below the line (negatives are cut to zero); all bars share one scale, the largest value in the whole picture, so a tall bar is large in every box; the output box has one bar, the rating; +k says how many values are not drawn.
A pulsing blue frame marks the stage the current step talks about; the red-framed box is the output, green when the prediction is in; the footer gives the architecture and the total parameter count. Press + to enlarge the diagram; it then scrolls inside the tab and keeps the active stage in view. (The dark theme keeps the hues and picks tones that suit its ground.)
## How to present it
1. **Ids in, rating out.** Start from the black box: it takes a user id and a film id and returns one number, the predicted rating. Everything in the picture is what happens in between.
2. **An id is not a feature.** A row number says nothing by itself. The embedding table turns it into numbers: one learned vector per user and per film. That is the matrix factorization idea, now a layer of the network.
3. **Two branches** (NeuMF, He et al. 2017). GMF is the matrix factorization inside the network; the MLP can learn interactions a product cannot express; the output layer decides how much each counts. Each box's own tip says which part it is.
4. **Training is the loop you know.** Predict, compare with the rating, nudge the numbers - the FunkSVD loop, with the Adam optimiser instead of plain gradient steps; the validation curve and early stopping decide which epoch's weights are kept. On a few thousand ratings (the class set has about 8 k) the best epoch is often the first: the network starts to memorise at once - capacity against data, a lesson, not a defect.
5. **Limits.** One seed, no hyper-parameter search, offline numbers: an offline gain is no promise of an online one.
## If asked how the advanced versions differ
- Wider embeddings and deeper layers.
- Side information: the hybrid variant here adds the film's genres through a tower of its own.
- Ranking losses with sampled negatives instead of rating regression.
- Sequence models over what the user watched before.
- Two-tower retrieval for millions of items: user and item vectors are made separately, so the best items are found by a nearest-neighbour search.
- Graph neural networks over the user-item graph.
- Context features and multi-task heads in production.
- A well-tuned dot product often matches or beats the MLP (Rendle et al. 2020).
mf.layer_tip_input: The traced user / film: the id the embedding tables are looked up with. Not a layer: no parameters, no bars.
mf.layer_tip_embedding: Embedding table: one learned vector of k numbers per user (or film); the id picks its row, the bars are that row. This lookup is the matrix factorization idea inside the network. |θ| = rows × k.
mf.layer_tip_branch_gmf: This table feeds the GMF branch (element-wise product); NeuMF keeps a separate table for each branch so each can learn its own geometry.
mf.layer_tip_branch_mlp: This table feeds the MLP branch (concatenation + dense layers).
mf.layer_tip_product: GMF product: the user vector times the item vector element by element (k numbers); summed with weights by the output layer it is a dot product, the MF prediction inside the network.
mf.layer_tip_concat: Concatenation: the pieces side by side, no arithmetic, no parameters; the dense layers read them together.
mf.layer_tip_concat_mlp: Start of the MLP branch: the user and item vectors side by side, no arithmetic, no parameters; the dense ReLU layers after it learn a non-linear interaction the product cannot express.
mf.layer_tip_concat_item: Concatenation: the film's embedding and its genre summary side by side, no arithmetic, no parameters.
mf.layer_tip_concat_out: The two branches meet: GMF product and MLP output side by side; the output layer's weights decide how much each counts.
mf.layer_tip_dense_relu: Dense layer: every output is a weighted sum of all inputs plus a bias, then ReLU cuts negatives to zero (that is why no bar hangs below the line). |θ| = inputs × outputs + outputs.
mf.layer_tip_dense_linear: Dense layer: every output is a weighted sum of all inputs plus a bias. |θ| = inputs × outputs + outputs.
mf.layer_tip_features: Genre multi-hot: 1 for each genre of the film, 0 otherwise; the only side information in the hybrid model.
mf.layer_tip_genre_dense: Dense layer over the genre vector: compresses the genres into a few numbers before they join the film's embedding.
mf.layer_tip_output: Output unit: a weighted sum of the last layer plus a bias, linear; its one number is the rating (clipped to the scale only when the page's clip option is on).
mf.layer_tip_cb_terms: The target film's input terms: its TF-IDF row cut to the terms the network uses and scaled to length 1. No parameters; the bars are the first few terms' values.
mf.layer_tip_cb_hidden: Hidden layer: {n} units, each a weighted sum of all the film's terms (weights W, no bias) cut at zero by ReLU, which is why no bar hangs below the line. |θ| = terms × {n}.
mf.layer_tip_cb_output: Output unit: a weighted sum of the hidden units (weights v, no bias), linear. Its one number is the deviation from this user's mean rating; the user's mean plus this deviation is the prediction.
mf.layer_tip_item_content: The film's content row: its TF-IDF weights over the selected fields (genres, keywords, themes), cut to the most frequent terms and scaled to length 1; a term's weight is high when it is typical for this film and rare among films. Catalogue data, no rating in it, the same row for every user. No parameters. Effect: switch the film terms group off and the network stops seeing what the film is about.
mf.layer_tip_user_profile: The user's taste profile over the same terms (Rocchio): each training film's terms weighted by the rating minus the user's mean - liked films push up, disliked ones down - then scaled to length 1. From the training ratings only. No parameters. Effect: switch the user profile group off and the network stops seeing what this user likes in terms of content.
mf.layer_tip_user_stats: The user's rating statistics from the training ratings - how many (as log(1 + n)), their mean and their spread - each standardised over all users, so 0 is the average user. No parameters. Effect: switch the user statistics group off and the network no longer knows whether this user rates high or low.
mf.layer_tip_item_numeric: The film's numbers: its release year and how many training ratings it has (as log(1 + n)), each standardised over all films, so 0 is the average film. No parameters. Effect: switch the film numbers group off and the network no longer sees how old or how widely rated the film is.
mf.layer_tip_item_dense: The content tower: a small sub-network - dense ReLU layers - that squeezes the film's long content row into a short vector before it is joined with the rest. |θ| = inputs × outputs + outputs. Effect: wider layers = more capacity for the content and many more parameters; the last layer's width is how many numbers the join receives from this tower.
mf.layer_tip_user_dense: The profile tower: a small sub-network - dense ReLU layers - that squeezes the user's taste profile into a short vector before it is joined with the rest. |θ| = inputs × outputs + outputs. Effect: wider layers = more capacity for the profile and many more parameters; the last layer's width is how many numbers the join receives from this tower.
mf.layer_tip_embedding_features: Embedding table: one learned list of {n} numbers for each user (or film); the id picks its row, the bars are that row. Training adjusts the lists so that similar users and films get similar ones. |θ| = rows × {n}. Effect: a larger size = more capacity and more overfitting on few ratings; with the ids group off this table is gone.
mf.layer_tip_join_features: The join (concatenation): everything the network reads, laid side by side as one vector of {n} numbers - {parts}. No arithmetic and no parameters: nothing here multiplies a user vector by a film vector. The dense layers after it (the MLP) mix the numbers, and that mixing is where who, what and content meet. Effect: switch an input group off and its part leaves this vector.
mf.layer_tip_mlp_features: MLP layer ({n} units): every output is a weighted sum of ALL the numbers of the stage before it plus a bias, then ReLU. |θ| = inputs × outputs + outputs. This is where the network mixes who, what and content. Effect: more or wider layers can learn more complex interactions and overfit sooner.
mf.network_features_reading: What you see: the user's side on the left, the film's on the right, from the top down to the rating. The join receives {sum} numbers laid side by side (its box adds them up); nothing multiplies a user vector by a film vector, the dense layers after it mix them. Hover a box for what it does.
mf.layer_tip_item_content_nz: For this film {nz} of the {n} terms are non-zero ({fields}); every other term is zero, so most of this vector is empty.
mf.layer_tip_user_profile_nz: This profile has {nz} non-zero terms of {n}: the terms of the {films} films the user rated in training ({pos} pushed up, {neg} pushed down); every other term is zero.
mf.layer_tip_relu_zeros: “{nz} of {n}” counts the units that are on for this pair; the other {z} output zero, and a flat bar at the baseline is one of them.
mf.no_side_inputs: This network has no side inputs: only the ids go in.
mf.side_count_item: {nz} of the {n} terms are non-zero for this film.
mf.side_count_user: {nz} of the {n} terms are non-zero in this profile.
mf.layer_tip_bars: The bars show the first few of this stage's values.
mf.layer_tip_relu: ReLU keeps a positive value and turns a negative one into zero, so no bar of this box hangs below the line. It is what makes the stack non-linear: without it the layers would collapse into one linear model and could not learn how user, film and content interact.
mf.layer_tip_bars_features: The bars are this box's numbers for this pair - the first six when there are more, “+k” counting the rest - in order, on one scale for the whole diagram: up is positive, down is negative, a flat bar is zero.
mf.layer_tip_bars_largest: The bars are this box's six largest numbers for this pair, biggest first, on one scale for the whole diagram: up is positive, down is negative; “+k” counts the numbers not drawn, all of them smaller.
mf.layer_tip_read_n: “n = {n}” is how many numbers the box holds.
mf.layer_tip_read_n_theta: “n = {n}” is how many numbers the box holds, |θ| how many weights it learned.
mf.values_note: The vectors the network passes on for this pair, stage by stage, in the order of the walk. Outlined: the stage the step is on; tinted: the stages that feed it. Each row shows its first six numbers (a wide input its six largest) and the same six as bars on one scale for the whole diagram - up positive, down negative, flat zero.
mf.values_largest_tip: A wide input shows its six largest numbers, biggest first; every number not shown is smaller.
mf.values_none: This trace has no network stages to list.
mf.factors_idle: No factor matrices for this trace. The factor view exists for FunkSVD and ALS: BPR learns scores for ranking, EASE is not a factorization, and a trace with no refit has no training run.
mf.factors_info: The model's value for EVERY cell of the watched users × films, rated or not: R̂ = μ + b_u + b_i + P·Qᵀ. Rows and columns are those of the sub-matrix tab (the active user and the target film first). P has one row per watched user, Qᵀ one column per watched film. Under a training rating: r − r̂, what training shrinks. A faded cell is a rating held out for validation: the model was not trained on it. An unrated cell has no residual. The target film's value stays hidden (?) until the prediction phase. The two frames are the initial weights and the epoch the trainer kept.
mf.factors_hidden: The first {shown} of the {k} factors are written out.
mf.factors_basis: With k = {k} the latent-space panel shows the first two principal components of these factors; the numbers here are the factors themselves (raw P and Q).
mf.factors_key: Under a trained cell: r − r̂ (the rating minus the model's value). Faded: held out for validation. ?: the target, hidden until the prediction.
mf.factors_p: P: the factors of the watched users (one row each)
mf.factors_q: Qᵀ: the factors of the watched films (one column each)
mf.factors_target_hidden: the target film's value is the answer: it is shown from the prediction phase on
mf.factors_cell_valid: rating {r}: held out for validation, not trained on
mf.factors_cell_none: no rating: the model's value alone
mf.factors_formula_with_bias: R̂ = μ + b_u + b_i + P·Qᵀ, μ = {mu}
mf.factors_topk_formula_with_bias: r̂ = μ + b_u + b_j + p_u · q_j for every film j, μ = {mu}; the {k} highest are the list
mf.factors_topk_formula_no_bias: r̂ = μ + p_u · q_j for every film j, μ = {mu}; the {k} highest are the list
mf.factors_topk_key: One row: the user's factors times each film's column of Qᵀ give a score per film. Outlined: the films the cut keeps. Under a film the user has rated: that rating and the residual.
mf.factors_topk_info: The same fitted model, asked about every film at once: the user's row of P (and bias) against each film's column of Qᵀ gives its score r̂. The first columns are the films at the top of the list, then some films the user has rated, for comparison (their r̂ is the model's fit to a known rating). The scores stay hidden (?) until the scoring step; the cut outlines the films the list keeps.
mf.factors_topk_hidden: the scores are written at the scoring step
