rs.title: Recommender systems
rs.text: A recommender system starts from what users did — ratings, clicks, lists — and predicts what they have **not** seen yet: a missing rating or a ranked list. Everything on this board is a different answer to one question: what fills the gaps in the matrix?

clas_vs_rs.title: Not classification: matrix completion
clas_vs_rs.text: In classification one column is the target and every row has its features. In a recommender **any cell can be missing and any column can be the target**: the ratings matrix has holes everywhere, so rows and columns both carry information — the seed of user-based and item-based CF.

problem_types.title: Problem formulations: prediction vs ranking
problem_types.text: What exactly must the system produce? Two formulations, and they decide both the model **and** the metric: **1 · predict a rating** or **2 · produce a ranking**. Two variants cut across both - implicit feedback (no ratings at all) and context / sequence awareness (time, place, order). Step through them (Space) or click an item on the card.
problem_types.rating_text: Explicit ratings in, one missing cell out: "how many stars will U1 give I5?" — on the toy matrix uCF says **5.11**. Judged by MAE / RMSE. The Netflix-Prize formulation, and the matrix-completion picture at the centre of this board.
problem_types.topn_text: An ordered list of N unseen items: "which ten films go on the home screen tonight?" Only the top of the list matters, so P@K, nDCG and AUC judge it. Most deployed systems solve this one, even when they were trained on ratings.
problem_types.implicit_text: No stars, only actions: watched, clicked, added to a list. Positives exist, negatives do not — an unwatched film is not a disliked film, and the missing entries are not missing at random (MNAR). BPR and EASE rank from positives alone.
problem_types.context_text: "What next — tonight, on a phone, after this film?" Time, place, device or the order of past items become inputs. The textbook's advanced chapters; in this course time only decides the train / test split and is never a feature.

goals.title: Goals & metrics
goals.text: Two lists that steer everything else on the board. The **operational goals** say what a good recommendation is; the **performance metrics** say how we measure it — and a metric that ignores a goal quietly optimises it away. Step through the items (Space) or click one on the card.
goals.relevance_text: Recommend what the user will actually like: the obvious goal, and the one every model optimises first. Measured by how close r̂ is to the true rating, or how many relevant items reach the top of the list. Relevance alone yields the safe, obvious list — hence the next three goals.
goals.novelty_text: Something the user does **not** already know. The ten most popular films score high on relevance and near zero on novelty. Measured as the mean unpopularity of the recommended items: the less often an item is rated, the more novel it is.
goals.serendipity_text: Pleasantly unexpected **and** liked: a film the user would not have found alone and enjoyed anyway. Harder than novelty — it needs a baseline of "obvious" recommendations to compare against, and a way to know the user liked the surprise.
goals.diversity_text: Not ten sequels: the list should spread across genres, eras and styles. Intra-list diversity is one minus the mean pairwise similarity of the recommended items; it usually costs a little accuracy and buys a lot of usefulness.
goals.side_user_text: For the user a recommendation must be relevant — and **trusted**. An explanation ("because you watched …", "members like you rated it") turns a guess into advice they can act on; a list they cannot read is ignored. Every step-through in this lab is such an explanation.
goals.side_provider_text: The provider wants **conversion** (a click, a purchase, a play), **retention** (come back tomorrow) and **long-tail sales** (move the whole catalogue, not only the hits). These goals can pull against the user's; the evaluation protocol decides which one the model is actually optimising.
goals.side_society_title: Society: fairness and the filter bubble
goals.side_society_text: A third party never clicks: the public. A recommender decides who gets **exposure**, so it can starve new creators and small catalogues; and by feeding everyone more of the same it narrows what each person sees - the **filter bubble**. Coverage and Gini on the Metrics page measure the concentration; the remedy is a re-ranking rule, not a better predictor.
goals.accuracy_text: For rating prediction: how far r̂ is from the true rating over the held-out cells. MAE = mean |r − r̂|; RMSE squares the errors first, so large misses weigh more. On the toy matrix the popularity baseline reaches MAE 1.4 on the five test cells.
goals.ranking_text: For top-N: judge the top of the list, not every rating. Precision@K (how many of the K shown are relevant), recall@K (how many relevant items were shown), nDCG (relevant items near the top count more), AUC (a relevant item outranks an irrelevant one). Report at least two cut-offs (K = 10, 20) over the full ranking of the unseen items.
goals.coverage_text: Can the system recommend the whole catalogue, or only its head? Item coverage counts the items that ever get recommended; the Gini of item exposure shows how concentrated they are. A system that only ever shows 50 films is "accurate" and useless for discovery.
goals.beyond_text: The goals above, turned into numbers: mean novelty of the list, intra-list diversity, long-tail share. In the classroom lab the baseline battery on the Metrics page printed them next to MAE and nDCG, because a single accuracy number hides exactly these.

challenges.title: Challenges
challenges.text: Four things every recommender fights, whatever its family: cold start, sparsity, popularity bias and scale. They decide which branch of this tree is usable for a given dataset - and they are why the branches exist at all.
challenges.cold_start_text: A new user has no row to compare, a new item has no column: neighbourhood CF has nothing to work with. Content-based methods can recommend a described item on day one, knowledge-based ones ask the user, hybrids switch between the sources until the data arrives.
challenges.sparsity_text: Most of the matrix is empty: under 2% of the cells in MovieLens small, while the toy matrix is 90% full. A few items collect most of the ratings and a long tail collects almost none, so neighbours are scarce exactly where a recommendation would be most valuable. The Data page shows the Lorenz curve and the Gini of every dataset.
challenges.popularity_text: Learn from a skewed log and you recommend the skew: popular items get more exposure, gather more ratings and become more popular. Accuracy metrics reward this; coverage, Gini and novelty expose it. A popularity baseline is the first thing to beat - and the first thing to inspect.
challenges.scalability_text: User neighbourhoods are recomputed at every request and grow with the number of users; item neighbourhoods and latent-factor models are computed once and answer with a dot product. With millions of users the model-based branch is not a preference but a necessity.

cf.title: Collaborative filtering
cf.text: CF uses **only the ratings matrix**: no genres, no descriptions. Users who agreed in the past will agree again; items rated alike will keep being rated alike. Two families: **memory-based** (neighbourhoods, computed at prediction time) and **model-based** (a model is fitted first).

memb.title: Memory-based: the matrix is the model
memb.text: Nothing is trained. To predict a cell, look at the rows and columns around it: a user is a **row vector**, an item a **column vector**, and similarity between vectors is the whole machinery. The uCF and iCF pages are this idea with Pearson, cosine or Jaccard plugged in.

ucf.title: User-based CF (uCF)
ucf.text: Compare the active user's **row** with every other row over the items they co-rated. The most similar users are the neighbours; their ratings of the target item, centred on their own means, are combined with the active user's mean. On the toy 5×6 matrix, U1's rating of I5 comes out as **5.11**.

icf.title: Item-based CF (iCF)
icf.text: Now compare **columns**: how similar is the target item to the items the active user has already rated? Item neighbourhoods are more stable than user neighbourhoods, which is why large catalogues (the classic Amazon paper) went this way. Same toy cell, item-based: **4.61**.

modelb.title: Model-based CF
modelb.text: Fit a model on the observed cells first, predict from the model later. The family is wide — association **rules**, **Bayesian** classifiers, decision trees — and two members matter most in this course: latent-factor models (matrix factorization) and neural black boxes.

mf.title: Matrix factorization
mf.text: Give every user and every item a short vector of latent factors; a rating is their dot product plus biases. Fitting by SGD (FunkSVD) or alternating least squares fills the whole matrix at once; EASE is a closed-form cousin. Toy FunkSVD predicts **4.51** for the same cell (true value 4.5).

blackbox.title: Neural black boxes
blackbox.text: A neural network takes (u, i) — ids, embeddings, maybe genres — and outputs r̂. It can fit anything, including noise: on a toy matrix with a few dozen ratings an MLP overfits within a few epochs. That is exactly why the next node exists.

eval_protocol.title: Evaluation protocol
eval_protocol.text: A recommender is judged on cells it never saw, against a baseline it has to beat, with metrics that match the problem type, and with the traps named in advance. Four steps, in this order; in the classroom lab the Metrics page ran them and the pitfall gallery showed what happens when one is skipped.
eval_protocol.baseline_text: Before any personalisation: rank the items by how many users liked them and hand everyone the same list. It is the reference engine of the Metrics battery and the fallback a live system serves to a brand-new user. A method that cannot beat it on the held-out cells has learnt nothing about the user - and the list itself is where popularity bias enters.
eval_protocol.split_text: Hold out each user's latest interactions (or everything after a global cut-off) as the test part; tune and stop early on a validation part carved from the training data; touch the test part once, at the end. A random split leaks the future into the past. Toy matrix: 22 training cells, 5 test cells.
eval_protocol.metrics_text: Rating prediction: MAE / RMSE. Top-N: precision, recall and nDCG at two cut-offs over the full ranking of the unseen items, plus AUC. Always next to them: coverage, Gini, novelty, diversity. Five seeds, mean ± std, paired tests against a baseline battery (Popularity, ItemKNN, MF, EASE). Online, the same question is asked with clicks and conversions in an A/B test; that ladder is on the system board.
eval_protocol.pitfalls_text: k-core or normalisation **before** the split, a library correlation instead of the course's Pearson, a signed denominator, a binarised AUC: each looks plausible and is wrong. Observed ratings are **missing not at random (MNAR)**: a cell is empty because the user never saw the item, not because they disliked it, so an offline gain never guarantees an online one. The gallery shows right and wrong side by side.

cbrs.title: Content-based RS
cbrs.text: Content-based systems describe **items** by their attributes (genres, keywords, text) and build a model **for the target user alone**, from that user's own ratings. Other users never enter the picture: a brand-new item with a description can be recommended on day one, but the user stays inside their own taste.

cbrs_table.title: Item profiles and the user's verdicts
cbrs_table.text: Each row is an item's feature vector (which genres it has); the last column is what the target user thought of it. Learn which features go with high ratings — TF-IDF weights, a nearest-neighbour rule or a small classifier — and score the unseen items. Toy, genres only: **4.65** for U1 → I5. Today the columns are usually embeddings learnt from text or images rather than hand-made genre flags; the classifier on top is the same idea.

kbrs.title: Knowledge-based RS
kbrs.text: When purchases are rare and expensive (cars, flats, cameras) there is no rating history to mine. Knowledge-based systems ask the user for **requirements** and match them against item attributes with explicit constraints or similar past cases. No lab module: the course's data has no such interaction.

gbrs.title: Graph-based RS
gbrs.note: No graph recommender in the lab.
gbrs.text: Put users and items on a bipartite graph and let similarity travel along **paths**: two users are related through the items they share, an item through the users who rated it, and random walks reach beyond direct neighbours — useful when the matrix is very sparse. The similarity atlas shows the neighbour graph of this idea.

hybrid.title: Hybrid RS
hybrid.text: No single source is enough: CF fails on new items, content fails on taste it has never seen, knowledge needs a dialogue. Hybrids **combine** them — weighted blends, switching by confidence, cascades, feature augmentation — and the ensemble is usually the strongest single system. In the lab: CF and content blended with α, or switched by neighbour count.
hybrid.weighted_text: Two scores, one weighted sum: r̂ = α·CF + (1 − α)·CB. The hybrid walk (weighted and switching, with the TF-IDF profile) lives in its own section two lectures ahead; the content-based pages show the content side. At α = 0.5 the toy cell U1 → I5 comes out at **4.63** (CF alone 4.61, content alone 4.65).
hybrid.switching_text: One recommender per situation: content when the CF neighbourhood is too thin, CF otherwise. The lab switches on the number of usable neighbours — the cold-start user gets content, the well-known user gets CF.
hybrid.cascade_text: One recommender ranks, the next refines: CF proposes the candidates, content or business rules re-rank them. This is the candidate generation → ranking → re-ranking chain of the system board.
hybrid.feature_aug_text: The output of one recommender becomes an input feature of the next: the content profile (the +i on the board) enters the collaborative model as an extra column, so CF can score an item nobody has rated yet.
hybrid.meta_level_text: Not a score but a whole learned **model** is handed over: the target-user content model of one step becomes the representation a collaborative step compares users by.
hybrid.mixed_text: Both lists are shown, side by side: a home page with a collaborative row and a content row is a mixed hybrid — the user does the combining.

wrap_up.title: The whole map
wrap_up.text: Every leaf on this board is a family of answers to the same question; in the classroom lab you picked a user and a film and watched the numbers appear step by step. Same data, same question, five families of answers.

what.title: What it is
what.body: Content-based filtering recommends items that are **similar, in their own attributes, to items the user liked before**. It needs two things: a description of every item (genres, keywords, cast, a text) and a profile of the target user, built from that user's own ratings. The ratings of other users play no role. That is the difference from collaborative filtering, which looks for correlations between the rating patterns of many users and does not look at what the items are. The consequence runs both ways: a new item can be recommended as soon as it has a description, but a new user has to rate something before the method has anything to work with.

pipeline.title: The pipeline
pipeline.figure_label: The three stages of content-based filtering, from left to right: preprocessing and feature extraction, learning the user profile, filtering and recommendation

s1.name: Preprocessing and feature extraction
s1.tip: Turn each item's description into a vector of features in a common vector space. Which features count, and how much, depends on the domain (a film's title or lead actor may matter more than a word of its synopsis).

s2.name: Learning the user profile
s2.tip: From the user's own ratings, build a model that belongs to this one user. It is a classification problem when the feedback is categorical (like or dislike) and a regression problem when it is numerical (a star rating).

s3.name: Filtering and recommendation
s3.tip: Apply the profile to the candidate items and rank them. This step has to be fast enough to run while the user waits.

pipeline.lab: **In this lab.** Step 1 is the **Fields** choice (genres, keywords, themes, people, text) and the TF-IDF weights that follow from it; step 2 is the **User profile** view; step 3 is the ranked list, optionally re-ranked for diversity.

families.title: Memory-based or model-based?
families.intro: The split that organises the collaborative chapters runs through content-based methods as well: a **memory-based** method goes back to the user's rated films every time it predicts, a **model-based** method fits a summary of them first and predicts from that summary alone. The three methods of this week sit at different points of that line. The table says, for each method, what is kept between two predictions, where the work happens and what the answer is.

knn.kept: The TF-IDF vector of every film over the chosen fields. Nothing about the user is stored.
knn.train: No training. At prediction time the target film's cosine to each film the user rated is computed, and the prediction is the weighted average of the user's own ratings of the k most similar films: a **predicted rating**, by the same two steps as item-based collaborative filtering.
knn.book: Section 4.4.1, nearest-neighbour methods; the two steps are those of the item-based method of chapter 2.

profile.family: **A Rocchio profile**, under its own name: the profile is built before any prediction, but nothing in it is fitted, so neither label is used here.
profile.kept: One vector per user: the sum of the vectors of the films the user rated, each weighted by the rating's signed distance from the user's mean (liked films pull the profile towards them, disliked films push it away), divided by the sum of those distances without their signs. Its length does not matter: the score is a cosine.
profile.train: One pass over the user's ratings builds the profile. Prediction is the cosine between the profile and the film: a **similarity score** between −1 and 1, not a rating.
profile.book: Named in section 4.3.3 as the Rocchio classifier; the method is Rocchio's relevance feedback (Manning et al., 2008).

model.kept: One set of parameters per user, fitted on that user's own films: for ridge regression a weight per term; for the small network a hidden layer of sixteen units (terms × 16 weights) and sixteen output weights, no bias.
model.train: Training first, prediction from the fitted parameters alone. Ridge: the weights minimise the squared error on the user's ratings with a penalty on their size, and the prediction is the user's mean plus the weighted sum of the film's term weights. Network: the same squared error without a penalty, lowered by a fixed number of Adam steps, and the prediction is the user's mean plus the output of the hidden units. Either way a **predicted rating**; the rated films are not consulted again.
model.book: Sections 4.4.5, regression-based models, and 4.4.6, other learning models.

families.src: Aggarwal (2016), sections 4.3.3, 4.4.1, 4.4.5 and 4.4.6; the memory-based / model-based split is the textbook's division of collaborative filtering into chapters 2 and 3. Rocchio: Manning et al. (2008).

vs.title: Content-based or collaborative?
vs.same_steps: The item-similarity method runs the same two steps as item-based collaborative filtering: a similarity between items, then a weighted average of the user's own ratings of the most similar items (Σ w·r / Σ w, the neighbours being the films the user rated). What changes is where the similarity comes from: not the columns of the rating matrix but the item × term TF-IDF matrix. That single change explains the rest of the table: no other user is needed (a brand-new film can be recommended on day one), the method cannot surprise (it recommends more of the same, overspecialisation), and the similarity lives in [0, 1], so there is no negative neighbour to argue about. The literature calls this the nearest-neighbour content-based method (Aggarwal 2016, §4.4.1); 'memory-based' is the name Breese, Heckerman and Kadie (1998) gave the collaborative family, borrowed above for the content-based methods that keep no model.
vs.callout: A neighbourhood method predicts what you gave the look-alikes; its largest errors land on your favourites.

new_item.label: New-item cold start
new_item.cb: Covered: the item's description is enough to place it next to the others.
new_item.cf: A problem: an item nobody has rated has no pattern to correlate.

new_user.label: New-user cold start
new_user.cb: A problem, and possibly a worse one: the profile is learned from this user's own ratings, and a classifier needs enough examples not to overfit.
new_user.cf: A problem as well: a user with no ratings has no neighbours.

explain.label: Explanations
explain.cb: In terms of item features: "because of this genre, this actor, these keywords".
explain.cf: Often not possible: the reason is a pattern among other users.

effort.label: Engineering effort
effort.cb: Low: off-the-shelf text classifiers apply, and each user's problem is small.
effort.cf: Higher: one model over all users and items.

overspec.label: Overspecialization, novelty, serendipity
overspec.cb: Tends to find items like those the user has already seen, so little novelty and little serendipity.
overspec.cf: Peer groups can bring in items unlike anything the user has seen.

other_data.label: Use of other users' data
other_data.cb: None: the ratings of everyone else are set aside.
other_data.cf: It is the basis of the method.

combo.label: Combination
combo.cb: Rarely used alone; it complements collaborative filtering, which is the idea behind hybrid systems.
combo.cf: Gains from content knowledge in a hybrid.

vs.source: Aggarwal (2016), section 4.5. The table is the lab's reading of the book's points, not a table from the book.

cold.title: Cold start
cold.intro: What each method can do when the user or the item is new.

known_known.cb: **Works:** the profile can be compared with the item's description.
known_known.cf: **Works:** there are rating patterns to correlate.

known_new.cb: **Covered:** the item's description is enough to place it next to the others.
known_new.cf: **A problem:** an item nobody has rated has no pattern to correlate.

new_known.cb: **A problem, possibly a worse one:** the profile is learned from this user's own ratings, and a classifier needs enough examples.
new_known.cf: **A problem as well:** a user with no ratings has no neighbours.

new_new.cb: **A problem:** there is no profile to compare with the description.
new_new.cf: **A problem:** no ratings on either side, so no pattern and no neighbours.

field.title: Where the field went
field.intro: Content-based ideas did not disappear; they moved into larger systems and richer content.
field.b1: **Surveys of the trend.** The content-based literature has been surveyed as a whole (Lops et al., 2019), and as the semantics of content, that is, what the words and tags mean and not only which words occur (Musto et al., 2022).
field.b2: **More than keywords.** Content can be an image, a sound or a video clip as well as a text; the multimedia line of work builds recommenders on such content (Deldjoo et al., 2020).
field.b3: **Learned representations.** Recent work asks whether a model that works from the content itself (its modality) can replace a model that sees only item identifiers (Yuan et al., 2023), and surveys language models used for recommendation (Wu et al., 2024).
field.lab: **What the lab shows this week.** Three ideas from this literature are built into the pages: **re-ranking a list for diversity** (maximal marginal relevance: Carbonell and Goldstein, 1998; applied to recommendation lists by Ziegler et al., 2005), which is the usual answer to overspecialization, a **table of feature-level explanations** (in the spirit of Vig et al., 2009), which shows which features produced a score and how much each contributed, and a **per-user content model** (Aggarwal, 2016, sections 4.4.5-4.4.6), which learns the user's taste from the features of their own films: one model per user and no other users - small data, small model.
field.named: **Named, not built.** Calibrated recommendations (Steck, 2018), Rocchio's original update with separate weights for liked and disliked films (the user-profile page uses one centred weight instead), BM25 weighting, factorization machines, the tag genome, and sentence embeddings of the film overview.

what.guide: Say it in one line: "similar to what you liked, judged by the film's own description, never by other people's ratings"; then show the two things the method needs, a description and a profile.
what.q1: Why does it ignore other users' ratings?
what.a1: That is what makes it content-based: the similarity comes from the attributes of the items and the only ratings used are the target user's. The price is lower diversity and novelty, because nothing from other people's tastes can widen the list.
what.q2: What is an item description here?
what.a2: The attribute lists of the film table: genres, keywords, themes, people (cast, directors, writers), and optionally the text of the overview. In a text-heavy domain it would be the words of the description.
what.q3: Can it recommend a film nobody has rated?
what.a3: Yes, as long as the film has a description: its position among the other films does not depend on ratings.
what.q4: Is this the same as keyword search?
what.a4: No. A search matches a query typed now; here the "query" is a profile learned from what the user rated, and the match is a similarity score.

pipeline.guide: Walk the three boxes left to right and say which are offline (the first two) and which online (the third); then recall the same three steps in the classroom lab's walk.
pipeline.q1: Why is the profile learned offline but the filtering online?
pipeline.a1: Learning can take its time and be redone when ratings change; filtering has to answer while the user waits, so it must be efficient.
pipeline.q2: Is learning the profile classification or regression?
pipeline.a2: It depends on the feedback: a categorical rating (like or dislike) makes it a classification problem, a numerical rating (stars) a regression problem. The lab's profile is built from numerical ratings.
pipeline.q3: Why not use every word as a feature?
pipeline.a3: Noisy words invite overfitting. Words can be removed before learning (stop words, rare or uninformative terms), and the lab's feature selection ranks the features by how well they separate liked from disliked films.
pipeline.a4: A weight per feature and item: how often the feature occurs in the item, damped, times how rare the feature is among the items that carry that kind of feature (the inverse document frequency: the logarithm of the number of those items divided by the number that carry this feature).
pipeline.q5: Why does the textbook example turn "hoping" into "hop"?
pipeline.a5: Stemming cuts a word to a stem so that its forms count as one feature; the example is the textbook's. The lab's stemmer (Snowball English, Porter2) writes the stem as "hope" (hoping, hope, hopes → hope); the slide keeps the textbook's spelling "hop".
pipeline.q6: Why is the "log" damping 1 + ln(count) and not log(count)?
pipeline.a6: A feature that occurs once has a count of 1, and the logarithm of 1 is 0: every tag would vanish. Adding 1 keeps it at 1 and still damps larger counts.
pipeline.q7: Is the profile score a predicted rating?
pipeline.a7: No. It is a similarity between the profile and the film, between −1 and 1. Turning it into a rating would be a regression model, which the textbook treats separately.

families.guide: Point at the three rows and say what each page keeps between two predictions: only the film vectors, one profile vector, or fitted parameters. Then ask which rows answer with a rating: the first and the third; the second answers with a similarity.
families.q1: Is the Rocchio profile a model?
families.a1: It is built before prediction, as a model would be, but nothing in it is fitted or optimised: it is a weighted average of the rated films' vectors. The page keeps it under its own name for that reason.
families.q2: Why is kNN item similarity memory-based when the film vectors are computed in advance?
families.a2: Because every prediction still goes back to the user's rated films one by one and averages their ratings; the vectors only make that lookup fast, they are not a model of the user.
families.q3: What makes the per-user content model model-based?
families.a3: Its parameters are fitted by minimising an error over the user's own ratings, and a prediction uses those parameters alone; the rated films are not consulted again.

vs.guide: Read the table row by row and stop at two rows: cold start (what each method can and cannot do) and overspecialization (what the list looks like in a few weeks). The last row, combination, is the bridge to hybrid systems, which get their own section two lectures later.
vs.a1: Neither: they fail in different places. Content-based copes with a new item and explains itself; collaborative finds surprising items. That is why they are combined.
vs.q2: Why can a new user be worse off with content-based?
vs.a2: Its profile comes only from this user's own ratings, and a classifier needs enough training examples to avoid overfitting; collaborative methods can borrow from other users once the new user has a few ratings.
vs.q3: Why can content-based explain and collaborative often cannot?
vs.a3: Content-based scores are sums over item features, so the reason is a list of features; a collaborative score comes from a pattern among other users that has no name.
vs.a4: The tendency to keep recommending items like those already seen. A user who liked three horror films gets horror films; a peer group might bring in something else.
vs.q5: Is the table from the book?
vs.a5: No: the book states points and the lab arranged them into a table, so the cells follow the book's points but the layout is the lab's.

field.guide: One minute: the idea survived by moving into hybrids and richer content; then name the three things the lab does build this week, a diversity re-ranking, a feature-level explanation table and a per-user content model.
field.a1: The book describes it as rarely used alone and usually combined with other methods, and the surveys of the area (Lops et al., 2019; Musto et al., 2022) are recent; the work listed here is about richer content and about combining it with learned models.
field.q2: Why is there no text-embedding step in the lab?

taxonomy.title: Taxonomy of hybrid systems
taxonomy.intro: No single recommender uses every kind of information well. Collaborative methods read the ratings of a community, content-based methods read the attributes of the items, and each is weak where the other is strong. A **hybrid system** combines them. The textbook sorts the ways of doing it into a tree with three branches: an **ensemble** takes the outputs of ready-made recommenders and merges them into one, a **monolithic** design is a single algorithm built to read several kinds of data, and a **mixed** system shows the outputs of several recommenders side by side. Every ensemble is a hybrid; not every hybrid is an ensemble. The seven leaves are the seven types of the table below. Hover a box to read what it means.
taxonomy.figure_label: The taxonomy of hybrid systems as a tree. Hybrid systems split into monolithic, ensembles and mixed. Monolithic holds feature combination and meta-level. Ensembles split into sequential (feature augmentation, cascade) and parallel (weighted, switching). A dotted line joins monolithic to feature augmentation.
taxonomy.open_hint: Click to open the lab page.

dotted.tip: The dotted line: feature augmentation is an ensemble as long as the next recommender is used as it is. When that recommender has to be adapted to read the new features it is technically monolithic, and the textbook marks the possibility with a dotted line.

taxonomy.lab: **In the classroom lab.** The weighted blend, switching and the Hybrid DNN had pages of their own; the meta-level hybrid is future work. Cascade, feature augmentation and mixed are named here without a lab page.
taxonomy.src: Aggarwal (2016), chapter 6, section 6.1: the textbook's taxonomy of hybrid systems, redrawn.

root.name: Hybrid systems
root.tip: Any recommender that combines more than one source of information or more than one algorithm.

monolithic.name: Monolithic
monolithic.tip: One algorithm, built to read several kinds of data at once. It cannot be taken apart into ready-made recommenders.

ensembles.name: Ensembles
ensembles.tip: Ready-made recommenders are run as black boxes and their outputs are combined into one output.

mixed.name: Mixed
mixed.tip: Mixed: nothing is merged; several recommenders present their lists side by side, each in its own labelled row. This is the design of the term project: the group projects of the second half of the term build a home screen of labelled rows.

sequential.name: Sequential
sequential.tip: The output of one recommender is the input of the next.

parallel.name: Parallel
parallel.tip: The recommenders work independently on the same input and their predictions are combined at the very end.

combination.name: Feature combination
combination.tip: Content features and collaborative features go into one representation, and a single algorithm (a regression, a factorization, a network) learns from all of it. It cannot tell which input came from behaviour and which from a profile.

meta.name: Meta-level
meta.tip: The model one recommender has learned becomes the input of the next. The usual case: the collaborative system finds its peers through content profiles but still predicts from the ratings.

augmentation.name: Feature augmentation
augmentation.tip: The output of one recommender is turned into features for the next, for instance a content model filling the empty cells of the rating matrix with pseudo-ratings before collaborative filtering runs on the denser matrix.

cascade.name: Cascade
cascade.tip: Each recommender refines the list of the one before it: a rough first ranking prunes the items, the second stage breaks the ties.

weighted.name: Weighted
weighted.tip: The predictions of several recommenders are added up with one weight each; the weights can be fixed or learned.

switching.name: Switching
switching.tip: A rule picks one recommender for the case at hand: content-based while the collaborative method has too little data, or whichever has the lowest error on held-out ratings.

designs.title: Parallel and sequential designs
designs.intro: The figure sorts the ensembles by how their recommenders are connected. In a **parallel** design the recommenders never see each other: each one reads the same input and the combiner works on their predictions at the very end. In a **sequential** design the output of one recommender feeds the next, so the order matters. Weighted and switching are parallel; cascade and the meta-level systems are sequential, and so is feature augmentation, with the caveat that it sometimes needs a small change to the recommender it feeds (the dotted line of the taxonomy). Meta-level is filed under monolithic in the tree because the second system has to be built to read the first one's model, but the model still flows from one to the next.
designs.figure_label: Two diagrams. Parallel design: the input goes to recommenders 1 to q side by side, their predictions P1 to Pq meet in a combiner, which gives the output. Sequential design: the input goes to recommender 1, its output to recommender 2, and so on to recommender q, then to the combiner and the output; dashed lines carry the input forward and every output to the combiner.

tip.input: The data and the question: the ratings, the item attributes, and the user and item to predict for.
tip.rec_parallel: A ready-made recommender used as a black box. It never sees the others: each one reads the same input.
tip.rec_sequential: A ready-made recommender used as a black box. It reads the output of the one before it, so the order matters.
tip.combine_parallel: Where the predictions meet: a weighted sum (weighted) or a rule that picks one recommender (switching).
tip.combine_sequential: Where the chain ends: the last recommender's output, or a combination of every output along the way.
tip.output: The one prediction, or the one ranked list, that the user sees.
tip.rail_input: Dashed: the later recommenders may read the original input as well, not only the output of the one before.
tip.rail_pred: Dashed: the combiner may read every recommender's output, not only the last one's.

designs.lab: **In this lab.** The weighted walk is the parallel design with a learned combiner: base recommenders predict the same held-out ratings, then a weight vector is fitted over their columns. Switching, the other parallel type, picks one of them instead of adding them up.
designs.src: Aggarwal (2016), chapter 6, section 6.1: parallel and sequential ensembles, redrawn.

types.title: The seven types
types.intro: The same seven names as the leaves of the tree, with what each one combines, how it is wired, and where the lab stands. The textbook gives each type a few lines; the lab's pages carry the numbers.

detail.weighted:
**What it combines.** The predictions of several base recommenders for the same user–film pair. In the lab: user-based kNN, item-based kNN, matrix factorization and the content-based model, each fitted on the training part of the ratings only.
**How it decides.** The blend is r̂ = β₀ + Σ αᵢ·pᵢ with the weights summing to one. The weights are learned on held-out ratings, the newest ratings of every user, never on the training ratings the bases have already seen; a ridge closed form and a projected gradient trajectory give the same answer. The intercept β₀ absorbs a level shift: the bases over-predict the newest ratings, and most of the gain in this cohort is that correction.
**Scope.** The weights are class-wide: learned on every user's held-out ratings. The literature also fits the weights per user, adapted from each user's feedback, or per group of items; this lab keeps one set for the whole class.
**In the classroom lab.** The split, the base table, the trajectory with β₀, the closed form and the blended prediction. Switches show the foils next to the right way: equal weights, weights fitted on the training ratings, no sum-to-one constraint, no ridge penalty.
**Pitfalls.** Weights fitted on the training ratings reward the base that memorised them. Heterogeneous bases, one reading ratings and one reading content, disagree for informative reasons, which is where the weights matter most. **Examples.** The Netflix Prize blends (Jahrer, Töscher and Legenstein 2010); the P-Tango newspaper recommender, as described in Burke (2002).
detail.switching:
**What it combines.** The same base recommenders, but only one of them answers a given case.
**How it decides.** A rule picks the base. **Bucket of models:** every base is scored on the active user's own newest held-out ratings (an MAE or RMSE leaderboard) and the winner predicts the target. **Neighbour rule:** use collaborative filtering while it has enough neighbours, otherwise the content-based model, which is the cold-start case.
**Scope.** The bucket chooses per user, once, on that user's own held-out ratings; the neighbour rule chooses per pair; the literature also switches on confidence, rating counts or a learned selector.
**In the classroom lab.** The bucket, the leaderboard, the winner's answer, the neighbour rule with its coverage. The foil picks the winner on the training ratings, shown next to the right way.
**Pitfalls.** A winner chosen on the training ratings is the base that overfits them. With few held-out ratings the leaderboard is noisy: the chosen base changes from student to student and rarely beats always-MF in this cohort, so a rule's gain is checked against the noise level. **Example.** DailyLearner, a news recommender that switches between its content-based and collaborative components (as described in Burke 2002).
detail.combination:
**What it combines.** Ids and content features in one model. There are no separate recommenders: the collaborative signal (who rated what) and the content signal (genres, keywords, themes, the user's taste profile) are input columns of a single learner.
**How it decides.** The network embeds the user and film ids, encodes the film's content fields and the user's profile in towers of their own, joins everything and predicts the rating; training stops early on a validation split and keeps the best weights.
**Training settings.** The feature network is trained with a small learning rate (0.001), mini-batches of 128 ratings, a little weight decay (0.0001) and 10 % dropout, for at most 30 epochs, with early stopping (patience 5) on a validation tail made of each user's newest ratings. With the plain recipe of the neural page (learning rate 0.01, batches of 16, no regularisation) the validation error fell to 0.850 by epoch 3 and jumped to 0.928 four epochs later; with this one it falls for five epochs to 0.845 and then stays flat, so the early-stopping rule has a clear best epoch to keep.
**In the classroom lab.** The named towers, the fit curve with its stop reason, the comparison with the ids-only variant (what the content adds), the training controls.
**Pitfalls.** The content tower helps most where ids are rare: new films, few ratings. A network trained past its best epoch overfits, which the page shows with and without early stopping. More inputs are not more signal unless they carry what the ids cannot. **Examples.** A rule learner over collaborative and content features (Burke 2002); Wide & Deep (Cheng et al. 2016) and neural collaborative filtering (He et al. 2017) are the modern monolithic designs.
detail.cascade:
- **What it is.** A strict order: the first recommender produces a ranking and the second only refines it, breaks ties and reorders the top; it can never bring back what the first one discarded.
- **Example.** EntreeC, where knowledge-based recommendation ranks restaurants and collaborative filtering breaks the ties (Burke 2002).
- **In the lab.** Not a page: the lesson is sequencing, which the switching page shows in its simplest form.
detail.augmentation:
- **What it is.** The output of one recommender becomes an input feature of the next: a content model fills the empty cells of the rating matrix with pseudo-ratings, then collaborative filtering runs on the denser matrix.
- **Example.** Content-boosted collaborative filtering (Melville, Mooney and Nagarajan 2002).
- **In the lab.** Not a lab page: it would reuse the content pages' profiles and the user-based page.
detail.meta:
- **What it is.** Two stages. The model learned by one recommender, not its output, becomes the input of the next: per-user content profiles, vectors of term weights, are compared to find peers, and the ratings of those peers make the prediction with the user-based formula. Same formula as the user-based page, different peers.
- **Example.** "Collaboration via content" (Pazzani 1999); Fab, as described in Burke (2002), used the idea for web pages.
- **In the lab.** Future work.
detail.mixed:
- **What it is.** Nothing is merged: the recommendations of several systems are presented together, each in its own labelled row, for instance a home screen with a collaborative row, a content row and a popularity row.
- **Example.** PTV, a television guide that lists content-based and collaborative suggestions side by side (Burke 2002).
- **Term project.** The group projects of the second half of the term build a mixed hybrid: a home screen where every recommender the group built fills its own labelled row (popularity, collaborative, content-based, a blend), nothing merged. Expected: each row names its method and the signal it reads, the rows can be compared for the same user, and the group can explain why a row recommends what it does. Groups state the scope of every choice their system makes: for the whole class, per user, per film or per pair.
- **In the lab.** Not a page: a presentation design, there is no single prediction to trace.

weighted.combines: The scores of several recommenders, added up with **one weight each**.
weighted.lab: A walk: base recommenders, their predictions on held-out ratings, the weights found by gradient steps and by regression, and the blend for one user and film.

switching.combines: Several recommenders, **one of which is chosen** for each case: by the data available, or by the lowest held-out error.
switching.lab: A walk: a leaderboard of the models on held-out ratings, and the rule that picks the winner.

cascade.combines: A chain: a first recommender **prunes and ranks roughly**, the next refines the list and breaks ties.
cascade.lab: No lab page: a content stage that proposes candidates and a collaborative stage that re-ranks them.

augmentation.combines: The output of one recommender becomes **features of the next**: content fills the empty cells, collaborative filtering then runs on the denser matrix.
augmentation.lab: No lab page: content-boosted collaborative filtering, with the pseudo-ratings given less weight than real ones.

combination.combines: Content and collaborative inputs in **one representation**, learned by a single algorithm.
combination.lab: A network over film ids, film content, the user's profile and activity statistics, on the classroom lab's Hybrid DNN page.

meta.combines: **The model** of one recommender is the input of the next: peers found through content, the ratings still make the prediction.
meta.lab: Future work: peers found through the taste profiles of the content-based pages, the user-based rule predicting from their ratings.

ensembles.title: Ensembles: bias and variance
ensembles.intro: Why combine at all? The expected squared error of a predictor splits into three parts: **bias**, a consistent miss because the model's assumptions are too narrow; **variance**, the answer changing when the training sample changes, which is overfitting; and **noise**, what no model can know. An ensemble can lower the first two. On the dartboard, bias is how far the centre of the hits lies from the bullseye, and variance is how widely they spread.
ensembles.figure_label: A two-by-two dartboard: rows are low and high bias, columns are low and high variance. Low bias and low variance: the hits are tight around the bullseye. Low bias, high variance: the hits are scattered around the bullseye. High bias, low variance: the hits are tight but off-centre. High bias, high variance: scattered and off-centre.

cell.ll: Low bias, low variance: the hits are tight and centred. This is the aim of a well-tuned model, and of an ensemble.
cell.lh: Low bias, high variance: the hits centre on the bullseye but scatter widely. A model like this overfits: a different training sample gives a different answer. Averaging many of them (bagging) pulls the scatter in.
cell.hl: High bias, low variance: the hits are tight but off-centre. The model is wrong in the same direction whatever sample it sees, so averaging copies of it does not help; a more expressive model, or one that corrects the previous model's mistakes (boosting), does.
cell.hh: High bias, high variance: off-centre and scattered, the worst of both.

ensembles.equation_caption: The error decomposition: the expected squared error is the squared bias plus the variance plus the noise.
ensembles.callout: Bagging attacks variance; boosting attacks bias.
ensembles.cf: The result carries over from classification to collaborative filtering. A missing rating can sit in any column of the matrix, but predicting one column from the others is the same kind of problem, so averaging models trained on resampled data lowers variance there too.
ensembles.netflix: The Netflix Prize shows it at scale: the two best entries of the contest, BellKor's Pragmatic Chaos and The Ensemble, were both ensemble systems (Aggarwal, 2016).

weighted.title: The weighted blend
weighted.intro: A weighted hybrid is the simplest ensemble: every base recommender predicts the rating, and the blend adds the predictions up, each times a weight. The weights start equal and are then **fitted on held-out ratings**, never on the ratings the bases were trained on: a base has already seen those and looks better there than it is.
weighted.blend_caption: The blend of q base recommenders; the weights start at 1/q.
weighted.loss_caption: The error to minimise over the held-out entries H, with a penalty on the size of the weights (ridge).
weighted.closed_caption: The regression alternative: the same minimum in one step (written for free weights; with the sum-to-one constraint the system gets one more equation). P holds one column of held-out predictions per base, r the held-out ratings.
weighted.b1: **Bases.** q recommenders, each fitted without the held-out ratings: user-based and item-based neighbours, matrix factorization, content-based.
weighted.b2: **Held-out entries H.** The newest share of every user's ratings (the lab's temporal rule), kept aside while the bases are fitted.
weighted.b3: **Gradient descent.** Start at equal weights and move them downhill on the loss; each step shortens the held-out error. The step size is one over the largest curvature of the loss: the steepest direction is corrected in a single step, the flatter ones creep.
weighted.b4: **Closed form.** It jumps to the minimum in one solve, as a check on where the descent is heading. The penalty keeps the weights stable even when the bases agree with each other.
weighted.b5: **Sum to one, or free.** By default the weights add up to one, so the blend is a weighted average of the bases and its level stays where the bases put it; the free option lets the weights rescale the level too. Either way a weight can be negative: the regression may use a base to correct the others.
weighted.kinds: **Homogeneous or heterogeneous?** Blending a neighbourhood method, a factorization and a regression model that all read the same rating matrix is the homogeneous case. Blending a collaborative recommender with a content-based one, which read different data, is the heterogeneous case; there the weights matter more, because the two disagree for reasons that carry real information.
weighted.lab: **In this lab.** The walk fits the weights on held-out ratings with gradient steps and with the regression, side by side, and shows the blend of one user and film with its numbers. Switch the bases on and off to compare the homogeneous set with the heterogeneous one.

weighted.label: The weighted walk
weighted.text: Pick a user and a film, and follow the split, the base predictions, the weights and the blend.

weighted.src: Aggarwal (2016), chapter 6, section 6.3. The three formulas are the textbook's recipe written out; the numbers come from the walk.

families.title: Ensemble families
families.intro: The textbook's ensemble methods, grouped by what they do to the error. Most of them need many fitted copies of one model; the lab starts with the learned blend and the choice of a winner, and names the others here.

bagging.name: Bagging adapted to rating matrices
bagging.how: Fit q copies of one algorithm on resampled rating matrices and take the **simple average**: rows drawn with replacement (a user can appear three times or not at all, and is predicted only where present), rows drawn without replacement, entries drawn with replacement (some ratings gain weight), or entries drawn without replacement (like dropout: part of every user and film stays). Equal weights, because the copies are exchangeable.

injection.name: Randomness injection
injection.how: Keep the data and randomise the algorithm: a neighbourhood method keeps k neighbours at random out of its top α·k, a factorization starts from different random initialisations; average the results. It can work where bagging does not, because the copies of bagging are too alike.

bucket.name: Bucket of models
bucket.how: Hold out a quarter to a third of the ratings, score every model on them with the mean squared or absolute error, and let the lowest win; the same rule tunes a parameter (each model is one value of it). The winner can change from user to user.
bucket.lowers: Neither: it **selects**, it does not combine.

stacking.name: Weighted blend and stacking
stacking.how: Learn the weights of the blend (or a small model on top of the predictions) from held-out ratings: a layer of base models with an ensemble model stacked above it.
stacking.lowers: **Bias**: the stack can express what no single base can.
stacking.lab: The weighted walk; a small network as the combiner may follow.

boosting.name: Boosting and cascades
boosting.how: Boosting works in rounds: the examples the last model got wrong gain weight, so each new model works on what the chain still misses. A cascade is the ranking version: a first stage prunes and roughly ranks, the next refines and breaks ties.

walk.left_out: in neither the bases nor the weights
walk.bridge: The four bases are the methods of the earlier pages with the same defaults, fitted here on the training part of the ratings only; the blend learns only how much to trust each of them.

text.class_split: Scope: the whole class. One held-out set from every user; one set of weights for everyone.
text.class_fit: Scope: the training ratings of the whole class; each base is one model for all users, and the content base builds one profile per user from the training ratings.
text.user_split: Scope: this user only. Only the active user's newest ratings are held out; everyone else's stay in training.
text.user_bucket: Scope: per user. The winner is chosen once for this user and answers every film of theirs.
text.user_film: Scope: per user × film. The choice is made for each pair from its neighbour count.

lit.class_weights: The literature also fits the weights per user, adapted from each user's feedback, or per group of items; this lab keeps one set for the whole class.
lit.user_bucket: The literature also switches on the first recommender's confidence, on rating counts (the cold-start rule), on ranking quality instead of error, or with a learned selector.

walk.blend_line_tip: The blend of the target film with its numbers in it: the intercept, then each weight times what its recommender says, added up. The table below spells out the same sum.
walk.profile_alpha_tip: {row}: the closed-form weight of {term} = {x} (above zero its answer is added to the blend, below zero it is subtracted)
walk.profile_says_tip: {term} predicts {x} for {row} - what this base says before the weights count
walk.chip_weights_tip: The weights that predicted the target: the closed form, the gradient steps or the equal start. Σα is their sum: 1 when they add up to one, anything else for free weights.
walk.chip_heldout_tip: The newest {frac} of the ratings of each user with at least {min} ratings were held out: the weights were learned on them and no base was fitted on them.
walk.chip_rmse_tip: The root mean squared error on the held-out ratings: the best single base against the blend with the weights used. A blend can be worse than its best base, and this is an offline error, not a promise about new ratings.
walk.chip_fit_train: weights fitted on the training entries (the right way: held-out entries)
walk.chip_fit_train_tip: The foil: the weights were fitted on the ratings every base was trained on, where the bases look better than they are. Switch "Weights fitted on" back to the held-out entries to see the difference.

bases.guide: Read the bases table top to bottom: how long each base took to fit, how many of its answers were fallbacks, how well it does alone on the held-out ratings. Then the held-out table: the active user's ratings come first, each with what every base said.
bases.q1: Why are the bases fitted without the held-out ratings?
bases.a1: So the weights can be learned on ratings the bases have not seen: a base looks better on its own training ratings than it will on new ones. The target film's rating is out of everything, the held-out entries included.
bases.a2: A base that cannot answer (a user with no neighbour, a film nobody else rated) answers with its own fallback, such as the user's mean. The table counts those answers instead of hiding them: a base with many fallbacks is weaker than its error alone suggests.
bases.q3: Why does one user's share of the held-out table matter?
bases.a3: The weights are global: one set for every user. If one user supplied most of the held-out ratings, the global weights would be that user's; the per-user cap keeps every share small, and the split step says how many held-out ratings the active user contributed.

weights.lead: What the gradient steps do: start from equal weights, projected gradient descent on the held-out RMSE under Σα = 1 with the intercept; the rows of the table are the weights after each step; the closed form is where they end.
weights.learns: The weights are learned on the held-out ratings of EVERY user: the newest ratings of each student (at most a fixed number per user; the split step gives the numbers), this student's included; one set of weights serves the whole class, and the target rating is never among them. Switching differs: its bucket scores the bases on the active student's own held-out ratings only.
weights.flat: Why the curve flattens: near the minimum the gradient shrinks, and with a fixed step size each step moves the weights less; the closed form is the limit the steps approach. Later steps change the error by less than 1e-4: diminishing returns.
weights.guide: Follow the curve: it starts at the equal weights, every gradient step moves the weights downhill and the error falls. The dashed lines are the best single base and, once the walk has computed it, the closed form. The table under the curve holds the weights after every step, their sum and the intercept: a constant added to the blend, set again after every step as the mean error of the weighted average, so the weights only have to get the differences between bases right. The intercept absorbs the shift of the newest ratings (the held-out entries are the newest of each user's); the compare step says how much of the gain over the best single base is this level.
weights.a1: It is the neutral guess: every base counts the same. The curve's first point is the error of that plain average of the bases.
weights.q2: Why do the weights move so little in the first steps?
weights.a2: The step size is one over the largest curvature of the loss: the steepest direction is corrected in a single step and the flatter ones creep. With the weights constrained to add up to one the remaining directions are of similar steepness and the descent settles in a few dozen steps; free weights spend the first step on the level of the predictions and then creep.
weights.q3: Why does the closed form stand apart from the descent?
weights.a3: It is the exact minimum of the same loss, found in one solve; the descent is the iterative way to reach it. If the last point of the curve is still above the closed-form line, more steps would get closer: the descent creeps, the closed form jumps.
weights.q4: Which line is the fair comparison for the blend?
weights.a4: The best single base: a blend that does not beat it has not earned its complexity. The walk reports the gain with its sign, because the weights are fitted on a finite sample of held-out ratings.

blend.lead: Blend applies the learned weights to the base predictions of the target film.
blend.guide: Read the weights (first row) against what each base says about the target film (second row): the prediction is the intercept plus the sum of the products, which the table spells out (the intercept is its last row; free weights have none). Then say what the error is and what it is not: one pair, one number.
blend.q1: Why do the cells have two colours?
blend.a1: The colours are the centred diverging scale: one hue for a negative value, another for a positive one, grey at zero. A base can get a negative weight when the regression uses it to correct the others.
blend.q2: Must the blend beat every base on this film?
blend.a2: No: the weights are fitted for all the held-out ratings together, not for this film. On one pair any base can be closer; the gain the page reports is the held-out error over all of them.
blend.q3: Is a gain here a gain for the real system?
blend.a3: Not necessarily: it is an offline gain on ratings held out of the same data, which guarantees nothing online, where users and films change. A real system would refit the bases on all the ratings before it applied the weights.

switch.bridge: The same four bases as the weighted walk: the methods of the earlier pages with the same defaults, fitted on the training part only. Switching does not blend them; a rule picks one of them for the case at hand.
switch.bridge_rule: The two bases of the rule: the collaborative base and the content base, the methods of the earlier pages with the same defaults, fitted on the training part only.
switch.left_out: in neither the bases nor the leaderboard
switch.legend_mae_tip: MAE: the average size of a miss on the held-out ratings.
switch.legend_rmse_tip: RMSE: the misses are squared before they are averaged and the root taken, so big misses count more.
switch.board_winner_tip: The lowest {criterion} on the board the choice uses: this recommender answers about the target film.
switch.board_right_tip: The best on the held-out ratings - what the right way picks. The winner above was picked on the training ratings (the foil).
switch.rule_row_tip: The cold-start rule's own misses on the held-out ratings: {cf}'s answer where it had enough neighbours, {cb}'s elsewhere. The rule helps only if it beats both alone.
switch.coverage: {cf} answered {n_cf} of {n} held-out ratings (at least {m} neighbours); {cb} the other {n_cb}
switch.coverage_tip: Which recommender the rule let answer each held-out rating: the collaborative one where it found enough neighbours for the film, the content one where it did not.
switch.chip_rule_bucket: bucket of models: the winner by {criterion} answers
switch.chip_rule_bucket_tip: One recommender is chosen for the user - the one with the lowest error on the user's own newest held-out ratings - and answers about every film.
switch.chip_rule_neighbours: cold-start rule: {cf} with at least {m} neighbours, else {cb}
switch.chip_rule_neighbours_tip: The choice is made per film: the collaborative recommender answers when it found enough neighbours for the film, the content recommender when it did not.
switch.chip_heldout: {n} of the user's {n_user} ratings held out
switch.chip_heldout_tip: The newest {frac} of the active user's own ratings (at most {cap}) were held out for the leaderboard; every recommender was fitted on the rest, and on every other user's ratings.
switch.chip_winner_tip: The recommender with the lowest error on the held-out ratings, and how far the runner-up is behind it. This is an offline estimate on a handful of ratings: one rating more or fewer can change the winner.
switch.chip_select_train: winner picked on the training ratings: {winner} ({criterion} {value}; the right way, held-out ratings: {right})
switch.chip_select_train_tip: The foil: the winner was picked on ratings every recommender has learned from, where the one that memorised them looks best. The right way's winner - on the held-out ratings - is named beside it; switch "Winner picked on" back to see the walk choose it.
switch.chip_rule_result_tip: The rule's own error on the held-out ratings against the two recommenders alone: a switch pays off only when the second recommender is better exactly where the first is thin. An offline estimate, not a promise about new ratings.

taxonomy.guide: Walk the tree from the root: three ways to combine, then the seven leaves. Say how the ensemble branch splits (sequential, parallel) before the leaves, and point at the dotted line.
taxonomy.q1: What is the difference between a hybrid and an ensemble?
taxonomy.a1: Every ensemble is a hybrid, because it combines several recommenders; the converse fails. A monolithic hybrid is one algorithm that reads several kinds of data, and a mixed hybrid combines nothing: it shows the outputs side by side.
taxonomy.q2: Why does the tree have a dotted line?
taxonomy.a2: Feature augmentation uses ready-made recommenders as black boxes, so it is an ensemble; but sometimes the next recommender has to be adapted to read the new features, and then it is technically monolithic. The dotted line marks that.
taxonomy.q3: Where do the Netflix Prize winners sit?
taxonomy.a3: In the ensemble branch: the two best entries of the contest were ensemble systems.
taxonomy.q4: What do the pills under the boxes say?
taxonomy.a4: Where the course stands: “future work” for the meta-level hybrid and “term project” for the mixed hybrid; the other types have no pill. In the classroom lab a leaf with a lab page opened that page on a click; this edition has no lab pages, so no leaf is clickable.

designs.guide: Say who sees whom: in a parallel design nobody sees anybody, in a sequential one the next recommender sees the previous output. Then say where the combination happens.
designs.q1: Why is the cascade sequential but the weighted blend parallel?
designs.a1: In the blend the recommenders run independently on the same input and only their predictions meet, at the end. In a cascade the second recommender starts from the first one's ranking, so it cannot start before the first has finished.
designs.a2: Both readings are in the textbook: the model flows from one recommender into the next, which is a sequence, but the second recommender has to be modified to read a model instead of ratings, which is why the taxonomy files it under monolithic.
designs.q3: What do the dashed lines mean?
designs.a3: In a sequential design the later recommenders may also read the original input, and the combiner may read every recommender's own output, not only the last one's.

types.guide: One row per leaf of the tree. Read the first three columns aloud, then say which rows had a page in the classroom lab and which did not.
types.a1: There is no general winner: the types answer different problems. Weighting and switching are the simplest to build, because they treat the recommenders as black boxes; feature combination needs one model built for all the data.
types.q2: Why is mixed not an ensemble?
types.a2: An ensemble merges the predicted ratings of the same item from several recommenders into one. A mixed system never does: the user sees each recommender's list. It fits where the recommendation is a whole composite, such as a day's television programme, or where each row has to justify itself.
types.q3: What does switching have to do with cold start?
types.a3: A recommender that works with little data (content-based, or knowledge-based) can serve a new user, and a collaborative one takes over as ratings accumulate; the rule switches between them.
types.q4: What is the difference between feature augmentation and feature combination?
types.a4: Augmentation is sequential: the output of one recommender (pseudo-ratings, say) becomes features of the next. Combination happens at once: all the inputs are put into one long feature row and one algorithm reads it, without knowing which feature came from behaviour and which from a profile.

ensembles.guide: Point at the dartboard: bias is where the hits centre, variance is how widely they spread. Then give the one-line rule: bagging attacks variance, boosting attacks bias.
ensembles.a1: Noise is the part of a rating that no model can predict (a bad day, a mis-click). The equation keeps it as a floor, so the ensemble's job is only to lower the other two.
ensembles.a2: A model that fits its training sample too closely changes a lot when the sample changes: the same test case gets different answers from different samples. Averaging many such models cancels the part of the error that changes.
ensembles.q3: Does the classification result really apply to ratings?
ensembles.a3: Yes. The only difference is that a missing entry can sit in any column of the matrix; predicting one column from the others is still the same problem, so the same argument holds. The cost is that resampling a rating matrix needs care, which is why bagging has four versions for it.
ensembles.q4: Do ensembles lower bias or variance?
ensembles.a4: Either, depending on the method: bagging and randomness injection lower variance, boosting and stacking lower bias. A statement that ensembles reduce bias is true of the second group only.

weighted.guide: Read the three formulas top to bottom: the blend, the loss on the held-out entries, the closed form. Then recall the classroom lab's walk: the same three things with numbers.
weighted.q1: Why fit the weights on held-out ratings and not on the training ratings?
weighted.a1: Every base has seen its training ratings, so it looks better on them than it will on new ones, and the weights would trust the bases that overfit most. Held-out ratings are the ones none of them has seen. The walk shows the two side by side.
weighted.a2: It is the neutral choice, every base counts the same. The fitted weights are then compared with it, and the walk reports the error of the equal blend as the first number.
weighted.q3: Why a penalty on the weights?
weighted.a3: With few held-out ratings, or with bases that agree with each other, an unpenalised fit lets the weights jump to large values of opposite sign. The ridge penalty keeps them small and stable.
weighted.q4: Do the weights have to sum to one?
weighted.a4: In the walk's default, yes: the blend is a weighted average, and the descent walks along the plane where the weights add up to one. Switch the constraint off and they are free, as in the textbook's recipe: they can then also rescale the level of the predictions, and the walk says by how much. A base can get a negative weight either way, when the regression uses it to correct the others.
weighted.q5: Why can the blend be worse than the best single base?
weighted.a5: Nothing guarantees a gain: the weights are fitted on a finite sample of held-out ratings and the bases may already agree. The walk reports the gain with its sign. And a gain on held-out ratings is not a promise of a gain online.

families.guide: Read the column on what each family lowers first: it explains why the families differ. Then show which rows the lab has a page for.
families.q1: Why is bagging a simple average and the blend a weighted one?
families.a1: The copies in bagging come from the same algorithm on resampled data, so there is no reason to trust one more than another. The bases of a blend are different algorithms that may differ a lot in quality, so their weights are worth learning.
families.q2: Why does bagging a rating matrix need four versions?
families.a2: A rating matrix can be resampled by rows (users) or by entries (single ratings), each with or without replacement. Resampling rows can leave a user out, who then cannot be predicted by that copy; resampling entries keeps every user and film present, with fewer ratings.
families.a3: It sits in the ensemble branch (parallel), but it does not combine predictions: it chooses. The textbook notes that switching is often used for model selection without being recognised as a hybrid at all.
